events.title: I'm a 24-year-old data center engineer making six figures. There are pros and cons, but my career has advanced faster than I thought.
events.summary: Joseph LeGare works at a data center site in Maryland. Photo courtesy of Joseph LeGare Joseph Legare landed a six-figure data center job after a six-month-long internship. His community college had a partnership with the local data center construction company. He says deadlines, budgets, and relationships make the job more stressful than expected. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Joseph LeGare, a 24-year-old project engineer based in Frederick County, Maryland. He works at Rowan Digital Infrastructure, a hyperscale data center developer, which introduced Business Insider to LeGare. It has been edited for length and clarity. It has been edited for length and clarity. I studied philosophy for two years at The Catholic University of America before dropping out and working as an assistant superintendent at a construction company. After about a year, I moved into residential and did administrative work, including daily reports, county inspection scheduling, quality verification, and weekly safety meetings with foremen. I even worked as a materials management specialist at a residential home manufacturer. At the same time, I was taking night classes in construction management at Frederick Community College. I assumed I'd go into residential construction, but my classes made me realize I really wanted to pursue commercial construction. I wanted to get out of office work and back into the field. My professor said that if I wanted field experience, getting into the data center industry would be a game changer. The data center industry caught my eye because it's so fast-paced Rowan Digital Infrastructure, which builds data centers , ran an internship program with my school, and one of my professors recommended I apply. They hired me full-time after six months. The data center industry uses the most up-to-date technologies to build projects — whether those technologies are related to safety equipment, heavy equipment, or tools — and it's fascinating to see. I enjoy working in the data center industry, as there is a massive need for it, and I want to help build the infrastructure that keeps the world running. As an intern, my mornings started with reviewing data center drawings I learned to read construction drawings and specifications while gaining hands-on field experience. These are data center-specific , but they share many similarities with general commercial construction drawings. The only real difference is that when we follow our drawings, we build a data center. It could just as easily be for a warehouse or apartment building. Most mornings, my mentor and I reviewed the drawings and specs. Then we'd head out with an iPad or printed drawings to watch the crews work, whether they were installing or lifting a wall. In data center construction project management, you don't need specialized skills beyond those required for any other construction project. However, data center construction is extremely fast-paced work. You'll need to adapt to constant changes, whether that's new details being released, deliveries being delayed, or a schedule being pulled in. I got to be in the field, and the pay was generous My main focus was on being in the field and learning. I was also learning how requests for information, or RFIs, work and how to move between the architects, designers, engineers, general contractors, and subcontractors. The internship pay was generous , in the high five figures. I thought I might be taking a pay cut going into commercial construction. Instead, Rowan offered me a full-time job with a six-figure salary after my internship. I'm making more than I was earning at my last job. My full-time data center role focuses on getting answers One of the biggest responsibilities after being hired was overseeing the RFI and submittal process with the general contractor. I went from observer to main point of contact . Now the GC comes to me practically daily with a problem or an RFI, and I assemble the right people to get an answer. Basically, I keep all the documentation moving. Much of my job is closing the gap between what's on the drawings and what's happening in the field. When something doesn't line up, I track down the answer. That means going back through the specs, talking to the trades, and getting questions to the design team. I'm constantly coordinating to make sure everything lines up. The specific problem is different almost every day. However, probably the most common issue is that field conditions differ from the construction documents. Sometimes the issue is easy to fix, and we can make a call right then and there. Other times, we have to reach out to the design team for guidance. We also focus heavily on testing and commissioning before turnover because everything has to work reliably. Additionally, our project is a brownfield site, which means the soil contains higher amounts of regulated materials than is typical. This is because the site used to be an aluminum smeltery, so we have to work hand in hand with the Maryland Department of the Environment to ensure we avoid adding to that regulated soil and remediate it. There are pros and cons, but overall, I'm happy working in the data center industry The biggest pro is how fast my career has advanced . The opportunities I've been given are crazy, and so is the knowledge and skill I've been able to build. I thought it would take five to 10 years to get here, but the company gave me the opportunity right off the bat. The biggest con is the stress, which I didn't fully expect. Every job has its stressors, but here you're constantly on deadlines, watching budgets because there isn't endless money for a job, and maintaining relationships. There are a lot of days I go home thinking, "Man, that was a really long day." Eventually, I'd love to be a construction manager or project manager and take on more responsibility, even with the added stress. But I'm happy where I am. As hard as the stress is, it's rewarding to look at something and know I helped build it. Do you work at a data center and want to share your story? Email this editor, Manseen Logan, at mlogan@businessinsider.com. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Jim Farley is right about Gen Z and blue-collar work. We see firsthand how the industry is failing them
events.summary: Ford CEO Jim Farley recently said “the air we breathe is a four-year degree.” In other words, college is the default path we steer every kid toward. He’s right, and he deserves credit for pushing back on it. Ford has even commissioned Ad Council research on how students, parents, and teachers see the trades. The Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, which Ford launched with Google, BlackRock , and Carhartt, just released a detailed new look at what the country needs. The headline most outlets ran with is that employers will have to fill about 1.7 million skilled trades openings every year through 2035. Training programs are preparing roughly 55 people for every 100 of those jobs. But the number that stopped me was further down in the report. Much of the public conversation has focused on persuasion, and this number suggests that isn’t where the biggest gap is. Seventy-one percent of teens say they would be proud to pursue a skilled trade, and 81% of parents would be proud if their child did. Yet of every 100 people who start an apprenticeship, only 48 finish. Just 29 are working in a trade five years later. We are losing people after they’ve already said yes. America can’t afford to waste young talent on the way to work. The bigger lever is what happens after enrollment, and much of that is in employers’ hands. Why people walk away Finishing isn’t cheap. Getting to class can mean a car payment or a two-hour bus ride, and childcare doesn’t pause for an apprenticeship. Ford’s new investment in getting trades students to class goes straight at one of these barriers, and that matters. Other barriers are ones employers built. Apprentices earn little while they learn, and in some trades they carry costs that employers used to cover. Many auto technicians, for example, are paid a set rate per repair regardless of how long the job takes, and they buy their own tools. A new tech who is still learning works slower and absorbs the loss. No awareness campaign fixes that. Employers control the destination, and a pathway only holds people if the destination pays enough to make finishing worth it. What finishing looks like At the International Youth Foundation, we’ve spent more than a decade building automotive talent pipelines in Mexico and South Africa. One lesson keeps holding up. People finish when the training is built with the employers who will hire them. In Mexico, we worked with automakers, suppliers, and coatings companies to design technical tracks in automotive painting, tool and die manufacturing, and automation. Then we embedded them across 28 campuses of the State of Mexico’s technical college system, so they would outlast any single grant. An evaluation of graduates from two of those tracks found 82% were employed within five to six months. What made it work isn’t unique to Mexico. Employers help decide what gets taught. Students get mentoring and career guidance alongside technical training. And there’s a real job waiting. Teach the job as it is now Outdated training is another way we lose people. A graduate who learned last decade’s version of the job shows up unprepared, and either doesn’t get hired or doesn’t last. Matt Sigelman, whose Burning Glass Institute co-produced the report, said the jobs most resistant to automation are the ones built on varied, complex tasks that require human judgment. That means the training has to keep up with the work. When electric vehicle manufacturing arrived in Mexico, we worked with the National Auto Parts Industry Association to define what the new jobs actually require, then built training around them. Industry defined the standard. Schools taught it. What the Alliance can do next Ford and its partners have done the hard first step by measuring the problem, including how many people never finish. The next step is accountability. Every Alliance member should publish completion and five-year retention rates for the training programs it funds or runs, so we can see which ones actually get people to work. Employers should be inside public technical schools co-writing curriculum instead of building parallel programs on the side. They should pay people while they learn and cover the tools the job requires. With DEWALT and Milwaukee Tool among the Alliance’s newest members, the companies that make those tools are now at the table, and that’s real progress. And the jobs at the end should pay a living wage. The country doesn’t need to convince young people that the trades are worth it. They already believe it. Our job is to make sure the ones who say yes make it all the way to work. events.title: Mini scandal clouds Dubai's Michelin Guide
events.summary: There’s a mini-scandal brewing in Dubai’s elite food scene. The latest Michelin Guide awarded stars or distinctions to 11 restaurants that have temporarily or permanently closed because of the war. Food writer Samantha Wood questioned why shuttered restaurants made the cut. The speech recognition model has 1.6 billion parameters, but is more accurate than a 30-billion-parameter model, according to TII. AI training in Arabic has lagged behind other languages, partly because dialects vary widely and can be incomprehensible to people who know only the formal Arabic used in news reports and textbooks. TII aims to eliminate those errors by training models on local dialects, idioms, and cultural references, ultimately making AI more useful in the region. — Mohammed Sergie

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Broadcom partner 11:11 picks ‘em up ahead of channel death deadline Nine in 10 VMware customers eye the exit as licensing bills bite 1 day ago KPMG tells staff facing the axe: Here's £100, now zip it 2 days ago Palantir's fondness for French food cooked up tech's latest fad – forward-deployed engineers 5 days ago Amazon sellers watch as inventory vanishes into pending-order purgatory 13 days ago India’s outsourced software industry grows 9.5 percent to reach $239 billion 14 days ago IBM has sold “hundreds” of its cloudy VMware customers to Broadcom partner 11:11 Systems. Under Broadcom’s ownership, VMware slashed the number of cloudy partners it keeps on the books and retained only partners that go all-in on the Cloud Foundation (VCF) private cloud stack. Partners that Broadcom decided not to work with lost the right to resell its software as of October 2025 and may not run VMware-powered clouds after March 2027 . IBM was once a top VMware partner, but last year stopped selling new cloudy VMware services , suggesting it wasn’t invited to continue as a Broadcom partner. Sources tell The Register that soon-to-be-former VMware partners often have a contractual obligation to provide a Virtzilla-powered cloud beyond the March 2027 cutoff, and that their customers want whatever happens next to be non-disruptive. One option for partners leaving the VMware fold is to turn to a wholesaler like 11:11, which runs its own VMware cloud. Another option for departing partners is selling contracts for ongoing VMware cloud services to one of the remaining Broadcom partners. 11:11 Systems told The Register IBM sold contracts for “hundreds” of customers who use VCF in the Big Blue cloud. 11:11 CEO Brett Diamond said the contracts are for customers running versions 7 and 8 of VCF and who are therefore “ripe for migration.” IBM did not respond to our questions about the transaction, which included a request for information regarding some customers that we understand are not making the move to 11:11. Diamond said 11:11 has 40 to 50 points of presence for its VMware cloud, and a migration methodology it will apply to the customers it bought from Big Blue. He’s confident his newly acquired customers will want to stick around. “The customers we manage are very large multinationals and Fortune 5000s who want to stay on VMware,” he said. “No other hypervisor can handle the mid-to-large enterprise.” The CEO hopes to shift his new customers to VCF 9, a necessity given VMware ends support for VCF 8 next year. 11:11 also uses its VMware cloud to sell other services, by delivering it through a custom console that integrates around 50 other tools spanning backup, storage, and security. The IBM buy is 11:11’s eight acquisition of a VMware service provider. It’s not hard to guess why Broadcom binned Big Blue, given that it sells Red Hat OpenShift which is a competitor for VMware – and a stronger one after recent improvements to its VM-hosting capabilities. Other VMware partners feel Broadcom did not have clear-cut reasons for excluding them from its partner program. Broadcom argues that services outfits that don’t dedicate their practices to VCF won’t meet customer needs, and it is therefore building a better channel composed of expert partners. Lobby group CISPE (Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe) argues Broadcom’s actions mean it has improperly concentrated the market for VMware cloud providers and is pursuing an antitrust case in EU courts. ® AI giants promise to play nice with personal data after UK watchdog scrutiny Amazon, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and six others agree to changes, but the ICO isn't done asking questions The VMware exit is a protection upgrade PARTNER CONTENT: VergeIO says an exit is also an opportunity Samsung eyes $80B quarterly profit as memory buyers pay the price AI demand fattens chipmakers' margins while cheaper PCs and phones become harder to produce profitably Brighter isn't better and more is less.

events.title: Amazon launches premium Alexa tablets to take on Apple and Samsung
events.summary: When Amazon .com hired Panos Panay from Microsoft in 2023, senior executives hoped he could bring some of the devices magic he pulled off at the software giant to the e-commerce company. Three years later, Panay is back in his comfort zone. Amazon on Thursday unveiled an entirely new product lineup: premium Alexa tablets meant to take on devices from Apple and Samsung . The tablets, featuring aluminum casing à la Apple, puts Amazon in direct competition with the iPhone maker after years of offering lower-budget Fire tablets that have primarily served as entertainment devices. Panay, senior vice president of Amazon devices, Alexa, and Leo, led the development of Amazon’s new tablets. The tablets are made for “the moment you need it, in the background when you don’t. That’s the whole idea,” Panay said in a statement to Fortune . “We built these around how real people actually live. How they watch. How they read. How a family shares a single screen.” With the new line of Alexa tablets, Amazon is also taking a different approach to software. Unlike Fire tablets, which are heavily optimized for Amazon services, the Alexa tablets run Android with full access to the Google Play Store. The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is the most premium offering at $499.99 for the 128-gigabyte version. It is 6.5-millimeters thin and features a 12-inch, 280 pixels-per-inch display. A pricier, $549 version has a “Nanomatte” display that the company said dramatically reduces screen glare. The tablet can be paired with a new Alexa Tablet Pro Pen and Pro Keyboard, creating a laptop-like setup similar to what Apple offers. There is also a $329.99 Alexa Tablet 11, an 11-inch device, and a 8.7-inch Alexa Tablet 8 entry-point version. Amazon also launched two kids tablets. While the prices are a notable step up from the Fire line of devices — the Fire HD 10 tablet with a 10.1-inch display has a list price of $154.99 for 32 gigabytes and is often on sale — Amazon is pricing the new Alexa tablets below Apple’s tablets. Apple’s 11-inch iPad costs $449 for the 128-gigabyte version. And the 11-inch iPad Pro, which has 264 pixels per inch and is 5.3-millimeters thin, starts at $1,199 for the 256-gigabyte version. Although Amazon is undercutting Apple on price, Apple leads in display technology, connectivity, thinness, and storage options. Samsung, meanwhile, has its new Galaxy Tab S12+ starting at $1,199.99 for the base 256-gigabyte model. Amazon is moving upmarket as tablet shipments decline. Market research firm IDC reported that global tablet shipments fell 12.3 percent year-over-year in this year’s second quarter to 33.6 million units, with U.S. shipments down 31.6 percent, as surging memory costs pushed prices up.  A boost for Alexa+ One of Amazon’s primary goals with the tablets is for people to use Alexa+ , the company’s updated AI-based virtual assistant which it rolled out in general release earlier this year. On the tablets, Alexa can read what’s on the screen to help with tasks like planning around a page of hiking trails, and “live sessions” allow hands-free conversation. Alexa+ gave the company’s flagship assistant a smarter, more human upgrade and added AI capabilities such as booking restaurants. It is free for Prime members and $19.99 per month as a standalone subscription. Amazon has not said how many subscribers it has, and the update has been overshadowed by leading chatbots from OpenAI and Anthropic. Amazon struggled initially to roll out the smarter Alexa, and its original financial strategy with the assistant was to sell underpriced Echo smart speakers with Alexa in hopes of getting people to spend more across its ecosystem. That failed to work, and when it became clear that Alexa+ couldn’t be profitable on its own, Amazon tied the new Alexa to its Prime memberships. Panay is known as the “godfather” of Microsoft’s Surface tablets, which were popular during his tenure at the company. At Amazon, he has tried to give the company’s products a more premium and focused feel , from Alexa+ to the Kindle Colorsoft, the first color Kindle e-reader, and the revamped Kindle Scribe models that compete with cutting-edge paper tablets like reMarkable. Panay has also streamlined the number of events the company holds and changed its tactics for its hardware, which for years included a flurry of product launches. Panay is also known as an effusive onstage showman, making product launches a flashy, intimate affair when he holds them that feel closer to Apple’s past legendary showcases than to the overwhelming Amazon events that predated him. The new Alexa tablets go on sale Oct. 14 in the U.S., Canada and Mexico, with a rollout to the UK, Germany, France, Italy, and Spain starting Oct. 19. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Diners saddened but unsurprised by Crystal Jade outlet closures; affected workers secure interviews
events.summary: The Crystal Jade Hong Kong Kitchen outlet at Suntec City, which closed in July. - Crystal Jade has closed four more Singapore outlets, after three shut last month, leaving diners sad but not surprised amid higher costs and strong competition. - About 120 workers received termination notices, and on-site job interviews were held by Paris Baguette, Neo Group Bakery and Din Tai Fung through union support. - Kroll says no more Singapore closures are expected, while the closures form part of a restructuring and proposed sale as L Capital Asia exits Crystal Jade. SINGAPORE – For generations of local diners, Crystal Jade has been a familiar choice for everything from casual dim sum to family celebrations. So, news that the homegrown restaurant group was closing four more outlets after three were shuttered last month came as a disappointment – but not much of a surprise to some. Mr Derek Wong, a 35-year old writer, said he saw the closure coming because “it seems like a really tough period for local F&B brands”, citing competition from overseas F&B brands, and increasing rental and ingredient costs. Wong, who has two sons, said he would usually frequent Crystal Jade restaurants for wider family gatherings. He recalled enjoying the xiao long bao buffet at the Holland Village outlet with his army friends, where they ate until “there was a tall stack of steamer baskets when we were done”. “We are sad because it means fewer options, but also because Crystal Jade is a homegrown institution,” he said. “They provide a wide range of offerings, from casual to more fine dining experiences.” He said he and his family may still go to the Takashimaya outlet for special occasions, or to alternatives such as Canton Paradise, which has an outlet at Bedok Mall near his home. At the Crystal Jade Palace outlet in Takashimaya, a couple in their 60s who were lunching with their adult daughter said that they were not surprised to hear the group had closed more outlets. They said they liked the service at the restaurant at Takashimaya, with the man saying that he liked how the “servers speak to you in Cantonese”. The couple, who declined to give their names, said they dined at Crystal Jade Palace about three to four times a year, and also go “dim sum hopping” at other restaurants, but eating out has become more expensive. The restaurant was about one-third full when ST visited around 12.30pm on Oct 8, though it quickly filled up within an hour. Staff at the Crystal Jade Palace outlet at Takashimaya and the Crystal Jade Golden Palace outlet at Paragon declined to speak to ST, directing queries to the group’s marketing team instead. The Crystal Jade Palace outlet at Takashimaya on Sept 30. When contacted, Crystal Jade said ST’s questions would be forwarded to advisory firm Kroll, whose representatives were appointed as receivers over Singapore-incorporated Crystal Jade Culinary Concepts Holding and Hong Kong-incorporated Crystal Jade Culinary Concepts Holding (Great China) on Sept 30. On Oct 7, Kroll representatives announced that Crystal Jade had closed four outlets in Singapore and issued termination notices to about 120 workers as part of a restructuring ahead of a proposed sale of the business. The four outlets – three Crystal Jade La Mian Xiao Long Bao restaurants at Bugis Junction, Toa Payoh and i12 Katong, as well as Crystal Jade GO at Oasis Terraces in Punggol – ceased operations on Oct 6. On Oct 7, representatives from Paris Baguette, Neo Group Bakery and Din Tai Fung conducted job interviews for affected workers at Crystal Jade’s headquarters in Lorong Chuan. A Paris Baguette human resources representative said they had shortlisted seven of the 15 workers they spoke to for a follow-up interview. Three workers will attend the interview at the Paris Baguette regional headquarters on Oct 9. The three companies were among the 86 employer partners that the Food, Drinks and Allied Workers Union (FDAWU) and the National Trades Union Congress’ e2i worked with to offer over 400 job opportunities in food manufacturing, food services, hospitality, wholesale and retail. Other employer partners include Raffles Hotel Singapore and Sheng Siong Group. Kroll and Crystal Jade have been engaging FDAWU and other associations since Sept 30 to support affected employees. The Food, Drinks and Allied Workers Union and NTUC’s e2i helped connect retrenched Crystal Jade workers with three companies for job interviews. PHOTO: FOOD, DRINKS AND ALLIED WORKERS UNION FDAWU general secretary Sankaradass S. Chami said the on-site interviews were an important first touchpoint between affected workers and potential employers. “We are encouraged that some workers have progressed to subsequent rounds of interviews with the potential employers,” he said.

events.title: Elon Musk says 'Bravo!' after Jeff Bezos reveals he's put $28 billion of his own money into Blue Origin
events.summary: Elon Musk (right) and Jeff Bezos have been space rivals for years. Blue Origin; NASA; Win McNamee/Getty Images; Mike Blake/Reuters; Samantha Lee/Business Insider Jeff Bezos said on Wednesday that he's piled $28 billion of his own money into Blue Origin. Elon Musk responded "Bravo!" on X, saying he's "glad" that Bezos "cares so much about space." Musk and Bezos, who are rivals in the space industry, have clashed many times over the years. There's no love lost between Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, but the Tesla and SpaceXAI CEO has openly applauded the Amazon founder for pouring nearly $30 billion of his fortune into building his spaceflight company. "Bravo!" Musk replied on X to a clip of Bezos telling Fox News during a live interview on Wednesday that he's "personally invested $28 billion" in Blue Origin since founding it in 2000. "I'm glad Jeff Bezos cares so much about space," Musk added. Bezos, who stepped down as Amazon CEO in 2021 but remains the e-commerce giant's executive chair, said Blue Origin had  just raised more than $10 billion in its first external funding round. The serial entrepreneur , worth $285 billion as of Wednesday's close per the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, told Fox News' Brett Baier that it was the right time to cease self-funding the company. "I see the financial future of Blue with some clarity now, and I didn't really want to take outside investors until I was sure it would be a good investment for them," he said. Bezos added that he expects Blue Origin to "be a public company at some point," but its IPO will be " several years from now ." @RedWavePress Bravo! I’m glad @JeffBezos cares so much about space. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 8, 2026 Musk and Bezos have historically  butted heads  over launchpads, government contracts, patents, talent, copycatting, and more, with Musk once labeling Bezos' company "Sue Origin." But the first- and third-richest people on the planet have also spoken admiringly of each other. Musk has said he pokes fun at Bezos because he wants to goad him into working harder at Blue Origin, so he may well have praised Bezos for piling $28 billion of his own money into the company because that's a clear sign of dedication. events.title: Chrysler Building to get its crown restored after being sold
events.summary: The skyscraper was briefly the world's tallest building The Chrysler Building, one of the most distinctive high-rises in Manhattan's skyline, will undergo a major renovation as part of a multi-million-dollar sale deal. The skyscraper, opened in New York nearly 100 years ago, will see its Art Deco crown polished and restored during a refurbishment that will also involve the restoration of the building's 77-storey façade. Developer Tishman Speyer has taken over the lease from the Cooper Union for the Advancement of Science and Art, a private college. Tishman Speyer and its partners will invest $235m (£178m) in the project, as part of which it will upgrade the 61st floor, which is home to huge eagle gargoyles and will also feature an "upscale" lounge. The developer is planning to use most of the building, which is close to Grand Central railway station, for office space. It is following what it calls a "prebuild approach" that will allow firms to move into their new premises quickly. Tishman Speyer explained that the area "has one of the lowest office availability rates in Manhattan", adding: "Construction of new office supply in the neighbourhood has been virtually nonexistent for decades." The renovation will include internal work, such as upgrades to the building's mechanical, elevator, electrical and air handling systems. At 1,046ft (319m), the Chrysler Building was once the world's tallest building - before being usurped less than a year later by the nearby Empire State Building. Financed by Walter Chrysler, the motor magnate, the skyscraper's construction began in 1928 and was completed two years later. Architect William Van Alen modelled the eagle gargoyles on hood ornaments found on the 1929 Chrysler car. Popping out for lunch: a worker eats a sandwich during construction of the Chrysler Building The Cooper Union college, whose alumni include inventor Thomas Edison, has owned the land on which the Chrysler Building stands since 1902. The land was bequeathed to it by the children of Peter Cooper, a manufacturer and industrialist who founded the college in 1859. As part of the deal, Tishman Speyer will make ground lease payments to the Cooper Union which the college wants to use to finance "a bold plan to restore full-tuition scholarships for all undergraduates". Cooper Union's president Steven McLaughlin, said: "The significance of this agreement is ultimately about what it makes possible for generations of Cooper Union students." events.title: Medium-term borrowing costs for UK government hit 19-year high
events.summary: Investors offload global bonds amid fears of rising inflation, increasing pressure on John Healey ahead of first budget Medium-term borrowing costs for the UK government hit a fresh 19-year high on Thursday, as investors continued to offload global bonds amid fears of rising inflation. Recent dramatic moves in government bond markets have been driven by international factors, but will increase the pressure on John Healey ahead of his first budget as chancellor on 28 October. The yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds had jumped 0.06 percentage points by lunchtime in London, to 5.515%. That was the highest level since July 2007, when the global financial crisis was starting to unfold. Yields on 20- and 30-year UK government bonds, which are known as gilts, had also risen significantly, to their highest level since as long ago as 1998. Yields go up when bond prices go down. Economists believe rising borrowing costs and a weaker growth outlook are likely to have wiped out around half of the £24bn buffer against Labour’s fiscal rules that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, built up at the time of her spring statement in March – perhaps significantly more. Healey is expected to raise taxes at the budget to partly rebuild that cushion, as well as paying for policy interventions including the six-month VAT cut on electricity bills and a modest energy support package for the poorest households . Some economists are warning the chancellor not to go too far in rebuilding the Treasury’s headroom, however. Andrew Wishart, of Berenberg Bank, said: “Raising taxes to keep the surplus close to the size it was in the March forecast (ie to ‘maintain the headroom’) would do unnecessary damage to economic incentives.” He argues that gilt yields are likely to come back down over the next year, with the Bank of England likely to make fewer rate rises than the four that investors currently expect. The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates at its November meeting to tackle surging inflation, echoing moves already made by the European Central Bank, Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan. The bond selloff has intensified across big economies in recent days, as oil prices have soared , with no resolution of the Middle East conflict in sight. Investors appear to be anxious about higher inflation and runaway government spending. France has been hardest hit, as Paris battles to pass a budget, but the selloff has been widespread. Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), has urged governments to tighten their belts in response to rising bond yields. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said, ahead of next week’s IMF annual meeting in Bangkok. Higher yields not only push up costs for indebted governments, but have knock on effects for borrowers across the economy, including homeowners and businesses. The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has tried to rein in yields on the US’s long-term debt by increasing buybacks of its government bonds, known as treasuries, but the policy appears to have had little impact. Yields on the 30-year treasuries targeted by Bessent’s policy were about 5.235% when he announced the doubling of buybacks in August, but have since surged above 5.7%.

events.title: Two killed after building partially collapses in Turkiye’s Istanbul
events.summary: Eight survivors rescued from the rubble as fears of further collapse slow operations in Istanbul’s Maltepe district. At least two people have been killed after a seven-storey building in Turkiye’s Istanbul partially collapsed, officials said. Emergency crews were trying to reach at least two people who were believed to be trapped, authorities said on Thursday. list 1 of 3 India teams search for survivors after Delhi building collapse kills six list 2 of 3 At least 100 dead in gold mine collapse in Central African Republic list 3 of 3 Brazil bus crash kills at least 23 and injures five in Parana state The cause of the collapse was not immediately known, and an investigation was under way. The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, caved in before dawn in the district of Maltepe, on the Asian side of Istanbul, a city that is bisected by the Bosporus Strait. Residents from the upper floors were safely evacuated while search teams rescued eight more people from the rubble. The rescuers recovered two bodies and were trying to reach two people still believed to be inside, according to the Istanbul governor’s office. Earlier, Istanbul Governor Davut Gul said rescuers had made contact with a 6-year-old trapped in the rubble. It was not immediately clear if the child was among those rescued. He warned that the building was at risk of further collapse, hampering the rescue efforts. Nearby buildings were also evacuated for safety, the governor said. Istanbul and other parts of Turkiye are undergoing an urban transformation programme that aims to replace old and earthquake-prone buildings with safer housing.

events.title: South Korea to recall Ukraine envoy in diplomatic row over POWs
events.summary: South Korea and Ukraine embroiled in a diplomatic row after President Zelenskyy revealed alleged transfer of two North Korean soldiers. South Korea says it will recall its ambassador to Kyiv following a recent revelation by Ukraine of a transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. The South Korean announcement on Thursday came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologise over the revelation. list 1 of 3 North Korea dismisses UN nuclear watchdog resolution list 2 of 3 Russia and North Korea deepen relations with symbolic road bridge list 3 of 3 Trump hints at new approach to North Korea’s nuclear programme “The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement. “The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.” South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his United Nations General Assembly address last month. South Korea accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement relating to the transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal. The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers have expressed their desire to resettle in South Korea because they could face persecution if repatriated to North Korea. South Korea had said it would accept them because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors. South Korean officials said the nondisclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. There have been no comments from North Korea’s state media on the soldiers’ transfer. But the North has previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and its key ally, the United States, and focused on bolstering its nuclear programme since 2019. South Korea has provided $445m in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100m in aid to Ukraine during a meeting with Zelenskyy.

events.title: Hundreds of new pro sports team ETFs lead world of retail investing to the edge of gambling
events.summary: Prediction markets have blurred the line between financial trading and gambling, and now fund companies have filed for hundreds of ETFs that track individual NHL and MLB teams through futures tied to single-season team performance metrics. There are sports ETFs that hold publicly traded shares of companies that own teams, a conventional investment approach allowing for balance sheet analysis, including Gabelli Funds' GOLS and Amplify Funds' planned PROS ETF. But investing experts put the individual team funds, none of which have yet launched, closer to wagering than investing, while issuers say they offer a transparent way for fans to put money behind their teams. In 1989, all-time hits leader Pete Rose was banned from Major League Baseball for life because of his gambling activities. He wasn't reinstated until last year, months after his death in 2024. Fast-forward to today, and Pete Rose's gambling might seem like just another day on Wall Street as financial firms expand the ways fans can put money behind their teams, beyond a beer and a $15 hot dog. You may soon be able to buy a ticker for your favorite hockey team, and it isn't a stake in the franchise. Multiple asset managers have filed to launch dozens of ETFs, one for every NHL team, with MLB baseball team funds filed as well, all built on new futures contracts that track a team's season statistics. None has begun trading but in all, hundreds of ETFs that track the single-season performance of one professional team across a mix of statistical categories have been filed at the SEC for approval. Some finance experts see the development as lacking any nuance whatsoever. "The line between gambling and investing has not simply been blurred, it has been erased," said Robert Johnson, a professor of finance at Creighton University. Among fund companies getting in on the novel trend are VolatilityShares , LeagueShares, Roundhill Investments , and Rex Financial . None of the four companies responded to requests for comment. Asset managers typically cannot publicly comment during the period between when funds are filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission for approval and when they become effective, if approved. Rex, a Miami-based ETF issuer, announced Sept. 21 that it was launching Alpha Sports Holdings, a new subsidiary built to turn team performance into exchange-traded funds. REX has filed with the SEC for BaseballShares and HockeyShares, suites of ETFs that would track Major League Baseball and National Hockey League teams through futures contracts that CME Group, the derivatives exchange, lists on indexes built by FutureSports, an index company. The underlying CME futures , which began trading for NHL teams in late September, need to first establish a trading history. Each team's index opens the season at a set number and moves as the team racks up statistics, including runs scored, stolen bases and strikeouts for baseball, then resets in the offseason. "The sports industry generates hundreds of billions of dollars a year, but there has never been a liquid, transparent investment product tied directly to what happens in live games," said Greg King, CEO of Alpha Sports, in a press release. "Alpha Sports exists to build that product for passionate investors who want to participate in the fortunes of their favorite teams." Johnson, though, said the sports-themed ETFs are far more gaming than investing. "I thought that the ETF world had jumped the shark with the introduction of the 2X and 3X leveraged and inverse ETFs. In my mind these were simply vehicles for short term speculators. But, at least these vehicles were based upon assets. The new structures — and I call them structures, not assets — are simply gambling dressed up as investing," Johnson said. In fact, the proposed team ETFs include in some cases leveraged versions of trades on single-team performance. The boom in prediction markets is already blurring the lines between sports wagering and market trading. Unlike prediction markets contracts, the sports team ETFs are tracking futures off an index rather than a single event (e.g. win or loss). But while structurally contracts in this market have a role to play for investors, in the case of sports performance, Johnson says the case is weak. "They have societal value in that parties are able to hedge natural positions and transact with other speculators willing to bear that risk. This allows a more optimal allocation of risk," Johnson said. But he added that is not the case when individual investors are making bets on the performance of sports teams they follow. "There are no natural positions being hedged. In the aggregate, they destroy wealth," Johnson said. Here's a look at other stories offering insight on ETFs for investors.

events.title: PepsiCo sees strong overseas demand but lackluster North American performance in Q3
events.summary: PepsiCo is reporting better-than-expected revenue in the third quarter despite lackluster North American demand PepsiCo reported better-than-expected revenue in the third quarter despite lackluster North American demand. Net revenue rose 5.6% to $25.27 billion in the July-September period. Wall Street had expected revenue of $24.95, according to analysts polled by FactSet. The company, based in Purchase, New York, said its global snack food volumes increased 4%, the highest rate of growth since 2021. That was largely due to its international business, which makes up 41% of the company's revenue. World Cup-related demand for Lay's snacks was strong, the company said, and PepsiCo gained share in key markets like China and Brazil. Snack food volumes rose 11% in the Asia Pacific region, PepsiCo said. Fast-growing categories include snacks with simpler ingredients, like Doritos and Gatorade Lower Sugar with no artificial colors or flavors, as well as protein-enhanced snacks, the company said. But PepsiCo's North American results were weaker, with Frito-Lay snack food volumes flat compared to the same period last year and beverage volumes down 2%. PepsiCo said growth in sales of U.S. salty snacks was offset by sales declines in Canada. The company said it is also planning to cut corporate costs and will begin other initiatives not directly tied to sales growth in the coming months. PepsiCo lowered its earnings expectations for the year, saying it now expects adjusted earnings per share to grow 2.5% to 3.5%. Previously it had expected growth between 5% and 7%. The company now expects full-year revenue growth of 6%, the high end of earlier forecasts of between 4% and 6%. Net income rose 17% to $3.07 billion in the third quarter. Adjusted for one-time items, the company earned $2.34 per share. That was higher than the $2.29 per-share profit analysts expected. PepsiCo share rose 1% in pre-market trading Thursday. events.title: From Vatican archives to Microsoft Word: Michelangelo’s lettering lives on
events.summary: How do you create a digital identity for something as storied as St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome? The Fabbrica di San Pietro , or St. Peter’s Factory, which is the institution in charge of maintaining the basilica, turned to Michelangelo Buonarroti, the architect of the building’s dome, sculptor of the Pietà (which resides in the basilica), and painter of the frescoes on the ceiling of the nearby Sistine Chapel. “This project grew out of a question: ‘How can the Fabbrica di San Pietro preserve a heritage while also making it part of how we communicate today?’” says the communications office of the Fabbrica di San Pietro. “There’s kind of a geometry, there’s kind of use of empty and filled spaces, his impatience, his precision, his energy are in his calligraphy.” Image courtesy of studiogusto: Stefano Caliandro, creative director of studiogusto. In connection with the 400 th anniversary of the consecration of the basilica, with a ceremony on Nov. 18, the Fabbrica decided to create a digital typeface inspired by Michelangelo’s handwriting. Called Michelangelus, the typeface will be used for digital and printed materials as well as for signage inside the basilica. The Fabbrica decided to share Michelangelus with the world by contributing it to the library of fonts in Microsoft 365 applications. For those who would like to use it outside of the M365 applications, it will also be available to download . “A typeface, a visual identity or a digital experience can tell a story. And that can represent culture, research and tradition,” says Mimmo Berterame, CEO of studiogusto , the Italian design agency that did the research and artistic and technical work to turn handwriting into a digital script. Turning a master’s penmanship into a modern typeface Berterame and Stefano Caliandro, creative director of studiogusto , visited the Vatican archives to examine Michelangelo’s original manuscripts. “There’s kind of a geometry, there’s kind of use of empty and filled spaces,” Caliandro says. “His impatience, his precision, his energy are in his calligraphy.” However, the goal was not to imitate Michelangelo’s handwriting but to adapt it through design into a modern tool. The designers identified “rules” inside the calligraphy, “and we try to reply to this invisible grid, architectural grid of this alphabet,” Caliandro says. They did keep some of Michelangelo’s flourishes, such as the small dot at the top of the ‘h’ or the bottom of the ‘y’. Michelangelo often wrote to his nephew, Lionardo Buonarroti, whose handwriting was a frequent source of frustration. In one letter, Michelangelo complained, “Do not write to me again: every time one of your letters arrives I get an attack of the fever because of the trouble I have to read it! I cannot think where you have learned to write. I believe that if you had to write to the greatest donkey in the world, you would write with more care than you do to me. Therefore do not add another to the troubles I have already.” (Lionardo kept writing and Michelangelo kept complaining. ) For Michelangelo, “writing was not just about expression,” Berterame says. “For him, it was about clarity and respect for the reader. So, beauty was important, but it also needed order. Our typeface needs character and personality, but it also needs to be clear and easy to read.” Finding Michelangelo in every letter The designers began with the lowercase italic letters, basing them closely on Michelangelo’s hand. The regular font and uppercase letters are largely derived from the artist’s inscription on the Pietà sculpture of Mary holding Jesus’s dead body, as well as some inscriptions inside St. Peter’s. In fact, the inscription on the Pietà, carved by Michelangelo, resembles a condensed typeface, in which letters are stretched slightly higher than usual, a style that is fashionable at the moment. For the uppercase letters, studiogusto began with M, because it is so present in the texts — Michelangelo’s name begins with it — and because it’s the largest letter. The team didn’t find any examples of numbers written by Michelangelo, so they had to base them off the letters. The number one, for example, is based on the letter I. In all, studiogusto produced more than 500 characters per style: regular, italic, bold and bold italic. From St. Peter’s Basilica to screens everywhere Using Michelangelus in the Fabbrica’s communications “allows that history to continue in the language of nowadays, and it brings the heritage of St. Peter’s into the messages we share every day with the world, with everybody, and on paper and on screens as well,” the Fabbrica’s communications office says. “Sharing it with everyone gives them a chance to form a personal connection with the history of the Basilica and of Michelangelo. If the typeface also makes people want to know more about the history, it will have achieved something important for us.” Michelangelus builds on the broader collaboration between Microsoft and the Fabbrica di San Pietro to use technology to help preserve and share the cultural heritage of St. Peter’s Basilica with people around the world. By bringing Michelangelus to Microsoft 365, the Fabbrica hopes to create another way for people to connect with the history of St. Peter’s Basilica and the artist whose vision helped shape it. Catherine Bolgar writes about AI and innovation at Microsoft, from advances in quantum computing to how AI is helping ordinary people. Previously, Catherine wrote about technology and business for a number of publications, and she was an editor at the Wall Street Journal in New York and Brussels. She taught high school math in Kenya, where she learned Swahili. She currently lives in France. You can contact Catherine on LinkedIn . AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Amazon, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and six others agree to changes, but the ICO isn't done asking questions Denmark's ID register spills more people's details than the country has residents 2 days ago Legacy sign-on service comes back to bite school software provider Bromcom 2 days ago Met Police suspends use of phone-hacking software over Russian links 6 days ago UK privacy watchdog starts over with new board and Manchester HQ 7 days ago More than half of UK businesses lack confidence in basic cyber skills 8 days ago Ten of the world's biggest AI developers have agreed to tighten their handling of personal data following scrutiny by Britain's privacy watchdog, which is now turning its attention to autonomous AI agents that don't always play by the rules. The recently rebranded Information Commission's Office (ICO) said Thursday that Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Cohere, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Stability AI have either made changes or committed to doing so after the regulator examined their compliance with UK data protection law. These include clearer explanations of how personal information is used to train AI models, better ways for people to exercise their data rights, and tougher assessments of developers' safeguards. The commitments follow a supervisory program launched in 2025 that initially covered 11 developers. That number dropped to ten after the ICO paused its engagement with Elon Musk's xAI to pursue a separate formal investigation into its Grok chatbot . The watchdog isn't declaring victory just yet. It's monitoring whether developers deliver on their promises and admits that current AI training practices still pose problems under UK data protection law. Developers still have some explaining to do over personal data buried in their models, particularly sensitive information, and how people are supposed to get their details removed once an AI has been trained on them. There's also the risk of personal information being extracted from models, including data developers never intended them to retain. The ICO acknowledged that some of these issues will require cooperation between industry, regulators, and government. Getting companies to promise changes is one thing. Making today's AI models comply with the law is another. "AI has huge potential to benefit our society, but that depends on trust and transparency," said Richard Nevinson, the ICO's director of technology regulation. "Our engagement with some of the biggest developers has secured real commitments that will help people better understand and control how their data is used, even in a fast-moving and complex area." Meanwhile, the regulator is turning its attention to AI agents, which can browse websites, use tools, and carry out tasks with limited human supervision. And some aren't sticking to the rules. The ICO confirmed it has contacted OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and the UK's AI Security Institute following reports of agents bypassing safeguards during testing and deployment earlier this year. "These recent reports show both how fast these systems are advancing, and the risks they pose if the guardrails aren't fit for purpose," Nevinson said. "Our message is clear: the fact AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance." The regulator has also launched a six-week call for evidence on agentic AI, covering security, transparency, accountability, and the lawful use of personal data. Responses are due by November 20 and will inform future guidance and the ICO's forthcoming statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. The watchdog is separately examining how consumer chatbots and AI companions use personal information as they become increasingly personalized. For now, the ICO has secured promises from some of the industry's biggest names, although whether they deliver remains to be seen. And with AI agents increasingly capable of acting on their own, the watchdog may have its work cut out keeping them in line.

events.title: Fires, barricades, and fraternité: 7 photos show the scale of the protests sweeping France
events.summary: Hundreds of thousands of students have taken to the streets all over France. Muhammed Said Tako/Anadolu via Getty Images Protests have taken France by storm over the past few weeks. Hundreds of thousands of high school students are protesting against underfunding in education. Clashes between protesters and police have led to injuries and arrests. What started as a peaceful demonstration in a southern suburb of Paris in late September has evolved into nationwide protests across France. Hundreds of thousands of high school students, parents, teachers, and union members have taken to the streets this week to protest what they say is underfunding in education, citing concerns such as dilapidated buildings and teacher shortages. The protests have spread to more than 40 French cities, including Paris, Lyon, Marseille, and Rennes. The protests spanned the whole of France. Miguel MEDINA / AFP via Getty Images In the photo above, student protesters can be seen taking to the streets in Marseille in the south of France. The streets of Paris were crowded with protesters on Tuesday, October 6. An estimated 450,000 people participated in the protests. GEOFFROY VAN DER HASSELT / AFP via Getty Images The French Government counted 265,000 demonstrators on October 6. Organizers said the number was closer to 450,000. Students are demanding renovations to run-down buildings, a mass hiring of teaching staff, and changes to the university application system. Protesters in Nancy, Northern France. Muhammed Said Tako/Anadolu via Getty Images Students have set up makeshift barricades outside high schools and universities and set fire to them in the streets. Protestors made blockades near schools. FRED TANNEAU / AFP via Getty Images In the photo above, a protester throws a street sign onto a burning blockade in Brest, western France, on October 2. France's Justice Ministry said 5,060 people have been detained since the protests began, with 87% of them minors. Police have been accused of excessive force. LOU BENOIST / AFP via Getty Images Police have been accused of excessive force against students. A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off on Monday by a stun grenade, a local official told media outlets. "High school students' voices are precious and must be heard," Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Wednesday. Fires burned in the streets all over France this week. Olivier CHASSIGNOLE / AFP via Getty Images In a post on X , Lecornu shared a link to an online consultation where high schoolers can express their issues and suggestions. As of publish time, the site had recorded more than 43,500 participants. On Wednesday, the French government said it was undertaking five projects to address the issues they are hearing about from the protestors. France's youth protests have put Parcoursup, its college-admissions portal, under fresh scrutiny. Dimitar DILKOFF / AFP via Getty Images The five projects, as outlined on the French government's website, are: replacing absent teachers, improving the state of buildings, better organizing students' days, making orientation — including the divisive Parcoursup website — more readable, and strengthening the role of student councils. events.title: British towns could soon look like American food courts. Here are 9 US chains making the move across the Atlantic.
events.summary: A Chili's restaurant in downtown San Antonio. Robert Alexander/Getty Images American fast-food chains are setting up shop across the pond. From Wendy's to Wingstop, these US chains are expanding rapidly in the UK. Chili's also recently announced it was looking for a UK-based franchise partner. American restaurant chains are setting their sights across the pond. From Wendy’s and Wingstop to chicken-focused newcomers such as Raising Cane’s and Dave’s Hot Chicken, US brands are expanding rapidly in the UK — and increasingly making London their first stop. Now, the American casual-dining revival is joining the invasion. Chili’s , which has staged one of the biggest restaurant-chain turnarounds in the US in recent years, recently said it was looking for a UK-based franchise partner, signaling a potential return to Britain after its previous UK locations closed years ago. A shared language, a similarly demanding market for grab-and-go options, and an appetite for American menu items largely driven by social media make the UK a natural fit for US chains looking to expand overseas. Early successes are also fueling the rush to grow across the pond: Wingstop UK and Ireland’s revenue surged 73% to £216.4 million (around $285 million) in 2025, while Popeyes’ UK revenue climbed 50% to £178 million (around $235 million) as it expanded to 108 restaurants in the UK and Ireland. From food-court classics to full-service chains serving burgers, fajitas, and margaritas, these American restaurants have their eye on the UK. Wingstop's model is proving successful in the UK. A Wingstop location in London. Tartezy/Getty Images Founded in Garland, Texas, in 1994, Wingstop has grown from a single chicken-wing restaurant into a chain with 2,728 US locations as of June. Revenue for Wingstop's UK-based restaurants surged 73% to £216.4 million in 2025, or around $285 million, driven by new restaurant openings. The chain hit its 100th UK restaurant milestone this summer and plans to open up to 30 more locations across England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland this year, The Independent reported. Chili's comeback in the US could also bring the casual-dining chain back to Britain. Chili's restaurant. sanfel/Getty Images Founded in Dallas in 1975, Chili’s helped popularize the casual-dining formula of burgers, fajitas, baby back ribs, and margaritas, and now has about 1,110 US restaurants, with plans to ramp up to 30 new Chili's a year by fiscal year 2029. Chili's closed all eight or nine of its UK restaurants in 2009, but the chain is now looking for a local franchise partner to help it make a comeback. It hasn't shared where or when it plans to open yet. "As we continue to expand globally, we are seeking strategic partners who share our vision for growth and success to join us in spreading #ChilisLove hospitality and establishing this iconic brand in the UK," the chain wrote on its website . Jersey Mike’s has built a US sandwich empire, and now it wants 400 UK and Ireland locations. Photography By Tonelson/Getty Images Jersey Mike’s began as a single sandwich shop in Point Pleasant, New Jersey, in 1956, before Peter Cancro bought it at age 17 and grew it into a chain with more than 3,300 locations across the United States and Canada. The company is now planning to enter Europe with a 400-store rollout in the UK and Ireland. The chain's British expansion will begin with a London restaurant on Argyll Street in Soho this November, with three more central London locations to follow, Restaurant Online reported. Popeyes wants to have 150 locations in the UK and Ireland by the end of 2026. Popeyes restaurant on a historic corner building on a busy shopping street in Liverpool. ASphotowed/Getty Images Popeyes was founded in New Orleans in 1972 and has grown into a fried-chicken giant with more than 3,000 US restaurants. The chicken chain opened its first UK location in London’s Westfield Stratford in 2021 and has since grown its footprint to more than 100 locations. The business is proving successful: In 2025, revenue grew 50% to £178 million, or around $235 million, and the chain's restaurant locations expanded from 64 to 108. It now aims to reach about 150 locations across the UK and Ireland by the end of 2026, according to FoodColumn . Raising Cane's will open its first London location in 2027. Raising Cane's restaurant. Joe Hendrickson/Getty Images Raising Cane’s opened near Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge in 1996 and has built a devoted following around its tightly focused chicken-fingers-and-sauce menu, with more than 900 US locations. Its UK reception remains untested: The chain’s first European restaurant is set to open near Piccadilly Circus in early 2027, with more London sites planned. This isn't the chain's first international expansion, however. Raising Cane's operates 49 restaurants in the Middle East — Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE — through franchise partner Alshaya. Chick-fil-A has three UK locations, with plans to add two more. Chick-fil-A restaurant. Wolterk/Getty Images Chick-fil-A’s roots date to 1946, when founder Truett Cathy opened a diner near Atlanta; it now has more than 3,000 restaurants across the US, Puerto Rico, and Canada. The chain has only recently begun its permanent UK rollout, so it has not disclosed British sales figures, but it is moving ahead with a five-restaurant, $100 million initial investment plan . Dave's Hot Chicken's first UK location was wildly successful. Dave's Hot Chicken restaurant. hapabapa/Getty Images Dave’s Hot Chicken started as a parking-lot pop-up in East Hollywood in 2017 and has expanded to nearly 400 restaurants worldwide, most of them in the US. Its first UK location in Soho reportedly drew four-hour lines, Time Out London reported at the time, and later welcomed more than 1,000 customers a day, The Times reported, leading its UK operator to plan 57 more restaurants across Britain as part of its greater 180-location European rollout plan. Denny's is eyeing a larger expansion in the UK. Denny's restaurant. miroslav_1/Getty Images Denny’s was founded in Lakewood, California, in 1953 and operates more than 1,300 restaurants across North America. The chain had announced plans to close 150 struggling locations by the end of 2025. However, Denny's has seen success in the UK. Denny's lone UK diner in Swansea has shown enough promise to serve more than 13,500 dine-in orders a year and generate strong margins, prompting the chain to seek a franchise partner for a broader British expansion, Elite Franchise Magazine reported. Wendy's hopes to eventually operate 400 restaurants in the UK. Wendy's restaurant. sevenstockstudio/Getty Images Wendy’s opened its first restaurant in Columbus, Ohio, in 1969 and now has more than 5,700 US locations. Wendy's previously operated about 10 restaurants in the UK, but, due to high operating costs, the burger chain closed those locations in 2001.

events.title: AWS pricing team turns 18-tab Excel model into an AI chatbot to evaluate customer deals, CFO says
events.summary: Good morning. For companies figuring out how to use AI, the conversation is changing from improving existing work to rethinking what the business can do. I spoke with John Felton, SVP and CFO of Amazon Web Services (AWS), Amazon’s cloud computing and AI platform, about that shift. Felton speaks regularly with AWS customers, including fellow CFOs, and said their AI adoption is still uneven. Many are still early in their broader cloud and IT modernization efforts, a prerequisite for deploying AI at scale. “I think in general, I would say it feels early across the board,” Felton told me. “It’s unbelievable the pace of change, how fast things are moving. I do think every company is in a different stage of it. I think everyone is still early.” That puts him at an interesting vantage point as AI drives a significant new investment cycle. Felton also pointed out that customer AI discussions about two years ago focused largely on productivity and cutting costs. That is changing. “There really is a lot more focus on: how do I use AI for new revenue products, for new customer experiences?” he said. That perspective carries particular weight given the scale of the business Felton oversees. AWS is now a $169 billion annualized business, and Felton has been with Amazon for more than 20 years. He previously led Amazon’s worldwide operations before becoming AWS finance chief in 2024, reporting to Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky. The bigger shift, Felton said, is from adding AI to an existing process to rethinking the process. What impresses him is seeing companies move toward an “AI first mindset,” using AI to rethink what the business should be in the first place. “That is where a bunch of customers, including ourselves, really see a lot more value,” Felton said. AI in finance Inside AWS’s finance organization, Felton is encouraging employees to participate in that transformation rather than wait for someone else to tell them how to use AI. His instruction is straightforward: “Use AI every day.” Rather than dictate which tasks employees should tackle or which tools they should use, Felton wants them to identify opportunities themselves. They understand their work better than he does, he says. He tracks whether employees are following through, although he did not detail those metrics. One example came from AWS’s pricing team. Employees had relied on a complicated Excel model spanning 18 tabs to evaluate customer deals. The team converted it into a chatbot interface that lets users explore scenarios through natural-language questions. They can ask what happens if a price falls 20%, how different payment terms affect a deal, or where the break-even point lies. Employees who prefer the spreadsheet can still export the model to Excel. The point isn’t simply that AI made an existing tool easier to use. It changed how employees interact with the underlying analysis. Another team built an AI agent to compare payment terms in customer contracts with those recorded in AWS’s payment system. Previously, employees checked a sample of contracts. The agent allows the team to check all of them. “Let’s not just do a sample size, let’s do all of it,” Felton said, describing the team’s approach. The two examples illustrate the broader shift he sees in companies’ AI strategies: using the technology not only to make existing work faster, but to expand what the organization can do. Felton also uses Amazon Quick , an AI assistant for work, himself, including to query supporting materials prepared for board meetings and locate answers in the underlying files. He sees that kind of everyday experimentation as important for CFOs figuring out where AI fits. Sheryl   Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: DNC sues to stop Trump's taxpayer-funded ad blitz
events.summary: President Trump said he will help pay for his administration's campaign-style ads after the Democratic National Committee sued Wednesday over their use of taxpayer money. Why it matters: Trump's funding announcement does not address the DNC's central allegation that the administration illegally used taxpayer money to finance the ads. What they're saying: Trump said in a Truth Social post that he considers the ads "to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A." and defended using taxpayer money for them. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself," Trump wrote. Trump said money from MAGA Inc., his superPAC, would also pay for the ads. A person familiar with the advertising plans said the existing taxpayer-funded ad buy will end this week, after which outside groups will begin paying for the spots. The White House defended the ads as public service announcements, arguing that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies. The White House said the ads are not political because Trump is not on the ballot and the spots contain no call to action. The other side: "These ads are a clear violation of the Congressional ban on the use of appropriated funds for 'publicity or propaganda purposes,'" the DNC's legal counsel wrote in the lawsuit . "The president has nationalized the midterm election, made himself the center of a two-day 'midterm convention,' and repeatedly directed voters to 'pretend that I am on the ballot," it added. "As the 2026 midterm election has approached, Republican poll numbers have plummeted in both traditional battlegrounds and typically favorable states, and Democrats are poised to take control of Congress, governors' mansions, and state legislatures around the country." Zoom in: The lawsuit alleges the White House crafted the ads to boost the president's approval ratings and help Republican candidates. The complaint largely focuses on its allegation that the ads were paid for with money originally allocated for Customs and Border Protection that was rerouted for the TV spots. The DNC argues that the ads violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the Antideficiency Act, and the Purpose Act. The DNC asked a federal judge to step in, declare the administration's actions illegal and immediately block them from airing any more ads paid for with taxpayer money. It's not clear how the judge will rule, given President Trump said Monday that a Trump-affiliated super PAC would begin paying for the ads moving forward. A White House spokesperson confirmed Tuesday to Axios that the administration would not repay the government for the ads. Catch up quick: According to the suit, Trump personally hand-picked the ads that aired on television, which were broadcast to millions of Americans, including during NFL and college football games. The lawsuit says the ads aired "nearly 90 times across national television networks, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now, and CBS" over four days in late September. Those spots likely cost around $337,000. In that same time period, the ads aired on local television stations at least 2,311 times and those placements cost around $1.4 million, the suit says. Advertisement tracking firm AdImpact estimates that over $2.5 million was spent on the ads the first week they were aired. Worth noting: Using public funds for campaign ads hasn't sat well with American voters. Nearly nine in ten voters said in a Reuters-Ipsos poll published Wednesday that using taxpayer money for campaign ads featuring a president or Cabinet member is inappropriate. events.title: Jay-Z, Serena Williams-backed Kenangan Coffee considering IPO on SGX within next 24 months: CEO
events.summary: For SGX to be selected, CEO Edward Tirtanata said he would like greater clarity on how companies could pursue dual listings in Singapore and on regional exchanges. SINGAPORE – T he Indonesian coffee chain backed by tennis star Serena Williams and rapper-turned-mogul Jay-Z is considering an initial public offering (IPO) on the Singapore Exchange (SGX) as it looks to go public within the next 24 months. “We have been speaking quite closely with SGX, and I think they’re doing great things to overhaul the exchange,” Kenangan Coffee co-founder and group chief executive Edward Tirtanata told The Straits Times on the sidelines of the Forbes Global CEO Conference. The United States, Hong Kong and Indonesia are also under consideration, while a dual listing remains a possibility. “In the next 24 months, we do want to go public. We just haven’t decided on the venue.” Tirtanata said the decision would depend on whether market conditions at a particular exchange were favourable to an ASEAN consumer company at the time. Hong Kong, for instance, may currently be more receptive to artificial intelligence and biotechnology companies, while consumer businesses are generally well regarded on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX), he noted. For SGX to be selected, Tirtanata said he would like greater clarity on how companies could pursue dual listings in Singapore and on regional exchanges. He sees SGX as a potential “nucleus” for dual listings involving exchanges such as IDX, Bursa Malaysia and Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, but noted that there is no clear precedent on how this can be done. “If I want to list on both IDX and SGX, how do I do it?” he said, adding that the group is waiting for clearer guidelines or another company to establish a precedent before making a move. Tirtanata cited the Nasdaq-SGX Global Listing Board (GLB) as an example of a framework that gives companies clear guidelines on matters including the transferability of shares between exchanges. However, the valuation threshold of $ 2 billion to qualify for a GLB listing means that many smaller companies would not make the cut, he said. Coff ee and food and beverage companies are “always the flavour of the month” on the IDX, but a coffee company could also be an interesting addition to SGX, which is seeking to diversify beyond sectors such as real estate investment trusts. “A coffee company could offer something different for local investors and make it more interesting,” he added. Kenangan Coffee was founded in 2017 by Tirtanata and two school mates. Williams and Jay-Z are among several high profile investors who have backed the company, investing an undisclosed sum during a seed funding round in 2019. An IPO would not primarily be used to finance Kenangan Coffee’s expansion, as its new stores are mostly funded by internal cash flow. Instead, listing would give the company’s early investors a more liquid market for their holdings and allow them to realise their investments, Tirtanata said. He added that he is not seeking to exit the business and intends to remain with the company for at least another decade. Kenangan Coffee has 10 outlets in Singapore, where it opened its first store at Raffles City in 2023. But while sales at its Singapore outlets are among the highest across the seven markets in which it operates, elevated rents and capital expenditure make rapid expansion here riskier than in Indonesia or Malaysia, where Kenangan Coffee will open about 85 in Malaysia and nearly 390 in Indonesia in 2026. In contrast, it has no fixed target for Singapore and will expand only when it can secure locations at rents that allow stores to generate an acceptable return. “One unprofitable store in Singapore can be equivalent to four to five profitable stores” in terms of the impact on earnings, he said. The group may still open one or two stores in prime locations for branding purposes, but Tirtanata said expanding rapidly in Singapore does not make financial sense. “Singapore is actually a great market for F&B in terms of the revenue side. But in terms of the cost structure, it does present a challenge, especially with rental,” he said. The local market is also fiercely competitive, with Chinese coffee giant Luckin Coffee already running 103 outlets here after just three years in Singapore. Meanwhile, there are plans to expand Starbucks’ coffee offerings after DFI Retail Group acquired control over the coffee chain’s licensed operations in Asia, including in Singapore, on Sept 30. But Tirtanata said he is less concerned about competition from the growing number of coffee chains in Singapore, as the dense market here generates enough demand to support multiple brands. Singapore records some of Kenangan Coffee’s highest daily transactions and average spending per customer across its markets. “I’m not concerned about the revenue side of things,” he reiterated. “I’m a lot more concerned with the cost structure.
