events.title: We pay $17 an hour for someone to tackle our household to-do list — from meal prep to laundry — while we're at work
events.summary: Our household manager has been a great extra support system when we need it most. She helps me have more time to be present for my family. Maria Satira Our family has had a household manager for about two years, and it is worth every penny. For $17 an hour, she helps us by running errands, doing laundry, preparing meals, and more. Having a household manager has helped my husband and me get time back to spend with our kids. Many  working parents  can probably relate to our hectic schedules. I'm a marketing executive, part-time MBA student, wife, and mom of two young daughters. My husband is self-employed in construction, real estate, and property management, which means he regularly works 60-hour weeks and answers calls at all hours. On top of work, our week recently included four doctors' appointments, gymnastics and art classes for our almost 4-year-old, a family friend's wedding, and a preschool friend's birthday party. Despite all the personal and professional commitments, our family ate healthy meals, our kids had clean clothes, our home stayed organized, our dogs got attention, and our household to-do list got completed. I even managed to get my hair cut and colored. My husband and I didn't magically figure out how to keep all these plates spinning on our own — our success is largely due to our household manager. It's been wonderful being able to outsource our to-do list I hired a household manager because I didn't want to lose precious time with my family doing things someone else could do. Maria Satira We started this arrangement about two years ago after I came across the idea of a household manager on social media. At the time, I was pregnant with my second daughter, in the middle of my MBA program, renovating a house, preparing to move, and drowning in household chores — all while trying to be present for my husband and toddler and keep growing in a career I love. Outsourcing some of that mental load felt like exactly what I needed. I wanted help keeping our household running so I could be more present at home and at work. So, I created a job description, researched household-employee requirements, determined an hourly rate we could afford, and posted the role in local Facebook groups. After reviewing over a dozen applications in the first week, we ended up hiring a young woman who was finishing her college degree and had experience in short-term rental cleaning and management. After about a year with us, she moved out of state, so we rehired for the position and quickly found another wonderful fit: a mom of adult children with decades of household-management experience. Our current arrangement works out to $17 an hour and about eight hours a week, and feels worth every penny. We keep a standing weekly to-do list, and I text her anything else I might need while she's at our house or running errands for us. She tackles the big things, like making sure our fridge and pantry are stocked and that our daughters have clean, seasonally appropriate clothes in organized closets , and small ones, like restocking toilet paper in all our bathrooms and washing dishes left in the sink. Sometimes, she'll return purchases and online orders for us or even prep extra dinners when one of us is going to be away on a business trip, and the other is solo parenting. On a regular week, we don't have to worry about prepping dinner, changing linens, tidying the house, unloading the dishwasher, or running errands. Maria Satira There aren't many drawbacks to this arrangement, though it can take time and organization to properly delegate. For instance, my husband and I still handle ordering groceries; we just set our household manager as the pickup contact. If there's a specific recipe that we'd like her to cook, we make sure we have the right ingredients, print it out, and leave it for her. It also took a while to figure out the best use of our household manager's time versus what I'd prefer to do myself. For example, she washes our daughters' clothing and household linens, but my husband and I do our own loads of laundry. Ultimately, the return on investment is worth it for us — and it's nice to have time back Our household manager is such an important part of our village , and we're so grateful to have worked with two incredible women over the past two years. I recognize that paying for this kind of help isn't an option for every family, and we're fortunate to be able to make room for it in our budget. Yes, around $7,000 a year is a significant expense, but we feel the return on investment every day. In this season of our lives, we've decided that getting hundreds of hours of our family time back is worth prioritizing. Instead of waking up early on a Saturday morning to do laundry or start meal prepping , we can go for a walk with our daughters. I no longer feel like we're falling behind if we decide to take a day trip to the beach or spend hours at our favorite playground. And there's no guilt if we choose to just have a lazy, relaxing day at home. Beyond that, I no longer stress so much about all the things that need to get done. Instead, I add them to my list and, knowing my household manager will handle them when she's here, I can mentally let them go. I used to think being a good mom and wife meant finding a way to do it all. Now, I think it means knowing what deserves my time and what I can let someone else take off my plate. events.summary: GCAP pact between the UK, Italy and Japan to build a new fighter jet welcomed Canada as an ‘observer’ in July Prime ⁠⁠Minister Andy Burnham says the United Kingdom is open to Germany ⁠⁠joining the GCAP programme, a partnership with ⁠⁠Italy and Japan to build a new fighter jet, after meeting Chancellor Friedrich ‌‌Merz in Berlin. “I’ve indicated to the Chancellor … our openness to Germany joining GCAP,” Burnham told a news conference on Thursday. list 1 of 3 Ex-German spy chief arrested: A history of spooks working for enemy powers list 2 of 3 Trump invites Putin to Miami G20: Why that matters list 3 of 3 Western militaries are undermining Ukraine’s defence, experts say “That is something ⁠⁠that we seek ⁠⁠to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy ⁠⁠and Japan.” There has been growing speculation that the ⁠⁠founding countries of the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) could open the door to ‌‌Germany after a rival Franco-German fighter programme collapsed in ‌‌June. The GCAP pact to build a sixth generation fighter jet welcomed Canada as an “observer nation” in July. As western nations seek to maintain air superiority over rival powers, the new warplanes will be equipped with AI, next-generation sensors and other technology. Burnham is on his first official visit to Germany since becoming Britain’s prime minister in July. The leaders are also expected to confirm a new UK-Germany joint security partnership to counter sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid threats from adversaries. “Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat. They reach into people’s homes and workplaces and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided,” Burnham said in a statement ahead of the visit. Burnham’s office singled out the threat posed by Russia in a statement on Thursday, but stressed that the partnership would confront security threats regardless of their origin. As part of the agreement, the UK and Germany will share security information and work together to monitor, deter and disrupt threats. British MPs have raised concerns in recent months about the potential threats posed by Russia, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warning last month that Russia and its President, Vladimir Putin, were the biggest threat to the country’s security. Germany has also raised concerns about what it sees as a growing security threat posed by Moscow. Last month, Berlin accused Russia of being behind a failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Moscow denies any wrongdoing. Reporting from Berlin, Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane said the security partnership is “supposed to send a message to several countries” about the intention to increase European security. “It’s a way of demonstrating German and British intent in so far as Ukraine is concerned, but also more broadly about where Europe goes next, remembering of course that the United States plays a role in so far as NATO is concerned,” Kane said. “We know that Merz and Starmer [Burnham’s predecessor] and we can assume Burnham want to show to the Americans, as much as to the Russians, how much European security means to them.” Burnham and Merz are also expected to discuss other key issues for Europe, including ongoing support for Ukraine in its war against Russia and disruption to global trade routes, including through the Strait of Hormuz. The leaders are also expected to formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty. The accord commits both countries to deepening cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and economic growth.

events.title: Derry firm becomes one of UK's biggest car park operators after buying NCP
events.summary: Published 8 October 2026, 12:48 BST A Londonderry company has become one of the UK's biggest car park operators after buying NCP out of administration. The deal means the Martin Group will control more than 100 sites. The NCP business collapsed in March 2026 after a sustained period of declining performance left it unable to pay its debts. At that time some of its sites were closed or transferred to other operators. The administrators, PwC, said the majority of NCP's 145 sites would now transfer to the Martin Group along with the staff who work there. Zelf Hussain, joint administrator and partner at PwC, said the deal protected hundreds of jobs and delivered the best outcome for creditors. "Keeping NCP's car parks open also helps keep Britain's town and city centres moving," he added. "We would like to thank all of NCP's staff and directors for their support and professionalism throughout what has understandably been a period of uncertainty." NCP's major problems included being locked into long-term leases with property owners and building up a large amount of debt. The Martin Group already has a substantial commercial property portfolio across the UK including the Fishergate Shopping Centre in Preston and the Mercury Shopping Centre in Romford. It has recently expanded its hotels business, developing The Bedford Hotel in Belfast and buying The Waterfoot in Derry. Gary Martin, director of Martin Property Group, said the company's goal was to "build on the strength and heritage of the NCP brand so it can once again deliver the lasting impact on the communities it serves". "NCP is an iconic brand with a loyal customer base and talented workforce," he added. Rob England, chief executive of NCP, said it was "a fantastic day for NCP". "We have had to make difficult, necessary decisions to keep the business moving forward," he said. England said NCP was "immensely grateful" to its employees, customers and suppliers and its priority was "to restore full operational momentum and build a sustainable platform for long-term growth". events.title: Ray Dalio warns the stock market's cushion against rising bond yields is shrinking
events.summary: Ray Dalio says earnings growth has helped stocks absorb rising bond yields, but that advantage is narrowing. Dalio expects free cash flow to deteriorate even as earnings continue to improve. He says the bond sell-off has further to run as governments and companies compete for capital. Billionaire investor Ray Dalio warned on Thursday that stocks face mounting pressure from rising bond yields and the prospect of weaker corporate cash flows, even as earnings continue to grow. The Bridgewater Associates founder told CNBC equities have so far weathered the global bond sell-off because earnings growth has kept expected stock returns attractive, relative to bonds. But that advantage will narrow, he said, potentially leaving equities more vulnerable as financial conditions tighten. "We're in the part of the cycle where interest rates can rise without sending the equity market down because there's enough earnings growth and there's enough expected return," Dalio told CNBC's Sri Jegarajah at the Milken Institute Asia Summit in Singapore on Thursday. "But when that cushion comes down, then you're coming later into that cycle. So that's where we are." His warning comes as U.S. Treasury yields hover near multi-decade highs. Investors are grappling with large government deficits, persistent inflation and rising borrowing tied to artificial intelligence investment. Dalio said equities entered the current cycle offering significantly higher expected returns than bonds, helping sustain demand for stocks even as borrowing costs rose. But as stock prices climb and bond yields increase, that relative advantage is diminishing, leaving less room for equities to absorb higher rates. "Because of that change in pricing, that cushion has come down, and so now you're starting to see credit spreads start to widen," he said. Dalio also cautioned that investors may be overlooking the risk of deteriorating corporate cash generation, even as headline earnings continue to improve. Asked whether companies could sustain strong profit growth in the third quarter, Dalio said investors should focus on free cash flow rather than earnings alone. "I think you have to pay attention to free cash flows. ... Not just earnings. Because if you're earning and then you're investing and you're not getting money out of that, you have a liquidity issue that's evolving," he said. "While earnings should continue to be improving, I would expect the free cash flows, I think, will be deteriorating." Dalio stopped short of predicting an earnings decline or an imminent stock market correction. He said financial conditions have not yet tightened enough to significantly curb credit and spending. Dalio also said he expected the global bond sell-off to continue as governments and companies compete for capital, as mounting debt issuance puts pressure on investor demand. Governments are borrowing heavily to finance fiscal deficits, while companies are raising funds to invest in emerging technologies, creating an imbalance that could keep upward pressure on interest rates. "We are in a bond bear market, that's I think, pretty clear, and I think that there's more to go would be my guess," he said. Higher borrowing costs will eventually force a reduction in credit and spending, weighing on economic activity and potentially spilling over into equity markets, Dalio said. For now, Dalio said the tightening process is only beginning, with earnings growth still providing support for stocks even as credit conditions start to weaken.

events.title: Amazon's detailed customer dossiers are just the tip of the iceberg in the AI era
events.summary: Peter Dazeley/Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Boxers or briefs? Don't worry. AI already knows. A new trend is making people realize the amount of data that tech companies have on them and how they're using it. Amazon's "About You" feature — an AI-created rundown of your preferences as a shopper — has been making the rounds on the internet. Amazon's specificity has been eye-opening, from "has flat buttocks" to "uses phone in the shower to read Kindle books." ( Here's a step-by-step guide for finding your "About You" feature .) Ben Shimkus canvassed the BI newsroom to see what Amazon thinks of his colleagues . Amazon's read on me wasn't all that surprising (or funny), with one exception: "performs manual work or construction." Yup, that's me, punching the clock at the old newsletter factory. Companies building profiles on us shouldn't be surprising. But the depths they're willing to go might be. When a Wired reporter recently requested a copy of his customer data from McDonald's loyalty program, he got back a 515-page dossier . And this wasn't necessarily someone you'd consider a frequent customer. McDonald's predicted he'd visit 2.16 times over a six-week period. McDonald's data collection is small fries when you consider other companies you're interacting with. AI giants are using their agents to get embedded deeper into users' personal lives. Instead of companies having to do some legwork to collect info on customers, people are actively giving them the keys to the data castle. From email, calendars, and texts to bank accounts, it's all fair game. And for those who don't want to have to think about reordering paper towels, it's worth it. But even if you want to overlook the security or privacy concerns , there's still reason to give at least a slight pause. AI companies are under pressure to generate revenue from the tools they're spending billions of dollars building. A subscription model is the most straightforward play, but that risks excluding a good chunk of users who won't be willing to cough up. Tapping into the troves of data they've collected on customers is another route. Suddenly it's not just ordering ahead for you, but ushering you toward certain brands. The South Korean company is among the major memory manufacturers benefiting from demand for chips used in datacenter servers and GPUs. Although Samsung will not report its full earnings until the end of this month, its guidance puts sales at between ₩194 trillion and ₩196 trillion (about $145 billion) for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. This is more than double the ₩86.1 trillion ($63 billion) for the same period last year. The company expects operating profit of between ₩107.3 trillion and ₩107.5 trillion (about $80 billion), compared with just ₩12.2 trillion ($9 billion) for Q3 2025, roughly 8.8 times last year's figure. Samsung's brief guidance note does not break down performance by business division. Demand for memory, including high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used alongside AI processors, is likely to be a major contributor. The demand for DRAM and NAND for AI applications is driving profits across the semiconductor industry. Analyst Gartner forecast that the sector as a whole will bring in $1.6 trillion during 2026, almost double the revenue seen in 2025. Rival chipmaker Micron posted similar gains last week , and the other Korean memory giant, SK hynix, will likely have the same story to tell when it discloses its own quarterly figures later this month. The boom is proving costly for buyers of everyday electronics. Memory manufacturers' shift towards more lucrative AI products is squeezing supplies for PCs, smartphones, and other devices, driving up component prices. As The Register previously reported, rising component costs are pricing budget PCs out of the market . US sales in that bracket fell 18.7 percent year-on-year in the first quarter, while average PC selling prices were forecast to rise by up to 12 percent by December. Smartphone makers face similar pressures, with budget devices becoming increasingly difficult to produce profitably . events.title: Italian law to give election winners bonus seats: Why that’s controversial
events.summary: Critics say the proposed law is undemocratic, potentially granting a winning coalition disproportionate power in parliament. Italy’s parliament is voting on Thursday on a new electoral law that would make it easier for election winners to form a majority government. The law, proposed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, would award extra seats to any party or coalition that obtains more than 42 percent of seats in both parliamentary chambers, ensuring it holds a majority. list 1 of 3 Italy’s Meloni slams protesters following clashes in Bologna list 2 of 3 Abderrahim Fakir’s death has reignited Italy’s police accountability debate list 3 of 3 ‘She doesn’t give up that easily’: France’s Le Pen eyes the Elysee Meloni has framed the legislation as a route to greater stability in Italy’s political system, which has often been run by fragile coalition governments. Her critics, however, say the move is actually aimed at boosting her own chances in elections next year. Here’s what we know about the electoral law and what it means for Italian politics: What is Italy’s current electoral system? Italy currently has a mixed electoral system for its 600-seat parliament, with about 36 percent of members of parliament elected directly in constituencies where the candidate with the most votes wins, and the rest decided through proportional representation. The system, called “Rosatellum”, has been in place since 2017. It encourages coalition-building but can produce fractured results that make a governing majority hard to forge. The new legislation would replace the mixed electoral system with a fully proportional one, as well as awarding extra seats to the party or coalition that wins the most seats if it secures at least 42 percent in both chambers. The bonus would be as many as 70 seats in the 400-member Chamber of Deputies, the lower house, and up to 35 seats in the Senate, which has 200 elected members. That means if a party or coalition meets the 42 percent share threshold in both chambers, it would have stronger power to govern. If no party or coalition meets the threshold, representation would be decided proportionally. The new law would also force coalitions to announce their candidates for prime minister before the elections. Rado Fonda, head of research at Italian pollster SWG, told the Reuters news agency this provision could “prove problematic for the centre-left, potentially forcing an early leadership contest and exposing divisions that could weaken the bloc”. Meloni, who currently leads the country’s longest-serving government since World War II, has said the reform will help stabilise the country rather than serve any one political group. “Whoever wins the elections will have the numbers to govern,” she said. The proposed law has already been approved by the Senate and must now undergo a final secret-ballot vote in the Chamber of Deputies. Giovanni Orsina, a political scientist at Rome’s Luiss Guido Carli University, predicted that the law is “extremely likely” to pass. If it fails, Meloni has said she will resign. Why is the legislation controversial? Opponents say the law is undemocratic because it could potentially grant a winning coalition a disproportionate level of power in parliament. They also say that the legislation is intended to favour Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy party (Fdl) is bracing for a tough election battle next year. Riccardo Magi, head of the liberal More Europe party, who is on a hunger strike to protest the proposed reform, has called it an “anti-democratic law” that risks giving a minority bloc a huge majority in parliament. Senator Matteo Renzi, who leads the Italia Viva party, has accused Italy’s governing coalition of pushing the electoral reform due to a fear of losing power. Other critics have pointed out that the law would do little to stabilise the political system if no party or coalition reaches the 42 percent threshold in both chambers – a relatively high bar. “This could produce a hung parliament, making post-electoral negotiations necessary to form a government,” Vincenzo Emanuele, a political science professor at Luiss Guido Carli University in Rome and a member of the Italian Center for Electoral Studies (CISE), told Al Jazeera. “Even relatively small changes in coalition composition could make the difference between a clear parliamentary majority and a situation of political deadlock.” When are Italy’s next elections, and what do the polls show? Italy’s next general election must be held by December 22, 2027, although the government can call elections earlier if it wishes. Currently, Meloni’s Fdl is polling ahead of all other parties, with 27 percent support, according to Politico’s polling aggregator. Her coalition partners, Lega and Forza Italia, have a combined 12 percent support, according to Politico, bringing the coalition share to 39 percent. Fdl’s polling has been dented by support for a new far-right group, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), Reuters reported.

events.title: The Download: AI roadblocks for humanoids and portable rubber dams
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI breakthroughs in robotics won’t change your life any time soon The hype around humanoid robots is reaching fever pitch. Much of it comes from the idea that the same AI advances behind ChatGPT and Claude could enable robots to imitate human movement the way chatbots imitate human language. But many researchers are skeptical. They argue that such assumptions minimize the challenges of using an intelligence built on language and images to master the infinite variability of the physical world. They also point out that conflating humanoids with so-called generalist machines is misleading. Across robotics labs, tensions have emerged over whether current forms of AI are all that’s needed to perfect all-purpose humanoids or whether an entirely new path is required. Read the full story on what it will take to build truly general-purpose robots . —Jamie Condliffe This story is a collaboration between MIT Technology Review and Aventine , a non-profit research foundation that creates and supports content about how technology and science are changing the way we live. 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WaveSave and its portable rubber dam WaveSave is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . As sea levels rise and flood risks worsen, WaveSave has emerged with an ingeniously simple tool: a portable rubber dam that’s quick to install when flooding starts. Anyone can unfurl the SlamDam on the ground along a riverbank or shoreline and pump it full of water until it swells into place. And there it stands, up to 1.3 meters high, shielding nearby property or structures from damage as waters rise.  WaveSave now plans to take its unusual approach to flood protection much further . —Amy Nordrum Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from smart turbines and sustainable cement to carbon dioxide batteries . Why we’re watching these climate tech companies —Casey Crownhart Our Climate Tech Companies to Watch list is always a little ray of hope for me—there are some fascinating ideas out there about how we power our world or move away from fossil fuels.  Our chosen companies also reflect several aspects of the current moment. One is that China is the center of the climate and energy tech world. Another is that everybody wants a piece of the data center pie. And then there’s the fact that the grid needs support, with energy storage a key piece moving forward. Here’s what this year’s list reveals about the state of climate tech . events.title: New generation of Gulf philanthropists want a seat at the table
events.summary: The Scene As Western governments slash foreign aid, many organizations are seeking Gulf philanthropy to fill the gaps. While wealthy individuals and governments in the region are ready to take on a larger role, a younger generation of donors isn’t content with plowing money into existing programs, and is instead seeking new approaches with more effective and measurable outcomes. Sonia Ben Jaafar, CEO of the Abdulla Al Ghurair Foundation, told Semafor that private donors from the Gulf want to be more involved in designing development programs rather than simply financing them. She said the region’s charities have developed their own expertise that can help inform changes to improve existing charitable programs. The foundation she runs — established in 2015 by Emirati billionaire Abdulla Al Ghurair and chaired by his son Abdul Aziz — has become one of the Arab world’s largest privately funded education initiatives, reaching about 500,000 young people over the past decade. The foundation runs like a business, using performance metrics to evaluate its grants and tying funding decisions to outcomes such as job placement rates, Ben Jaafar said. The approach fits within a broader push by Badr Jafar, the UAE’s special envoy for business and philanthropy, to bring private donors, businesses, and governments together to address humanitarian needs. In an interview in New York during the UN General Assembly, Ben Jaafar discussed the changing role of private wealth in the region, and why her foundation is quick to drop programs that don’t deliver results. Why is private philanthropy hesitant to step in to cover underfunded programs that have been abandoned by many governments? The narrative that philanthropic capital will just fill that up is not going to happen. What we’re hearing in the discussions, at least that I’m in, in the closed rooms, is: What does the new framework look like? Because it cannot be more of the same, and philanthropic capital shouldn’t be coming in as a gap filler. We need a new model of how public, private, and philanthropy — this is the new three Ps — are going to partner together. How does the Abdulla Al Ghurair Foundation measure the success of its programs? We have a strategy that would look like any business, except instead of generating revenue, we need to generate impact for the communities we serve. We have, on average, a [jobs] placement rate of 78%, which is a very high placement rate in my field. We don’t count just who we train. We want to know that that training landed them into a revenue-generating life. You were early to get into Syria after the war ended. What are you focusing on there? We’re training young Syrians to learn construction skills, and paying them to attend an apprenticeship program. Those graduates will then work on the schools we started to refurbish there. During the war, we started a fund in 2018 that was focused on educating refugees in Lebanon and Jordan. Some of those Syrians are now returnees and are being picked up by government administration and companies to support the reconstruction. Have you funded programs that didn’t work? We have funded programs that we were sure would work, and we were sure we had the right partner to implement it. Because it’s outcomes-based funding, if you cannot meet the milestone and you don’t have a good reason, or we can’t find a solution with you, then we will defund that. We’ll stop. We’ll sunset that, and we’ll find a new way of doing it. Notable Abdul Aziz Al Ghurair runs his philanthropy like a business. The foundation’s chairman urged donors to set measurable goals and work with governments and businesses to maximize impact. The Gulf’s wealth transfer could reshape charitable giving. Badr Jafar, the UAE’s special envoy for business and philanthropy, told Semafor that more than $1 trillion will change hands in the region by 2030 , accelerating a shift toward impact-driven philanthropy.

events.title: New rules to make long-term investment funds clearer
events.summary: The FCA has set out clearer expectations for asset managers about long-term investments, such as property. This will help give the market more confidence to invest in funds that support private markets.The new rules mean that investors will have to give 90 days' notice to access their funds but will be more certain that they will receive their money.For investors, this means the fund should be clearer from the start about how quickly they can get their money back and whether the fund is right for their needs.Currently some of these funds allow people to take money out daily with no notice period. During periods of stress or volatility there is a risk that some funds may suspend all payments due to lack of available cash. Some are also holding extra cash, leaving less invested in their intended assets.Rushed sales can lower prices, harm investors who stay invested and put pressure on markets.The new notice period would give managers time to sell assets in an orderly way and make liquidity-driven suspensions less likely.Existing funds would have 2 years to comply and give investors at least 1 year’s notice.The proposals bring the UK into line with new international liquidity standards for open ended funds.Michelle Beck, director, markets, at the FCA, said: 'Funds should be clear about whether they offer quick access or are built for longer-term investments like property. Our rules will help firms make that clearer and give the market more confidence to invest.'Notes to editorsRead CP26/35: Fair redemption terms for authorised funds investing in illiquid assets.The FCA is asking for feedback on the proposals by 11 December 2026.The consultation covers authorised fund managers of non-UCITS retail schemes, known as NURS.The FCA uses the term 'inherently illiquid assets' for assets that cannot normally be sold quickly without a significant loss in value. These can include property and infrastructure investments.Fund managers could set a notice period longer than the minimum where the fund’s assets or investment strategy require it.

events.title: Iraq devalues its currency but some MPs oppose it
events.summary: The move gives Baghdad more dinars for every dollar it earns from oil, at a cost MPs say will fall on ordinary Iraqis. Iraq has devalued its national currency again, undoing the previous government’s move to strengthen the Iraqi dinar and prompting calls in parliament to reverse the decision. The cabinet approved new exchange rates for the dinar on Tuesday, following an emergency recommendation from Finance Minister Falih al-Sari and the governor of the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI). list 1 of 3 Iraq grants Iranian airlines 40 daily Najaf flights after US exemption list 2 of 3 Iraq looks for oil export alternatives to the troubled Strait of Hormuz list 3 of 3 Iran urges Iraq to lift flight ban amid US sanctions From Wednesday, banks and exchange companies have been selling dollars to the public at 1,520 dinars each, 200 higher than the previous price. MPs who opposed the move had the agenda for Wednesday’s session of parliament cancelled in order to debate it instead. The finance minister and the central bank governor are due to appear before parliament on Thursday to discuss the devaluation. Why has Iraq devalued the dinar now? Right before instituting the devaluation, Iraq’s government adopted its annual budget for 2027. It plans to spend 217 trillion dinars (about $166bn) next year, and expects a deficit of more than 40 trillion dinars ($30bn). The massive shortfall reflects the difficult financial situation Iraq faces as a consequence of the US war on Iran. Since fighting began in late February, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been severely disrupted. Iraq’s oil exports – the majority of which must transit Hormuz to reach global markets – have fluctuated throughout the war, at one point falling by 90 percent to a trickle. In August, they were at 2.34 million barrels a day, far lower than their pre-war average of 3.6 million. Last month, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said his country was “facing extraordinary economic challenges”, having lost about $60bn in oil revenue as a result of the disruption. Oil revenues pay for more than 90 percent of Iraq’s federal budget. The lost income has made it harder to pay state salaries and the CBI’s foreign currency reserves fell from about $106bn before the war to roughly $80bn by late August. Speaking to the Reuters news agency, Iraqi analyst Mohammed al-Saffar said the measure “gives the government more dinars for each dollar of oil revenue, but raises import costs and reduces households’ purchasing power”. Why are some MPs opposing devaluation? Iraq’s Central Bank described the decision as a “strategic step” to steady the country’s finances. But many MPs have urged the government to reverse the change, saying it will raise the cost of living for Iraqis. In a joint statement on Wednesday, dozens of MPs opposed to the move said they had not been told how or why the decision came about – and that the CBI should have explained it to parliament before it was taken. Speaking on their behalf, MP Aziz Nasser al-Shammari, who sits on the Iraqi parliament’s integrity body, denounced the move, saying that they had been “surprised” by the decision. “Waging war on the poor like this is wrong,” he declared. Hassan al-Asadi, leader of the al-Nahj National Alliance bloc, rejected the measure and suggested alternative methods to balance the budget, such as cutting unnecessary spending. MP Saba al-Saadi was also among those who rejected using a weaker dinar to plug the budget gap. She blamed the Finance Ministry and the CBI for what she called financial mismanagement and vowed to bring the matter before parliament for review. What does it mean for ordinary Iraqis? A weaker dinar against the dollar means that imports will become more expensive for Iraqis, raising costs that have already been elevated by regional instability. Iraq relies on imports for much of what it consumes, from food and medicines to raw materials for industry. Last month, Iraqi consumers and business owners told Al Jazeera that prices had already risen significantly since the Iran war began, on top of delays and disruption to seaborne imports. Opposing MPs criticised the adoption of the measure at a time when Iraqis were already facing rising prices, import fees, taxes, unemployment and delays in government salary and welfare payments. Al-Asadi called attention to a growing gap between the official and parallel price of dollars in the country, warning it could “inflict severe harm on the poor and vulnerable”. After the new official rate took effect on Wednesday, the rate of the dollar on the parallel market rose as well, with the gap between them widening. In practice, most Iraqis cannot get dollars at the official rate and pay the parallel market price instead. Yes. In December 2020, Iraq devalued the dinar to 1,450 per dollar from about 1,182, after a crash in oil prices left the government short of cash.

events.title: Growing up, my 84-year-old great uncle and I barely knew each other. Now he's one of my best friends.
events.summary: My 84-year-old great uncle is now my best friend, even though I didn't know him well when I was growing up. Sean Loera Growing up in the US, I barely knew my great-uncle, who lives in London. In 2014, I spent the summer in his city, and we formed a close relationship. Now, I live in London and he's become one of my closest friends. Growing up in the US, I barely knew my family on the other side of the Atlantic. In my mind, my Uncle Brian was more of a name than a person, and I had only met him a handful of times. Two of those meetings were before I was old enough to remember, and the other two were when I was an angsty high school teenager with not much interest in getting to know someone more than twice my age. It wasn't until 2014, when I traveled to London for the summer to explore my ancestral home, that I connected with my uncle. Preparing for what I imagined to be a cordial, potentially awkward meet-up, I didn't expect much in the way of connection. He was, essentially, a stranger. I never expected our relationship to blossom that summer I was a little nervous to reconnect, since we had only met a handful of times while I was growing up. Sean Loera We met outside a café, and he took me into central London to one of his favorite pubs. When I ordered a pint of London Pride, he looked confused. "You like London Pride?" he asked me. We chatted over his shock at what he said was my pleasantly un-American good taste in British beer. That summer, we spent many days together exploring pubs, strolling through museums and parks, and seeing musicals on the West End. Experiencing London through his eyes was incredible, but what stands out to me most is how little time it took to develop such a close relationship. I had spent most of my life barely knowing him, yet somehow, that distance and those missed years disappeared. When we were together, I didn't see an age difference . I just saw my friend. I had always felt like something of an outlier growing up, restless in a way I didn't see reflected in the rest of my family. Getting close to Uncle Brian felt less like meeting someone new and more like being handed a mirror. My Nanny, his sister, says he and I are cut from the same cloth. We both have itchy feet, she says, and are always searching for our next destination. There's something oddly reassuring about discovering that the part of me I had always thought made me different existed in someone else, too. I remember being particularly nervous about coming out to him. After all, he is from a generation I worried might struggle with it. Instead, without missing a beat, he simply said, "So what? Do you want another drink?" I'll never forget that moment. Now that we live in the same city, we're making up for lost time. I moved to London in 2025. Sean Loera When I left London, we stayed in touch mostly through text, and when I moved to Los Angeles , the eight-hour time difference made those messages even more important. I visited him a few times over the years, picking up right where we left off, and always ending with a very tearful goodbye. But when I decided to move to London in the summer of 2025, knowing he was here made it much easier. Moving to a new country , looking for work, and trying to build a new life was still daunting, but I didn't feel like I was completely starting over. I had someone here I could turn to when things felt uncertain. These days, I see him a few times a month. We still meet in our favorite pub, go on nights out to the theater, and chat and laugh for hours. We love going to pubs together. Sean Loera We love to gossip, and I fill him in on family back home. He tells me stories about his past, and repeatedly reminds me about the time when I was 4 years old and he sat me on top of one of the lions in Trafalgar Square. Other times, our conversations become quite deep, and we find ourselves discussing everything from relationships to the choices we've made and what we've learned. And sometimes, we touch on harder topics like how we want to make the most of the time we have left together. We're there for one another, as best friends are. I can rely on him, and he on me. I used to assume that the people who knew me best would be the ones who had known me the longest. Uncle Brian has made me question that. I understand now that knowing someone isn't always about the years you've shared with them. Sometimes, you meet someone and recognize yourself almost immediately. events.title: Microsoft to sell $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra containing Nvidia AI chip
events.summary: Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra contains an Nvidia chip that can run large AI models without generating cloud bills. The device contains a magnetic USB-C port similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector. Microsoft also said that Meta will introduce its Muse AI agent for Windows. Microsoft said its new laptop containing an Nvidia AI chip will start at $2,599, as the software maker tries to bring more artificial intelligence capabilities to its consumer devices. The Surface Laptop Ultra is now available on preorder and will begin shipping on Oct. 16, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and devices, said at a company event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The computer has the world's first magnetic USB-C port, similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector, along with two other standard USB-C ports, Microsoft said in a blog post . While Microsoft Windows is the most popular operating system for PCs, the company isn't among the top six PC vendors in terms of unit shipments, according to an estimate from researcher Gartner. As the AI boom matures and chip technology advances, tech giants including Microsoft, Apple and Google are aiming to allow users to run more AI workloads from their devices rather than relying on the cloud. Users can install and run a variety of models on the new laptop without having to worry about racking up high monthly bills. Microsoft first talked about the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, but is just now providing specifics. "Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies, wrote on X after the announcement. Davuluri also said that Meta will introduce a version of its popular Muse AI agent for Windows, capitalizing on the surging popularity of the personal agent, which has jumped to the top of Apple's App store, surpassing ChatGPT. Microsoft is still trying to solidify its role as a key player in AI. The company offers its own AI models, but they're less popular than leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic and aren't at the forefront in terms of performance, according to one benchmark . Developers are more likely to have used alternatives, according to a recent survey . This isn't the first time Microsoft has sought to use the AI boom as a way to boost sales of its devices. In 2024, the company introduced the Copilot+ PC standard, requiring the inclusion of neural processing units that ensure a minimum level of AI performance, along with compliant Surface computers. But Microsoft has since "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences," a spokesperson said. The new device sports a 15-inch display and weighs 4.4 pounds. It can contain up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory and supply up to one petaflop of computing power. The Blackwell RTX Spark GPU inside the computer has as much processing power as Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server from 2016, which cost $250 million, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at Wednesday's event. A presenter showed how apps on the Surface Laptop Ultra can route some AI coding requests run on the computer's local GPU, displaying a green leaf icon, and others to the cloud. Through Windows 11, developers can confine coding agents to Microsoft Execution Containers that will prevent unwanted system access. Microsoft is updating its Windows 11 device setup experience to help people get started quickly with open-source OpenClaw AI agent software. Microsoft has been releasing its own computers since 2012, and CEO Satya Nadella indicated on Tuesday that the company's position in the market is evolving. "I think today is the day we'll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours two years from now, five years from now, 10 years from now," Nadella said at the event. "That classic edge that distributed computing will always remain distributed will be more true." WATCH: Microsoft unveils Muse for Windows

events.title: Europeans are drinking less beer. Heineken’s Europe boss has a plan to avoid a brewing hangover
events.summary: This summer was a bright moment for Europe’s brewers. Hot weather and the FIFA World Cup packed out beer gardens, and in Britain, the night that England beat Panama was pubs’ busiest of the year, with card transactions five times the daily average , according to Barclays .  But behind the sunny terraces, a longer slump has been brewing. European consumers drink less beer than they did before the pandemic. Consumption fell 3.2% in 2025 and is down 9.2% since 2019, according to a report by the industry trade body Brewers of Europe.  The slump has been pinned on sober-curious Gen Z drinkers and, more recently, weight-loss drugs like Ozempic. Glenn Caton, Europe president at Heineken , the world’s second-largest brewer, points to costs. “There’s no question that price inflation has impacted consumer consumption over time,” he told Fortune .   Brewers had barely recovered from the pandemic when Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine sent energy and grain prices soaring. “Clearly raising prices has been necessary,” Caton said. Heineken raised what it charges British pubs for draught beer by 2.97% in February 2025 and another 2.7% this February. The average U.K. pint rose 17p to £5.34 in the year to April, according to The Morning Advertiser .  Although Heineken returned to growth this year, volumes rose 1.6% in t he second quarter of 2026, this was not thanks to European drinkers. While beer sales in Asia Pacific and Africa and the Middle East rose, in Europe they’ve been falling. Across Europe and the U.S., Caton said, beer is in “structural decline.”  Cutting costs Europe is Heineken’s biggest region by sales but has its thinnest margins. Europe brought in nearly two-fifths ( 38.4%) of first-half sales but only a quarter of operating profit. Having already raised prices in the region, Caton is now focusing on cutting costs.  In February, Heineken announced plans to cut up to 6,000 jobs globally over the next two years under EverGreen 2030 , a strategy that aims to save the company up to €500 million a year ($559 million) and boost profits by focusing on its fastest-growing markets. The savings, Caton says, are also meant to offset rising energy and raw-material costs so the company can “mitigate price inflation for the consumer.”   About 3,000 jobs were cut in the first half of 2026, and chief financial officer Harold van den Broek has signaled that Europe will bear much of the burden. “Europe is a big component” of the cuts, he said at the half-year results in August.   Glenn Caton, President Europe at Heinken Heineken, 2026 Caton declined to say how many European jobs will go, citing ongoing consultation with staff and the European Works Council. Some of the changes will see roles move to Heineken’s business services hubs in places such as Kraków and India. “You never like to make difficult decisions that impact people you know and respect,” Caton said, “but it is necessary for the health of the company.”  Heineken is also merging nine country businesses into four multi-country operating units in Europe, including one bringing together Belgium and the Netherlands and another for Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. Caton says this is a departure from Heineken’s traditionally local-first way of operating. The aim, he said, is a business that is “lean, fast and agile,” with costs low enough to offer drinkers better value.   The overhaul also ran for nine months without a permanent chief executive. Rafael Oliveira took over on Oct. 1, but Caton insists the plan never slowed and that the new boss is there to help execute. “It’s not about a radically new strategy,” he said. “My job is to run Europe, and hopefully he’ll let me get on with that.”  Growing the non-alcoholic pie To keep drinkers who trade down, Heineken sells at every price point, from premium Birra Moretti to mainstream Cruzcampo and budget Foster’s. It is also betting on alcohol-free beer, which lets drinkers cut back without leaving its brands. Zero-alcohol beers, Caton said, is “enabling more consumers to moderate the decline in alcohol.”  Before Heineken 0.0 launched in 2017, the category’s big problem “was taste,” he added. Heineken’s version, designed to taste “near identical to the original” and backed by a Formula 1 sponsorship, is now one of the leading alcohol-free beers. The group’s low- and no-alcohol volumes rose 12% in the first half of 2026. Competition in the alcohol-free beer market is growing. “It makes our job harder,” Caton added, “but for the category overall, it’s a good thing, because it’s growing the whole pie.”  Alcohol-free accounts for one in 1 2 beers drunk in the E U, according to Brewers of Europe, and Carton admitted that take-up is uneven across the continent. As a result Heineken is innovating “in both directions,” with flavored 0.0s such as Lemon & Elderflower in the U.K., an orange Cruzcampo, and lagers of around 3.5% alcohol, below the usual 4.5% to 5%.  Pubs and bars make up about half of Heineken’s European business, according to Caton. In the U.K., it owns about 2,350 pubs through Star Pubs & Bars, mostly leased to independent operators, and is reportedly in talks to acquire Stonegate as part of a £300 million ($396 million) deal, which would add around 300 more pubs to its portfolio. Caton said the deal is still ongoing.   “Good pubs in the U.K. are thriving,” Caton said. “People still want to socialize physically.” The numbers only partly back him up. British pubs are struggling, with 161 shutting in the first quarter of 2026, up 26% on a year earlier. But the British Beer & Pub Association blames tax and overheads, and across the EU, the share of beer drunk in pubs, bars, and restaurants has stopped shrinking after years of decline.  Heineken is also making the case that bars are a key part of the economy. Tourists spend almost €2.5 billion a year on its beers, it estimates, mostly in pubs and bars, and 35% of tourists in a survey the brewer commissioned said they had visited a neighborhood specifically because of a local bar.  For Caton, returning Europe to growth will be reliant on creating more value for consumers by reducing the price of drinks in both shops and bars and creating new low-alcohol options for health-conscious consumers. “If you offer great value and a great experience, you bring punters in the door,” he said. And he isn’t worried about beer itself. “It’s been around 5,000 years. It’s not going anywhere.”  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: India to Turkiye, can new proposals to broker Russia-Ukraine truce succeed?
events.summary: India, Turkiye, Egypt and the US have put forward proposals for ceasefires in bid to protect global energy and shipping. Ukraine says it has received proposals from India, Turkiye, Egypt and the United States to broker talks with Russia. The offers come as the two adversaries escalate attacks on each other’s energy and port infrastructure with their war now in its fifth year. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha revealed the four proposals at a briefing in Kyiv on Friday and singled out New Delhi’s. “The most comprehensive is India’s proposal,” he said, adding that India had signalled a willingness to play a role for the first time. list 1 of 3 At least 20 killed as Russia launches ‘massive’ attack on Ukraine list 2 of 3 Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia? list 3 of 3 At least 24 killed as Russia launches massive attack on Ukraine None of the proposals aims to end the war. Each seeks a narrower truce, covering energy facilities, ports or commercial shipping in the Black Sea. India has not made its plan public. Quoting unnamed sources, however, Indian media have reported it has three parts. According to the Hindustan Times, it would aim to protect infrastructure, keep grain and energy supplies moving through Black Sea ports, and ensure the safety of commercial shipping. The first part – mutually halting strikes on energy facilities and ports – matches what Kyiv has been demanding. Sybiha said any deal must be a complete energy truce that covers port infrastructure as well. The second part builds on the Black Sea Grain Initiative , which Turkiye and the United Nations mediated in 2022 but Russia abandoned in 2023. The third part, protecting merchant ships and their crews, is particularly important to India because Indian sailors have been killed or harmed on Black Sea routes . The sources were quoted as saying India’s plan goes further than the other three proposals because it covers infrastructure and shipping together. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that it incorporates elements of the Turkish, Egyptian and US initiatives. The Kyiv Post reported that Sybiha also described the plan as addressing a possible ceasefire along the front lines, although other accounts said he gave no specifics. The proposal likely took shape during Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar’s first visit to Ukraine last month and in a later meeting with Sybiha at the UN General Assembly in New York, also in September. Jaishankar said New Delhi was “trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue”. What do we know about the Turkish and Egyptian proposals? Very little. Neither Ankara nor Cairo has published details. Both reportedly focus on keeping Black Sea grain supplies moving by suspending attacks on commercial shipping. Some reports said the two countries proposed a grain truce jointly while others described two separate plans. Turkiye has done this before. With the UN, it steered the 2022 grain deal, one of the few narrow truces of the war to hold for any length of time. Ankara and the UN are now organising new Black Sea talks with a round planned for October. Beyond its Black Sea focus, almost nothing is known about Egypt’s proposal. Its interest, however, is clear: Egypt relies on Ukraine for nearly one-third of its grain supplies. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Washington has proposed three steps: a mutual halt to energy strikes, a reopening of the grain corridor and a trilateral meeting with Ukraine and Russia, possibly in Abu Dhabi. The latest effort began in early September when US President Donald Trump’s envoys visited Kyiv and Moscow and secured an agreement in principle for a trilateral meeting. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on September 5 while Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev visited the US twice in September. The trilateral meeting has since been pushed back. It had been expected to take place in the United Arab Emirates in early October. Washington now wants it in late October, and people close to the talks blamed the delay on Russia. Washington has also invited Putin to the Group of 20 summit in Miami, Florida, in December. “We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said. The Kremlin said no decision has been made. At the same time, the US is applying pressure to try to end the war. Trump recently signed a law giving him sweeping powers to sanction buyers of Russian energy. He has also called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian diesel facilities amid a diesel prices crisis in the US, where Trump faces tricky midterm elections next month. “Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing,” he said on September 13. “He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.” This drew much criticism that Trump instead should focus his comments on Russia, which began the war with its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

events.title: Your next manager may have three employees and 19 agents. Who’s accountable?
events.summary: Over the past several months, we have been interviewing CIOs and other senior executives about how AI is changing management. We started with a fairly conventional question: Which parts of a manager’s job will AI automate, augment or leave alone? But the more conversations we have, the more we think this is too narrow for a framing. What we are seeing is not simply a smaller manager role, or a more automated one. AI is unbundling some parts of management while expanding others. The manager role is being reassembled around a different mix of responsibilities. For decades, organizations have bundled a remarkable amount of work into one position called “manager”: gathering information, coordinating people, reviewing work, tracking progress, translating strategy, allocating resources, coaching employees, communicating upward, making decisions and carrying accountability. That bundle is starting to change. At Edward Jones, CIO Kevin Adams has moved part of managerial memory and follow-through into an AI system that tracks context across enterprise programs and committees. At CVS, Alan Rosa described an operating process where agents now prepare the reports and dashboards that once consumed much of a two-hour daily management meeting. The meeting has fallen to roughly 15 minutes and is now largely about exceptions, problems and decisions. In many companies, AI is helping reduce the need for layers whose primary role was to collect, repackage and transmit information. At the same time, the definition of management is expanding. Broadridge CTO Tyler Derr is already considering how to balance human teams with digital workers Taken together, these examples point to two changes happening at once: Some traditional management work is moving out of the manager role, while entirely new management responsibilities are being added around AI and agents.The future manager may therefore be neither simply smaller nor simply more AI-enabled. The role itself is being reassembled. Some management work is becoming infrastructure The CVS example is useful because the change is not simply that a manager does the same work faster. The operating process itself changed. Agents run reports overnight, aggregate the results and prepare the dashboards before the team arrives. The daily stability meeting no longer has to serve as the mechanism for constructing a shared picture of what is happening. That picture increasingly already exists. The meeting can focus on the smaller set of issues that still need intervention. Historically, a lot of management work existed because someone had to assemble and move information. These were activities somebody had to find time to perform. Increasingly, they can become persistent systems. At Edward Jones, CIO Kevin Adams has created such an AI system. Rather than using AI as a series of isolated prompts, he continuously builds context within each environment by adding relevant documents, decisions, history, open issues and commitments over time. The accumulated institutional context allows the system to surface connections, preserve continuity and prompt follow-through across work that would otherwise depend heavily on individual memory. A colleague described it as his “chief of staff.” Adams puts the boundary this way: “I don’t let the machine tell me what to do. I let the machine prompt me about what I should be doing.” What interests us is less the metaphor than the organizational implication. Something that once lived almost entirely inside the manager including memory, continuity and follow-through can now partly live in the system around the manager. The same is increasingly true for reporting, preparation, monitoring and recurring operating rhythms. Those responsibilities do not necessarily disappear. They stop requiring the same amount of active managerial labor. Parts of management are becoming infrastructure. That creates a second question: what happens to the capacity? This is where the dialog elevates beyond simple productivity. If AI removes administrative work, what happens to the capacity it creates? Pushpendu Pal, Chief Digital and Technology Officer at CVS Health , described spending less time on budget administration, project-status reviews and implementation reporting. But he has not simply ended up with a shorter day. He is spending more time coaching people, working directly with engineers and developers, developing organizational capabilities and generating ideas for service and business improvement. AI is assisting in creating more time for leaders to perform their primary task more effectively, like coaching and mentoring, being consultative with business stakeholders and working with engineers in sculpting the improved services.  This demonstrates how removing management work and redesigning management are not the same thing. If AI saves a manager five hours and the organization simply fills those hours with more projects, more meetings or a larger workload, then AI improved capacity.  But the manager role itself did not necessarily change. A real redesign requires asking what responsibilities should grow as others shrink. That question will differ by organization. But it has to be answered deliberately. Otherwise, the role gets compressed without being redesigned. AI may also make certain management layers harder to justify The changes at CVS and Edward Jones raise an organizational question as well: Which management layers still perform a distinct function when information, context and status updates are available through shared systems? That does not mean AI automatically creates flatter organizations. It means some layers need a clearer reason to exist. If a management layer primarily exists to collect information, summarize it, translate it, carry it upward, and distribute it downward, then AI makes that role easier to question. The useful org design test is no longer simply “How many people report to this manager?” It becomes: What distinct management responsibility resides at this layer? If the answer is unclear, the layer may reflect an information architecture that AI is changing. At the same time, management is expanding to include digital labor While some traditional responsibilities are shrinking or moving into systems, another category of management work is growing. Someone has to direct the agents. That work can include assigning tasks, structuring workflows, inspecting outputs, coordinating multiple agents, resolving failures and deciding when a human needs to intervene. Individual contributors may take on some of it even when they have no human direct reports. At CVS, Alan Rosa described another part of that work: developing the agents themselves. Managers must give them relevant context, tune their performance and determine what they can safely handle. “I spend 70% of my time training it and 30% of my time using it,” he said. events.title: Trump says he doesn't want Iran deal as U.S. reportedly prepares for 'massive bombing'
events.summary: The U.S. president and his national security team have discussed possibly resuming large-scale U.S. military operations in the coming weeks, NBC News reported. Trump has seen his approval ratings fall to a record low amid concerns over high living costs spurred by soaring gasoline and diesel prices. Crude oil prices have remained elevated even as Middle East exports have been recovering to near prewar levels, according to Kpler. U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he no longer wants a deal with Iran, following reports that the U.S. military is preparing for possible strikes against the country, likely before the midterm elections. "I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop," Trump said at a campaign rally with Republican candidates in San Antonio late Wednesday stateside. Steve Witkoff, the U.S. special envoy to the Middle East, has been working on the deal and "doing very well," Trump added. The U.S. president and his national security team have discussed possibly resuming large-scale U.S. military operations in the coming weeks, NBC News reported Wednesday, citing a U.S. official and another person with knowledge of the talks. Axios reported earlier in the day that a possible resumption in armed conflict could include "massive bombing" of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, adding that military aggression could influence the outcome of the upcoming midterm elections. Earlier this week, Trump said the biggest problem for Washington was that nobody knew who was running Iran during the talks to end the conflict. Iranian officials rejected those claims, saying "the problem is actually the opposite." Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, pointed to the "contradictory positions and mixed messaging from U.S. officials." Crude oil prices have remained elevated even as Middle East exports have been recovering to near prewar levels, according to Kpler. Combined crude volumes exiting the Gulf, excluding Iran, plus volumes from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, were around pre-conflict levels of 18.5 million barrels per day. "Normalisation no longer needs to wait for a deal," said Matt Wright, lead freight analyst at Kpler, forecasting "slower, uneven normalisation" under continued conflict, with traffic recovering through operational adaptation rather than waiting for a diplomatic trigger.

events.title: Bid to run new trains on West Coast Mainline refused
events.summary: The West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, Stephanie Tobyn, from the Office of Rail and Road said Plans for new train services between London and Wrexham, Rochdale and Blackpool have been rejected by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR). The proposal to add more trains on the West Coast Main Line would "likely increase delays and cancelled trains for passengers", the regulator said. It rejected Wrexham, Shropshire and Midlands Railway's application for four daily Wrexham to London Euston return services, as well as Lumo's proposal for up to four return services between Rochdale and Euston on weekdays and Saturdays, and three on Sundays. Avanti West Coast's plans for additional services between Blackpool and Euston were also denied by the ORR. The regulator said: "Gaps in the current timetable need to provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers. "ORR concluded that adding more services into these windows in the timetable for recovery would reduce that resilience, increasing the risk of disruption spreading to other services and affecting more passengers." Stephanie Tobyn, from the ORR, said: "New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. "But the West Coast Main Line is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. "Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers." The ORR said its assessment and decision came after similar applications were rejected in 2025. events.title: My parents are getting older, but they've done a lot to prepare. Being honest and upfront has been the most helpful.
events.summary: The author's parents have taken helpful steps to prepare for their future. Westend61/Getty Images My husband and I are now firmly in the sandwich generation. Our attention is often split between our kids and our parents. However, our parents have taken steps to make this transitional time a bit easier. On a recent Tuesday, I received three text messages in a row: two from my daughter and one from my dad. For many of us, this is our everyday — sandwiched between our parents and our kids, and suddenly balancing both. Our parents are navigating big life transitions. So are our kids. In this sandwich generation , with little time and a lot on our plates, here are a few things our parents have done that have really helped our family navigate this tricky time of life. We're clear on our parents' wishes It goes without saying: this is new territory for everyone. Safety, stability, and continuous modifications have been themes my husband and I have prioritized as our parents enter this next chapter. Both sets of our parents have set up and periodically update wills and trusts ; they have their important documents in order. Having lawyer contacts and power of attorney has helped my husband and me, and our siblings know whom to contact in an emergency and which specific procedures to follow. While we can't predict the future or prevent emergencies, we can plan and prepare, so we're not operating in crisis mode — even if it is one. Carving out time to talk in advance helps everyone. It helps adult kids when parents' personal planning — for living arrangements or housing , care, and end-of-life wishes — can serve as a handy road map to follow, even if it's incomplete. As the oldest child, my 80-year-old dad made me the executor of his will about 10 years ago. We went to the bank, signed the papers, and then went to lunch. While it was weirdly emotional, I'm glad it's taken care of. In a way, it felt like he was still taking care of us, so that we can take good care of him. Knowing family medical history has been helpful Knowing ahead of time, especially as we adult children enter into our 40s and later, what medical conditions or health predispositions run in the family has also been helpful. Having a list of family members, too, who have struggled with or died from certain illnesses, chronic conditions, and other medical challenges has allowed us to keep up our own care, as we care for our own children. For example, I've been getting regular mammograms at an early age since breast cancer runs in our family, which gives me peace of mind. We have all their important accounts and information Our parents have given us all their personal information, knowing we won't look at it unless necessary. Having a list of important accounts and passwords ahead of time means we don't have to scramble mid-crisis. Nobody wants a scavenger hunt in an emergency. A password manager has really helped us with this. Our parents have their own accounts set up in a certain way. Taking time to talk through their systems is a technical and emotionally heavy lift, but it can benefit everyone in the long run. Our parents have told us what to do with special items Our families have many important historical items and artifacts, and we've learned which should be placed with a historical society. My in-laws created a detailed list, complete with pictures, dates, and the family significance of each item. This will come in handy — it's great to know where special pieces of furniture and family heirlooms need to be placed, and it's also helpful for our own kids, as a way to feel connected to generations of their family. Prioritizing honesty has been key While all these preparations have given us peace of mind, their honesty has been the most helpful thing of all. This might not work in all family situations, but having honest conversations about next steps has been crucial for us. Being kept in the loop, with our parents clearly articulating their needs, wants, and desires, has been such a gift. With our parents in their 80s, now is the time for clear and open communication. Carving out time to talk in advance , while difficult, has helped us to ease us all through this tender time. Whether it's in person, by phone, or via FaceTime, we have made a concerted effort to set aside time to process vulnerable topics together. We've also made time to have frank discussions with our teen and tween kids about their grandparents and this time of life. We've shared openly about how we've planned for them and their future. We might feel squeezed in this sandwich, as it's new territory for everyone. Our aging parents are shifting their mindset from being providers to receiving help, and we are helping to support them, while also managing our kids. It's delicate for all involved, but having time to talk about the hard things and share special memories can help everyone. Read the original article on Business Insider
