events.title: Russian attack on buses in Ukraine’s Kramatorsk kills at least 30 people
events.summary: Eighteen people were wounded in the Russian attack on city in eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region, local authorities say. A Russian attack on two buses has killed at least 30 people and wounded 18 others in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk, near the front line, authorities said. The local prosecutor’s office on Thursday posted photos of bodies and debris strewn across a road in front of the burning metal shell of a bus. list 1 of 3 Trapped in occupied Oleshky: Ukrainians face hunger, drones and landmines list 2 of 3 Ukraine says Russian drone attack sinks ship in Romanian waters list 3 of 3 Ukraine launches major drone attack on Russia’s Moscow region, killing two Police said the attack took place on a street where two city ⁠buses were operating at the time. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it as a bus stop. The Donetsk governor accused Russia of “deliberately targeting civilians”. “For them [the Russians], a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible,” Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram. Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb. There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022. Kramatorsk is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as part of Russia. It has been a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of Moscow’s war and is part of the so-called “fortress belt” that troops are fighting to keep hold of. Russian forces have edged close to the city’s eastern edge, which has prompted calls for civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine. Kramatorsk City Council said it was “yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population”. “Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets,” it added. Elsewhere in Ukraine, the death toll from Wednesday’s Russian missile attack on a residential building in the city of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region rose to 22 , including five children, Governor Vyacheslav Chaus said in a statement on Telegram. President Zelenskyy said a cruise missile directly hit the building in Pryluky, about 150km (93 miles) east of the capital, Kyiv. Meanwhile, in Russia, a drone caused a fire at a data centre belonging to Russian technology company Yandex, the firm told the AFP news agency on Thursday. Unverified images published on social media showed columns of thick, black smoke pouring from the roof of the building, which the company said was in the central Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with some of the latest Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses. The former head of Ukraine’s Centre for Countering Disinformation said Kyiv was responsible for the strike on the Yandex facility, writing on Telegram: “Two can play at this game”. The firm is Russia’s largest technology company. Often dubbed “Russia’s Google”, Yandex runs the country’s most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and ride-hailing application used by tens of millions of people across the Russian-speaking world.

events.title: 5 traders jailed for rigging key interest rates have their convictions quashed
events.summary: A British court has quashed the convictions of five traders accused of manipulating benchmark interest rates, in a scandal stemming from the 2008 financial crisis LONDON -- A British court on Wednesday quashed the convictions of five traders accused of manipulating benchmark interest rates in one of the biggest banking scandals to come out of the 2008 global financial crisis . The Court of Appeal threw out the fraud convictions of former Barclays employees Jonathan Mathew, Jay Merchant, Alex Pabon, Philippe Moryoussef and Colin Bermingham. The five were sentenced between 2016 and 2019 for offenses connected to influencing the London Inter-Bank Offered Rate, or Libor, and its euro currency equivalent Euribor. The rates were used to set the interest rates on trillions of dollars of financial products around the world. In July 2025, the U.K. Supreme Court quashed the convictions of two other traders: Tom Hayes, a former Citigroup and UBS trader, and Carlo Palombo, who worked for Barclays. It ruled that the convictions were unfair because the judges in their separate cases gave inaccurate instructions to jurors. Lawyers for the five others argued that juries in their cases received almost identical instructions and therefore “their trials were unfair and their convictions are unsafe.” The U.K.’s Serious Fraud Office said it would not seek retrials for Hayes and Palombo and did not oppose the five other defendants' appeals. They were based on figures submitted daily by major international banks, reporting the rate at which they could borrow money from other banks. During the financial crisis, regulators became aware that some banks were making artificially low Libor submissions to make their institutions seem more creditworthy, or submitting fake numbers to achieve a rate that better suited them. The Serious Fraud Office began investigating alleged efforts to manipulate Libor in 2012. That ultimately led to the conviction of nine bankers and the acquittal of 11 others. The rates were phased out in recent years, in part because they were seen as worsening the financial crisis. events.title: Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decade
events.summary: Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for change Tesco lifts profit forecast and says shoppers are resilient T hey may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade. This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – had held merger talks between last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away. News of the potential deal has relaunched speculation that the UK grocery market is now ripe for consolidation and revealed that the Sainsbury’s boss, Simon Roberts – who has been in post for six years – is at least willing to consider the possibility of buying one of his troubled rivals. Sainsbury’s, which has 600 supermarkets and almost 900 convenience stores, has until recently been seen as wary of trying to revive merger talks with its rivals after its bid to buy Asda for £7bn in 2019 was blocked . However, industry experts say Asda and Morrisons’ owners have held informal talks with each other – and both with Sainsbury’s team – and predict that talks could restart. “The three of them, one way or another, are talking to each other,” one said. He suggested that a combination of Asda and Morrisons could happen but was likely to be a weaker deal than a Sainsbury’s takeover of either, as both businesses struggle with costs and interest on debt piles. The industry has undergone significant change since the collapse of the Sainsbury’s-Asda deal. While riding the wider retail trends towards online shopping and convenience stores, the supermarket groups have been jockeying for market share. Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with less than 1 percentage point separating them. Aldi is rapidly opening stores while Asda has struggled to find growth since a £6.8bn, debt-fuelled takeover in 2020 and heavy price competition from the discounters and from its bigger rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s. Another big change could emerge this month when the UK’s competition watchdog is due to publish its final ruling on whether Aldi and Lidl should now officially be classified as “large grocery retailers” like Tesco , Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons. In August, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it had found provisionally that Aldi and Lidl no longer qualified as “limited assortment discounters” as they now carry a “full range” of groceries and operate stores larger than 1,000 sq m (10,700 sq ft) across the UK. The change means the German-owned discounters are now taken into account when assessing competition in different locations. This is the strongest hint yet that the CMA has changed its stance blocking the Sainsbury’s buyout of Asda on the basis that shoppers would be worse off. It also indicates that the CMA’s “balance of competition” – its estimation of the impact of a deal based on drive times for customers around stores – has shifted, meaning Sainsbury’s might have to dispose of dozens fewer stores to gain regulatory clearance for a merger. A figure of 150 was suggested when it tried to buy Asda. Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital and Sainsbury’s broker, says the CMA preliminary ruling indicates “the shape of the pitch has adjusted a little” and “the change encourages another chapter of consolidation”. It is a step-change from 2019 when analysts accused the singing former Sainsbury’s boss Mike Coupe and his board of directors of “arrogance” and “folly” for pursuing Asda. Now they say that consolidation is almost inevitable. That comes amid what is seen as a more welcoming regulatory environment backed by the UK government’s growth agenda combined with the appointment of Doug Gurr, a grocery industry veteran who has spent time at Asda and Amazon, to lead the CMA. One analyst described Sainsbury’s as the “kingmaker” in any industry consolidation as it uniquely has the resources to snap up a rival without the market dominance to immediately prevent any deal. Analysts agree it is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy Morrisons or Asda – Tesco is too big to buy a rival , while Marks & Spencer and Waitrose appear unlikely to have the financial firepower or desire to pursue such a deal. Amazon should not be ruled out as a player in consolidation, according to one analyst, who said the online specialist might be prompted into action by any of the supermarkets announcing plans to merge. “The last cards are coming on to the table,” he said, suggesting that Amazon might consider buying Asda, Morrisons or even Sainsbury’s, now that it had effectively disposed of Argos which may have caused competition concerns for Amazon. However, Amazon has not fared well with its dip into high street retail.

events.title: StarHub to acquire MyRepublic’s mobile business amid ongoing telco consolidation
events.summary: The acquisition will have no impact on MyRepublic’s mobile service customers, who are being progressively migrated to StarHub’s network. StarHub will acquire MyRepublic’s mobile business and move its 4G customers from M1’s network to StarHub’s network. MyRepublic mobile customers will keep the brand, while StarHub gains both broadband and mobile businesses after buying broadband in August 2026. The deal supports telco consolidation in Singapore, as smaller players face falling revenue and stronger price competition, with StarHub calling for more scale to invest in networks. SINGAPORE – StarHub said on Oct 8 that it will acquire MyRepublic’s mobile business. The value of the transaction is not fixed, but is dependent on the total 4G and 5G MyRepublic mobile subscribers, average revenue per user (ARPU) of active 4G and 5G subscribers, as well as subscriber lifetime. The transaction is expected to be completed by April 30, 2027. In addition to the transaction value, a bonus cash amount of $1 million will be paid by StarHub when 25,000 subscribers migrate from MyRepublic’s network to StarHub’s network. An additional $1 million will be paid when 50,000 subscribers migrate to StarHub’s network by March 14, 2027. MyRepublic’s mobile business attained a net profit of $2.4 million for the 12 months ended June 30, with about 85,000 active subscribers. MyRepublic’s blended ARPU stood at $13 per month. This follows an earlier agreement between the two parties to migrate all of the mobile virtual network operator’s (MVNO) 4G mobile customers from M1’s network – which MyRepublic mobile ran on – to StarHub’s mobile network. “The acquisition brings together complementary strengths while preserving the distinct MyRepublic mobile brand and proposition for customers,” said StarHub in a bourse filing. StarHub will then own both MyRepublic’s broadband and mobile businesses, having acquired the broadband business in August 2026. As Singapore’s digital needs continue to grow, the acquisition will allow greater scale to be directed towards sustained network investment, service innovation and customer experience, StarHub noted. In a statement to The Straits Times on Oct 8, StarHub said: “MyRepublic Mobile will retain its brand and offerings, with customers continuing on their existing plans and services without disruption. “There will be no workforce reductions arising from the acquisition.” At an earnings briefing in August for the first half of 2026, StarHub chief executive Nikhil Eapen said he expects smaller MVNOs to be bought by larger players as the industry consolidates. “There’s a natural progression in which MVNOs will gravitate (around) and then be absorbed and adopted by the large, well-capitalised players,” he noted. Analysts have long pushed for a consolidation of Singapore’s telco industry amid falling mobile revenue and ARPU. Mobile service revenue for StarHub fell 10.5% year on year to $245.3 million in the first half of the year ended June 30, from $274.1 million. StarHub’s underlying net profit, excluding Ensign, fell 76.1% to $12.4 million, from $51.9 million the year before, said CGS International analyst Prem Jearajasingam. Singtel Singapore’s first-quarter operating revenue fell 3.1% year on year to $901 million, from $929 million. Singtel attributed the dip to “continued intense price competition”. StarHub, in particular, has been “driving consolidation”, said Eapen in August. In addition to the consolidation of MyRepublic’s mobile customers, StarHub recently migrated customers from MVNO redOne to its budget brand, eight. More recently in September, both StarHub and Keppel confirmed that they are in talks over a potential deal involving M1 . “With ongoing consolidation, we are bringing greater scale to invest more effectively in the networks, resilience and innovation that Singapore will increasingly depend on,” said Eapen. events.title: I spent 3 days with pharma executives. They're suddenly taking longevity seriously.
events.summary: Pharma executives, scientists, and founders agree: this is THE aging conference to attend. Hilary Brueck/BI Longevity drugmakers gathered in Boston last weekend for their annual shindig. For the first time, the FDA showed up too. Longevity isn't a bad word in the pharma world anymore; it's an investment imperative. For decades, " longevity" was a word serious drug makers avoided. It conjured images of supplement gurus, Silicon Valley biohackers , and anti-aging hucksters — not legitimate medicines backed by clinical trials. That shifted last weekend. The 2026 Aging Research and Drug Discovery (ARDD) meeting — the most important longevity conference of the year — landed in the US. After more than a decade in Europe, it was held in Boston, the center of the US biotech industry. US regulators, executives from big pharma, and longevity upstarts came together for three days to discuss how drugs to combat age-related declines could become a reality, sooner rather than later. Executives from major drugmakers, including Pfizer, GSK, AstraZeneca, Novartis, and Eli Lilly , enthusiastically discussed their approach to "longevity drugs." "We think it's an important space to be in, because that's where the patients are going to be," Eli Lilly's associate vice president of healthy aging, Thomas Marron, said at the 13th annual conference, which was held for the first time this year with leaders from the US Food and Drug Administration joining the conversation. There was a breathlessness in the air, a can-you-believe-this tone from the longevity researchers who've spent their careers studying how we age, but hit a wall when it came to formulating actual therapies. Could their dreams of a future longevity pill be coming true? ARDD attendees were a mix of drugmakers, scientists, doctors, founders, and investors. The pharmaceutical contingent is growing. Donis Perkins for ARDD A couple of years ago, scientists were still arguing over whether aging was a disease, and lamenting that the FDA didn't have an approval pathway built for them. Now, they're starting to build the frameworks and discuss the data that the FDA will need to review to assess whether their longevity drugs can work. Here's what everyone was buzzing about on the ground. Panic is setting in about our aging population Wealthy countries are going gray. Governments around the world are panicking, including in the US. "The basic idea is to move medicine away from asking 'what disease does this person have?' towards asking 'what is this person still capable of doing, and how do we measure it?'" said Andrew Brack, program manager for the federal government's $144 million healthy aging and longevity drug trial initiative, started in 2024, called PROactive Solutions for Prolonging Resilience (PROSPR). Pharmaceutical companies are realizing they need to adjust their strategy to address aging patients who increasingly want preventative therapies that will keep them agile, able, and sharp for years to come. Why chase fixes for diseases that develop through the course of decades, when you could use all those years to preserve health and function instead? New blood tests can now measure aging in real time (kind of) New blood tests aim to measure aging in the body, assessing the health of internal organs. Stefania Pelfini la Waziya/Getty Images Until recently, we didn't have a good way to measure whether a drug was actually slowing down aging, in real time. New blood tests — often called biological age or organ "clocks" — are giving researchers a way to estimate whether someone's blood vessels, skin, heart, or entire body is aging slower or faster than expected. There are also new genetic screening tools that can identify our unique vulnerabilities to diseases like Alzheimer's and sensitivities to different foods or medicines. All of this new bloodwork is moving regulators and drugmakers towards a potential action plan for aging, as prevention becomes the preferred approach in healthcare and wearables become routine for tracking steps, heart rate, and sleep scores. In a historic move, the FDA took the stage on the first day of the conference, promising to release new clinical trial guidance next year. "We're the umpire and not the coach," FDA clinical pharmacologist Justin Penzenstadler said on stage at the conference, encouraging longevity drugmakers to come together and agree on how to design trials and present data. "You guys work out the cookbook." The Ozempic boom changed the game Can GLP-1s slow down aging? Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk are testing the idea. Viktoriya Skorikova/Getty Images Finally, there are new medicines showing signs they could help slow aging in humans, not just mice or dogs. Chief among them: the blockbuster GLP-1 drugs from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk. Both drugmakers presented data at ARDD this year on how their injectable weight loss drugs may slow aging, using blood test data. Lilly found that tirzepatide (sold as Zepbound and Mounjaro) may slow down aging in many internal organs, especially the heart, brain, liver, and kidneys. Novo's data was more impressive. The company analyzed blood samples from over 10,000 patients in semaglutide trials (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) over several years. Compared to people not on the drug, people on semaglutide saw their heart age drop 2 to 4 years, while their kidney, brain, lung, and pancreas ages decreased an extra 1 to 4 years. ARDD attendees mingled over lunches of chicken, salmon, and tofu, all served with whole grains and vegetables on the side. Donis Perkins for ARDD Regulators will need to see much more than this early data to approve a new drug for aging. The big question remains: can these GLP-1s be beneficial for people without diabetes or obesity? A new PROSPR longevity trial, funded earlier this year, aims to answer that question by giving healthy older adults semaglutide prescriptions and seeing what happens. Ultimately, researchers want to know if the drugs can functionally improve a person's overall health as they age. The financial opportunity is huge The payoff for improving human longevity ranges from big to enormous, depending on how you define the category. Bankers at TD Securities put the current longevity market at over $250 billion, including fitness, mobility, nutrition, lifestyle, and screening tests, a figure that doesn't account for the $560 billion-plus market for traditional age-related disease care, including cardiology, cancer, and neurodegenerative health. HSBC private bank thinks even bigger, imagining that healthcare advances like new drugs, coupled with more healthy years of labor force participation, could add up to a longevity-fueled "12.5 trillion global GDP uplift" by 2050. Any way you stack it, the opportunity is huge and growing. McKinley Carter Wealth Services CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list, now in its eighth year, recognizes the best financial advisors and top firms. Howland Capital Management, based in Boston, is CNBC's top-ranked firm for 2026. CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 methodology considers assets under management, years in business, regulatory and compliance records, firm size, and the number of investment advisors, among other factors. CNBC receives no compensation for placing advisory firms on the Financial Advisor 100 list. Many consumers face tough investing decisions amid rising inflation , the artificial intelligence boom and geopolitical uncertainty , among other factors that affect the stock and bond markets. An experienced financial advisor can help. But the best advisors do more than manage your portfolio . They can help craft a roadmap to meet competing goals such as saving for retirement , reducing your taxes , protecting your family , building a legacy and more. CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list ranks the country's best financial advisors and top financial advisory firms. Investors can use this list as a starting point — along with referrals — to find an expert who is well-suited for their family's needs. To make a list of prospective advisors, always verify credentials and check for complaints via the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority's BrokerCheck or the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission 's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure . Then you can interview your short list of candidates. CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list is determined through a blend of data analysis and editorial review. Firms do not apply or pay to be considered, and inclusion and ranking are based solely on the list's methodology. The list takes months to compile, with multiple steps and checks designed to ensure rigor and consistency. To prepare the 2026 list, CNBC worked with AccuPoint Solutions, a wealth management data and research firm specializing in advisor intelligence and industry analytics. The process started with 41,578 registered investment advisor firms, or RIAs, narrowed to 1,015 that met CNBC's requirements. These firms also passed a due diligence check, including any regulatory disclosures. To get more details, CNBC surveyed the finalists about their practices and fact-checked responses via publicly available resources. AccuPoint used CNBC's weighted criteria to rank the firms. Read more about the methodology below. For 2026, CNBC's top advisors collectively manage $329.7 billion. The firms have an average of 35 years in business. What is a fiduciary financial advisor? Finding the right financial advisor isn't easy, and there's a key question you should ask each prospect: Are you a fiduciary? A fiduciary financial advisor must act in the best interest of clients at all times, regardless of how it affects their compensation or profits. Certain financial advisors, such as RIAs, are bound by the fiduciary standard . By comparison, investment brokers must follow a suitability standard , which means recommendations must be appropriate but not always the best option for the client. What steps should you take when choosing a financial advisor? One of the first steps to finding the right financial advisor could be referrals from your colleagues, friends or family. You'll want to consider those candidates' credentials, including designations such as certified financial planner , or CFP; certified public accountant , or CPA; and chartered financial analyst , or CFA. You should also check each prospect for regulatory violations and customer complaints, known as "disclosures," via FINRA's BrokerCheck and the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure website. You can check state regulators for smaller firms. It's important to meet and interview prospective candidates before choosing a financial advisor. The CFP Board, which sets and enforces standards for CFP professionals, recommends 10 questions to narrow down your list: 1. What are your qualifications and credentials? 2. What services do you offer? 3. Will you have a fiduciary duty to me? 4. What is your approach to financial planning? 5. What types of clients do you typically work with? 6. Will you be the only advisor working with me? 7. How will I pay for your services? 8. How much do you typically charge? 9. Do others stand to gain from the financial advice you give me? 10. Have you ever been publicly disciplined for unethical or unlawful actions in your career?

events.title: The fight to uncover the Nigerian president’s FBI files
events.summary: The News Nigeria’s president is locked in a fierce reelection battle — one that is not just playing out among voters ahead of January polls, but pitting teams of lawyers and lobbyists against a lone litigant half a world away in California. Remarkably, this latter-day David just won a significant victory over Goliath. For three years, Bola Tinubu has fought to keep old FBI records tied to a 1990s Chicago drug probe about him sealed, hiring US lawyers to support the Justice Department in the fight. His main adversary is not a political rival or a diaspora activist, however. It’s a Freedom of Information Act litigant in California with no apparent connection to Nigeria who says he just wants to get to the truth. Tinubu’s efforts to prevent disclosure have partly failed. In August, the FBI acknowledged for the first time that it holds an investigative file on him and alongside the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has released hundreds of pages of partially redacted records. The fight now underway is over whether that is enough. On one side is Tinubu’s team of US attorneys, led by Chicago firm Henderson Parks. On the other is Aaron Greenspan, founder of legal document website PlainSite, who argues more documents should be released, with fewer redactions. The FBI declined to comment on this story. The DEA did not respond to requests for comment. Know More The case centers around an alleged heroin trafficking network run from Nigeria: A 1993 affidavit drafted by an Internal Revenue Service agent describes the scheme, and cites an associate of the narcotics-selling group as saying the network’s ringleader — allegedly Mueez Adegboyega Akande, a businessman who had returned to Nigeria in 1990 — directed its finances by phone and periodic US trips — and that Tinubu helped move money for him. In the 1990s, Nigerian rings often trafficked drugs from Southeast Asia to Chicago via couriers, according to the Justice Department . The Nigerian president has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. And his links to the case have been known and partially reported within Nigeria, often in the run-up to elections where opponents have used it to raise questions about his past. But the latest release — though unlikely to materially affect the results of the upcoming election — once again concentrates attention on Tinubu’s time in the US. A young Tinubu first arrived in Chicago in the 1970s to study accounting, graduating in 1979. By the time of the alleged scheme at the center of this case, he split time between Lagos and the US, having risen to treasurer at Mobil Oil Nigeria, and eventually winning a seat in Nigeria’s Senate — all while still opening bank accounts, and moving “large” amounts of money in the Chicago metro area, according to the IRS affidavit. Bank records cited show Tinubu went on to deposit nearly $1.9 million in Chicago-area accounts in 1990 and 1991. Tinubu’s then-employers at Mobil Oil told investigators his treasurer role did not involve moving large sums and that the company never authorized him to hold its funds personally. US authorities said that several of the transactions were linked to the alleged drug-trafficking ringleader Akande and seized roughly $460,000 from accounts tied to Tinubu in a 1993 civil forfeiture, alleging that the money was likely the laundered proceeds of drug dealing. Tinubu was not criminally charged, and the case was dismissed with prejudice after the money was forfeited. Tinubu’s US lawyers have argued that the latest files that Greenspan wants released are shielded by FOIA exemptions that protect against “an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.” In a filing, the lawyers said that curiosity about a foreign leader’s background was not a FOIA-protected interest, and described Greenspan’s requests as driven by Nigerian politics rather than by an effort to expose US agency misconduct. They also said the records concern Tinubu’s life as a private “student” who “should retain his full privacy interests because he was not a public official in 1993.” However, Tinubu was not a student in 1993 — he had graduated over a decade earlier — and he was, in fact, a public official for most of that year, serving in Nigeria’s Senate until November. Greenspan protested the inaccuracies in subsequent filings, and Tinubu’s team later recanted the claims. In a statement to Semafor, Henderson Parks attorney Christopher Carmichael argued that commentary on the case had outpaced the facts: “Interested persons and parties are attempting to infer what they believe may be in undisclosed records, but that is speculation.” He said Tinubu’s team would not speculate on non-public records while the FOIA case was pending. Tinubu’s aides have long presented the 1993 case as a closed civil matter. In a July statement, presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga called it “a civil forfeiture case from 1993 — a matter long settled, with no criminal conviction or finding of guilt ,” and added that the issue had been “thoroughly litigated, explained, and rendered moot” by Tinubu’s electoral victories. Representing himself, Greenspan said in an interview with Semafor that he had no personal or national stake in Nigerian politics and had kept his distance from partisans on both sides. He is not new to protracted fights with well-resourced opponents: A Los Angeles-area tech entrepreneur, Greenspan has spent years trading lawsuits with Elon Musk and Tesla, often alone and against larger legal teams. When a lobbyist for former Nigerian Vice President Atiku Abubakar — an electoral opponent of Tinubu — filed an amicus brief, Greenspan sought to make clear that the two were not working together. The case has been a political flashpoint in Nigeria for years, flaring up ahead of the 2023 election that brought Tinubu to office and again now with the 2027 vote fast approaching. An organization retained by the Nigerian government has targeted Greenspan online . Another of Tinubu’s main opponents called it “profoundly embarrassing” that Tinubu was asking a foreign court to withhold his records. Nonetheless, there are doubts about whether the matter is viewed as important by voters. Much like Tinubu’s presidential tenure, the campaign has been dominated by conversations around economic tumult and insecurity. “It is unlikely to impact [voters’] decision,” said Ebenezer Obadare, an analyst with the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington, “though the situation might change if a highly damaging piece of information unavailable previously were to suddenly turn up.” Notable One of Europe’s most wanted criminals is using close ties to Sierra Leone’s first family to transform the West African country into a hub for his drug dealing empire . Questions over Tinubu’s background persist, with critics citing educational records that have shifted from his initial campaigns to present day.

events.title: How much does France spend on education compared with the rest of Europe?
events.summary: Amid student protests, Al Jazeera visualises how French spending stacks up against defence and healthcare. French high school students have been protesting for more than two weeks over conditions in schools, including overcrowded classrooms and staff shortages, and they show no sign of stopping. The unrest began on September 21 when pupils blockaded a school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, and within a week, their protest had spread across the country with students and police clashing violently. On September 29 , the demonstrations coincided with a nationwide public sector strike, in which teachers joined other state workers against a proposed pay freeze. More than 6,100 people have since been arrested. With the government under pressure to rein in spending as its debt rises, Al Jazeera looks at how much France invests in education, how it compares with the rest of Europe and how it measures up against what the country spends on healthcare and defence. How much does France spend on schooling? According to the latest data from Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency, France’s public spending on education amounts to 5.1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP). That figure does not include private spending, such as school fees paid by families. The French Ministry of National Education uses a broader measure, known as domestic expenditure on education, which counts all the money that goes into education, whether from the state, local authorities, businesses or households. As well as teaching, it covers adult and continuing training and related costs such as school meals, boarding and transport. By this measure, France spent 199.2 billion euros ($223bn) on education in 2025, equivalent to 6.7 percent of its GDP and 2.4 billion euros more than in 2024, according to provisional ministry figures. Spending has more than doubled since 1980, even after accounting for inflation. But the economy has grown too, so education spending’s share of GDP is lower today than it was in the mid-1990s. Secondary education accounted for the largest share of spending at 73.7 billion euros (37 percent), followed by primary education at 60 billion euros (30 percent), higher education at 45.6 billion euros (23 percent) and adult and continuing education at 19.7 billion euros (10 percent), according to the National Education Ministry. How much do other European countries spend on education? Among European countries, Sweden spends the largest share of its GDP on education at 7.3 percent in 2024, followed by Iceland (7 percent) and Belgium, Estonia and Finland (6.3 percent each), according to Eurostat. The lowest spenders are Ireland (2.7 percent), Greece (3.9 percent), Romania and Italy (4 percent each), and the United Kingdom and Spain (4.1 percent each). At 5.1 percent, France is joint 13th, level with the Netherlands and Slovakia, and above the EU average of 4.8 percent. But above-average spending has not shielded France from a problem affecting much of the developed world. Teacher shortages are growing across countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, according to the OECD’s latest Education at a Glance report. Rather than leaving posts empty, many countries are filling them with teachers who lack full qualifications. In the 2024-2025 school year, 9 percent of primary and secondary teachers across the OECD were not fully qualified. In France, the strain is most visible in secondary schools. About 11 percent of secondary teachers are not fully qualified, compared with less than 3 percent in primary schools. Furthermore, lower secondary classes average 26 pupils, compared with 23 across the OECD. That echoes what pupils have been saying during the latest protests : Classes are large, and absent teachers are not being replaced. Some also described dilapidated buildings, a shortage of tables and chairs and, in some schools, rodent infestations. The intense heatwaves that hit France this year exacerbated existing problems in neglected buildings, many of which have no air conditioning, students said. Teachers also feel undervalued. Only 4 percent said their profession is valued in society, the lowest share of any country surveyed and far below the OECD average of 22 percent. Historical UNESCO data showed France’s education spending slipped from 5.5 percent of GDP in 2017 to 5.3 percent in 2022 although it remained the ninth-highest among 29 European countries with data. A brief rise to 5.7 percent in 2020 reflected the pandemic shrinking the economy, not extra spending. France was one of 14 countries where the share fell. Norway and Denmark saw the steepest drops while Slovakia, Slovenia, Lithuania and the Czech Republic recorded the biggest rises. What else are these nations spending on?

events.title: Republicans squirm as Latino support slips in South Texas
events.summary: Republicans are in a dogfight to defend the Latino gains that had them dreaming of a lasting political realignment just two years ago. Why it matters: Nowhere is that reversal of fortune more visible than in South Texas, where President Trump ran up historic numbers in 2024 — and Republicans redrew the map in 2025, assuming those Latino gains would last. Trump won 55% of Texas Latino voters in 2024 exit polls, carried 14 of the 18 counties within 20 miles of the border and won all four Rio Grande Valley counties. Polling shows Trump's disapproval ratings have skyrocketed among Latinos in Texas since 2024. Democrats and allied groups are now pouring money into races across the Rio Grande Valley. Zoom in: The reversal is starkest in TX-15, where Rep. Monica De La Cruz was one of the GOP's most visible symbols of its South Texas breakthrough. Trump would have carried the newly-drawn district by 18 percentage points in 2024. De La Cruz won her 2024 race under the previous map by 14 points. Cook Political Report moved the race from Lean Republican to Toss Up on Sept. 25, saying public and private polling shows the race tied or even favoring Tejano singer and Democrat Bobby Pulido . By the numbers: Democratic campaigns and allied groups are outspending Republican campaigns and groups on Spanish-language ads in two of the three competitive House districts covering the Rio Grande Valley, according to AdImpact data reported by the Texas Tribune . In TX-34, held by Vicente Gonzalez (D), Democratic campaigns and groups have spent $2.7 million on Spanish-language ads, compared with $1.6 million on the Republican side. In TX-15, Democratic groups have spent more than twice as much as Republican groups on Spanish-language ads. TX-28 bucks the trend: Republicans have narrowly outspent Democrats on Spanish-language ads to unseat Henry Cuellar (D). Zoom out: TX-34 is also a Toss Up, while TX-28 is Lean Democratic. The newly redrawn TX-35 has moved from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. House Majority PAC launched another round of ads Tuesday in TX-15, TX-28 and TX-34, defending two Democratic incumbents while continuing to target De La Cruz. The bottom line: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll shows Latinos nationally favor Democratic control of Congress 59%-35%, a 24-point advantage — roughly double the margin the same poll found for Democrats in 2024. A recent TelevisaUnivision poll found Latino voters in the three competitive Texas House districts shifting from a 44%-44% split in their 2024 presidential vote to 56%-36% Democratic on the 2026 congressional ballot.

events.title: Why we’re watching these climate tech companies
events.summary: This week, we released our 2026 version of our Climate Tech Companies to Watch list. It’s an annual project that the MIT Technology Review team puts together. Our goal is to highlight some of the promising, interesting advances and firms we think are worth paying attention to in the world of climate and energy technology. The list is always a little ray of hope for me—there are some fascinating ideas out there for changing how we power our world or moving away from fossil fuels to reduce the greenhouse-gas emissions that cause climate change.  Our chosen companies tend to reflect several aspects of the current moment. Here are some of the companies we picked and the key themes worth highlighting.  China is the center of the climate and energy tech world Forgive me—I know I’ve made this point before. Feel free to call me Captain Obvious. But I think China’s dominance in energy technology is a global trend that bears repeated mentioning.   China is home to the world’s largest grid, and renewables are coming online more quickly than I can wrap my head around. Contributing to that boom is Envision Energy , a renewables giant appearing on our list for the second time. The company has installed over 100 gigawatts of wind power worldwide, as well as over 50 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. Like many other Chinese companies right now, Envision is looking beyond the crowded Chinese market and setting its sights abroad, with projects in Germany, Brazil, and Australia and upcoming work in Vietnam. China is also leading innovation in key technologies. I’ve been fascinated by the potential for next-generation batteries coming out of its companies: All the big ones, along with a host of smaller ones, are racing to develop solid-state batteries. They could be both safer than existing EV batteries and longer in range. WeLion New Energy is particularly interesting. The battery company announced a big lab result last year, achieving 824 watt-hours per kilogram—more than three times the energy density of a standard lithium-ion battery today. Lab results in battery research are notoriously difficult to scale, but WeLion is also working to deploy semi-solid-state batteries, which could come to fruition faster than purely solid-state cells while still improving on lithium-ion’s performance. Everybody wants a piece of the data center pie We included just three companies from the US on the list, and two of them have received a major boost from Big Tech as companies look to power data centers. (The third, Brimstone , is leaning into another political hot topic, critical minerals.) Technologies that can provide consistent power are in high demand. Fervo Energy is bringing next-generation geothermal power to the grid by using horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to make it practical in more places. The company went public in May, raising $2.2 billion in its IPO, and plans to have a gigawatt’s worth of plants operational by the end of 2030. X-energy is building helium-cooled small modular nuclear reactors. The reactors’ small size lends flexibility, and the company is currently working on a 320-megawatt cluster of them in collaboration with Amazon in Richland, Washington. (For what it’s worth, I’m interested in what this technology could do for industrial facilities—the company has a deal with Dow that could see it deployed at one of the company’s chemical plants in the early 2030s.) The grid needs support, and energy storage will be a key piece moving forward I know, I know—I haven’t stopped talking about batteries since I started writing this newsletter four years ago. But the energy storage market has surpassed even my expectations over that time. And as solar and wind quickly come online, they need storage to help them meet more of the grid’s demand.  Form Energy is on the list for a third time for its iron-air batteries, which could enable cheaper long-duration energy storage. The company has a massive project in the works, to the tune of 30 gigawatt-hours, which will be used to help power a Google data center. It could be the world’s largest battery project in terms of capacity by the time it comes online, which is expected to happen in phases between 2028 and 2031. Taking another tack, Energy Dome is using compressed carbon dioxide to store energy on the grid. This technology is already cheaper than lithium-ion batteries for longer durations (think 10 hours or more), and the company is working to scale quickly. I covered the company in 2022 , before it had its first commercial plant running. Now it has plans for over 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of plants around the world, including one with Google in Ireland that’s slated to come online in 2028. And Moment Energy is working to use the million EV batteries that are expected to reach the end of their life by 2030. The company has a facility in Vancouver, British Columbia, that repurposes used batteries for backup power. This year hasn’t been all sunshine and rainbows for climate tech. But I’m hopeful that some of the companies on this list, and the technologies they build, will keep nudging us in the right direction.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. events.title: Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used Bystander Videos to Track Falling Debris
events.summary: Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica. Source images: FAA report obtained by ProPublica, Eric Gay/AP. When SpaceX’s giant Starship rocket exploded over the Caribbean last year, the internet lit up with videos from airline passengers, island tourists and locals showing flaming debris shooting across the sky. Even some airline pilots recorded the fiery aftermath as planes scrambled to move out of its path . Some of those videos of Starship’s seventh test flight — including ones taken from Disney and Royal Caribbean cruise ships and a Club Med resort — went on to play a role in the company’s efforts to count and track pieces of debris after the explosion, a report obtained by ProPublica says. The report — obtained by ProPublica from the Federal Aviation Administration through a freedom of information request — shows video captured a fireball, then a shower of sparkling debris in the sky moments after the explosion. It includes maps pinpointing where the images were shot, which helped the company understand how debris tumbled to earth after the blast. “At 1 minute 42 seconds, the debris cloud is observed transiting behind the cruise ship,” says the report, which SpaceX provided the FAA two weeks after the so-called mishap. Such reports are required by federal rules in the days after a rocket failure and are supposed to describe what happened and where hazardous debris landed. The information is key for the FAA’s efforts to keep busy air traffic corridors safe at a time of rapid growth in the commercial space industry as companies like SpaceX develop and test rockets that they hope will eventually reach the moon and Mars. During launches, the FAA preventively closes airspace. It has also been forced to clear areas quickly after test flights of massive spacecraft went wrong. Starship flights 7 and 8 broke apart last year and scattered debris above airline traffic over the Caribbean. Before Flight 9, the FAA moved to greatly increase the size of the airspace it walled off pre-launch. The agency defined its no-fly zones, which are closed to airplane traffic during a launch, and its so-called debris response areas, which are closed after a mishap, using information from SpaceX and modeling from Space Force, the branch of the military that deals with the nation’s space interests, to predict where debris might fall. Nearly doubling those pre-launch no-fly zones “only makes sense if the prior margin was judged inadequate rather than just unlucky,” said Moriba Jah, a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Texas at Austin. Read More “We’re Too Close to the Debris” Earlier this year, the FAA issued a warning that rocket launches could “significantly reduce safety” for airplanes, after ProPublica reported that 21 planes appeared to make sudden turns to exit or avoid an FAA-designated emergency no-fly zone in the minutes after the Flight 7 explosion. Such disruptions are likely to become more frequent. SpaceX is seeking to launch Starship up to 76 times a year from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The FAA provided ProPublica the reports on Starship flights 7, 8 and 9 — all of which involved mishaps — after we requested them under the Freedom of Information Act. The FAA redacted the vast majority of all three reports, citing, among other things, exemptions in the law that protect confidential business information from disclosure. The blackouts were, in part, a reflection of SpaceX’s objections; FAA allowed the company to challenge the release of information it deemed proprietary. The FAA refused to release information that would show SpaceX’s estimates of where debris fell during the three rocket failures. It’s unclear what the agency or the company knows about how close any airplanes came to falling debris. “Withholding the underlying debris estimates makes it impossible for anyone outside SpaceX and FAA to check whether that pattern is improving or repeating,” Jah said. “Given a regulator already revised its own safety margins once, the public has a real interest in seeing the data behind both the old margin and the new one.” The unredacted part of the report did not show whether the debris from the Flight 7 explosion fell where SpaceX and the FAA expected it to. But the references to Disney and Club Med guests’ video suggest SpaceX did not have a full picture of where the debris landed without them. “I would read it as evidence their own tracking did not carry cleanly through the debris cloud phase, so they used the public to fill the gap,” Jah said. A page from SpaceX’s report shows the company used public video, including from near a Disney cruise ship, to track debris from Starship Flight 7. Obtained by ProPublica. Redactions in original document. SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. The company has said that it learns from its mistakes and that each test improves Starship’s reliability. Last December, it said on X that “SpaceX is committed to responsibly using airspace during launches and reentries, prioritizing public safety to protect people on the ground, at sea, and in the air.” The FAA did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Disney, Royal Caribbean or Club Med. Ron Madler, a professor of aerospace engineering at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said the videos could help SpaceX “either confirm their breakup models or possibly to improve them.” The mishap report for Flight 8, which rained debris near the Bahamas, said before that flight’s explosive failure, SpaceX did not have the proper “test stand” that was capable of testing the rocket’s engines “for a full Starship mission.” The remainder of the page was blacked out, so it was unclear from the report whether the company had found another way to fully test the engines before launch.  Flights 7 and 8 both involved the same model. Both ended in engine-related failures. Text in the report around the statement about the test stand was redacted. But Jah said it “means some part of the engine’s actual flight behavior was being verified for the first time in flight rather than on the ground.” John Crassidis, an aerospace engineering professor at the University at Buffalo, said launching before having a fully capable test stand was likely “a cost-saving decision.” In building rockets, he said, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has used both the old approach of launching and then fixing any issues that arise, and the newer approach of running simulations and ground tests first to head off problems. “Doing too much of the old school can lead to too many mishaps and cost overruns,” he said. “Doing too much of the new school leads to long times to get things done and a reduction in flexibility.” The post Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used Bystander Videos to Track Falling Debris appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: NT government departments hit by massive network outage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NT government departments hit by massive network outage affecting hospitals, police Topic: State and Territory Government Hospitals across the NT, including Royal Darwin Hospital, were affected by the outage. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) A wide-reaching network outage has affected the whole of the Northern Territory government today. Systems experienced intermittent interruptions, forcing services such as hospitals to initiate continuity plans, and the NT Police Force says three Triple Zero calls were missed. The NT government says it has identified the problem and that systems should be back to normal by this evening. A massive network outage interrupted all government departments in the Northern Territory today, affecting services from hospitals to police. The widespread, intermittent outage began about 3am and affected all government agencies, from education to housing, in both urban and remote areas. Earlier today, NT Police said the outage was not affecting Triple Zero (000) calls. However, this afternoon, Assistant Commissioner Terry Zhang said three Triple Zero calls had been missed. Terry Zhang says police were informed by Telstra of the three missed Triple Zero calls "very soon after". ( ABC News: Michael Franchi ) "Since the start of the outage … there have only been three phone calls that we couldn't answer in time that were referred to us very soon after that by Telstra," he said. "We have conducted follow-ups with all three of those missed telephone calls, and there have been no issues identified. "None of them were high risk or had any consequences; it was just routine police follow-ups." NT Police advised there had been interruptions to the police non-emergency line throughout the day. The NT government said the issue occurred inside a "core" IT gateway for NT government services. The outage impacted police services across the NT. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the Territory-wide IT outage had caused "significant disruption to all of our IT networks". "We have mechanisms in place to continue with business as usual until we find the source, which will be subject to a serious inquiry," she said. Department of Corporate and Digital Development deputy chief executive Greg Connors said a team of up to 40 people had been working all day to isolate the cause of the outage. Mr Connors said workarounds had been implemented this afternoon and the systems were effectively back to normal. He also said the team believed it had identified the root cause and expected to resolve it this evening. Greg Connors says workarounds are now in place and the issue is expected to be resolved later today. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi ) "I can guarantee you this is not a cyber hack; this is something that is internal," he said. "It's a bit like getting in your car one day, and it goes, even though there have been no signs it was going to break down prior. "It is just one of those things that happens. We have found [the issue], which is great kudos to all my team that spent all day looking for it. "We are confident once we have fixed it, it will be back to normal." Mr Connors said the outage had a "widespread impact", including in hospitals, where staff had to initiate continuity plans. "Clinicians in hospitals would have experienced delays, [they] would have experienced not being able to get to services, not being able to get to impacted systems," he said. He said he could not rule out future outages, but said any that did occur would not be because of the same problem.

events.title: Andrew Garfield says he didn't trust AI after playing Sam Altman in 'Artificial:' I got a bit scared'
events.summary: Andrew Garfield plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in "Artificial," which hits theaters on Christmas Day. Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for FLC Andrew Garfield became wary of AI after portraying Sam Altman in "Artificial." Garfield said he became mistrustful and "a bit scared" of the technology. "Artificial" chronicles the time when Altman was temporarily ousted from OpenAI in 2023. Portraying OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in the upcoming film "Artificial" didn't make Andrew Garfield an AI enthusiast. In fact, Garfield said it had the opposite effect during an interview with Variety published on Tuesday. "I got a bit scared. I felt a little mistrusting of the technology," Garfield said. "It feels like the people who are creating and kind of encouraging us to use the technology don't exactly know its capacity themselves. So, that feels a little irresponsible to me, personally." Garfield said he's used ChatGPT for research or as a "kind of fancy Google," but doesn't need to rely on AI for his career. "Luckily, I don't need it in my life in the same way other people in other industries might as an actor," Garfield said. Directed by Luca Guadagnino, "Artificial" details the turbulent period when Altman was temporarily ousted from OpenAI in 2023. The film will be a who's who of Silicon Valley, with Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever, Monica Barbaro as Mira Murati, Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk, and Cooper Hoffman as Greg Brockman. The film hits select theaters on Christmas Day. In interviews, Altman has said he has some reservations about the film. "I'm sure it won't be accurate, but I hope it's funny and enjoyable to watch," he told Politico's Decoded this week. Altman told Vanity Fair he had seen the film's trailer and that Garfield had mastered some of his mannerisms. "They filmed outside of our house. There were these notices on our street that there was going to be some filming or whatever. I didn't realize what was going on. I paid no attention," he said. "And then one morning I was walking down the street to get coffee, and there were all these cameras, and there was a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something." He called the moment "very strange." "Then I immediately figured out what was happening. We waved and went on, but it was really weird. I mean, it's like a strange thing to see someone that has nailed your kind of quirky mannerisms or whatever," Altman said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A partial building collapse in Istanbul kills 2 and traps at least 2 more
events.summary: A seven-story building in Istanbul has partially collapsed, killing two and trapping at least two other people ISTANBUL -- A seven-story building in Istanbul partially collapsed on Thursday, killing two people, officials said. Emergency crews were trying to reach at least two people that remained trapped inside. The reason for the collapse was not immediately known and an investigation was underway. Rescue teams were working to reach those trapped even as there were warnings of a further collapse of the building. The building’s three lower floors, including a ground-floor shop, caved in before dawn in the district of Maltepe, on the Asian side of Istanbul, a city that is bisected by the Bosporus Strait. Residents from the upper floors were safely evacuated while search teams rescued eight more people from the rubble. The rescuers recovered two bodies and were trying to reach two people still believed to be inside, according to the Istanbul governor's office. events.title: Russia's internet giant Yandex halts operations at major data center after drone attack
events.summary: Russia's Yandex paused operations at one of its key data centers after a drone strike. The attack caused a fire to break out but the company said its core services were unaffected. Ukraine has ramped up attacks on Russia's infrastructure in the latest phase of the war. Russian internet giant Yandex suspended operations at one of its key data centers on Thursday after a drone strike as Ukraine continues to target the country's infrastructure. The attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan, in western Russia, and affected part of its infrastructure, Yandex said in a statement to CNBC. The data center has stopped operating entirely, and some Yandex services may be unavailable to users, it added. "There are no casualties, and emergency services are on site dealing with the aftermath," Yandex said. Moscow-headquartered Yandex, known as the Google of Russia, provides the country's most widely used search engine. It also developed the region's leading generative AI model, YandexGPT. Although Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for the Yandex attack, it has been stepping up its attacks on Russian infrastructure, including energy, over recent months, such as targeting Russian oil refineries , which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said are used to "finance the war and the killing of Ukrainians." Ukraine also increased attacks on Russian retail giant Wildberries , a critical part of the consumer infrastructure. Last week, Zelenskyy said the country will double down on its attacks on Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes from Moscow designed to force people to leave Kyiv and other cities. Emergency power cuts were enforced in Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, on Thursday due to ongoing Russian air strikes on the country's power grid. Last week, Russia hit key facilities in Kyiv and other major cities across the country, as it looks to destabilize Ukraine's energy foundation ahead of the winter season, threatening heating and other essential services for civilians. events.title: Nestlé's CEO says this is the most important skill for workers in the AI era
events.summary: Nestlé's CEO, Philipp Navratil, said understanding AI is the most important skill for today's workers. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nestlé's CEO Philipp Navratil said that understanding AI is the most important skill for today's workers. That doesn't mean understanding every technical aspect of AI, he said. He emphasized the importance of knowing AI trends and how the tech can transform your business. In today's workforce, getting good at prompting AI isn't enough. That's according to Nestlé CEO Philipp Navratil who oversees more than 270,000 employees worldwide. Navratil said workers still need to understand their business and how to use AI tools, but they also need to understand AI itself. That doesn't mean everyone needs to understand every technical aspect of how it operates, Navratil said. However, you might need a bigger-picture understanding of the technology. This is part of a series of stories from Business Insider's conversation with Nestlé CEO Philipp Navratil. To be alerted when the next piece publishes, follow reporter Ana Altchek here. The 3 qualities Nestlé's CEO says will get you a promotion "You need to understand what is it is capable of, what the trends are, what is happening, how AI can change anything at the company," the CEO of Nestlé, which owns brands like Nespresso and DiGiorno, told Business Insider. Too many people treat AI as just another tool, Navratil said, instead of recognizing that it should fundamentally change how they work. The real opportunity is rethinking workflows and processes around AI, rather than simply layering the technology on top of existing habits. "That's much more important in the sense of being successful in transforming a company using AI," Navratil said. He said if employees simply use the tools they're given without changing their approach, AI may add more layers of complexity instead of making work simpler. To unlock its potential, workers need to better understand AI's implications and rethink how it can streamline processes, eliminate unnecessary work. This can help free up time to analyze data, meet with business partners, and make the business move faster, Navratil said. His comments come at a time when many leaders are considering the most critical skills for workers in this new era. Other leaders, including the CTO of Coinbase, OpenAI's president Greg Brockman, and Y Combinator cofounder Paul Graham have emphasized the importance of skills like good judgment and taste now that AI can take on more tasks. "When anyone can make anything, the big differentiator is what you choose to make," Graham wrote on X . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: New direct train services from London to Wrexham and Rochdale rejected
events.summary: Regulator also vetoes extra Blackpool service, citing lack of space on west coast mainline for new trains to capital Plans to run direct train services to Wrexham and Rochdale from London have been rejected by the rail regulator because of “significant pressure” on the line. The Office of Rail and Road said that there was insufficient space on the crowded west coast mainline to introduce the two new separate train services. It also vetoed plans for additional London-Blackpool train services wanted by Avanti. The ORR had last year knocked back plans for a new independent open access service linking Wrexham and the capital put forward by the Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company (WSMR). WSMR had submitted plans for a slightly less frequent service but the ORR said the new routes would still put the reliability of the wider railway at risk. The new service could have allowed Wrexham to capitalise further on the town’s Hollywood-meets-football mini-boom, fuelled by the Wrexham AFC co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney. Proposals for a new Lumo service between London and Rochdale, again slimmed down after being rejected in 2025, were once more rebuffed. The ORR also said Avanti could not add more Blackpool services from London. However, it did approve one extra London-Chester evening service from Avanti, which would otherwise have run as a “ghost train”, with crew and the rolling stock returning north to the depot overnight. The decision follows the outcry over the ORR’s initial ruling on a Manchester-London service which was barred from taking passengers last year. The regulator said its assessment, backed by external reviews, was that the “capacity and performance of the southern section of the west coast mainline has not materially changed since similar applications were rejected in 2025”. It said gaps in the current timetable were needed to provide important space for trains to recover when things went wrong, rather than escalating chaos. Stephanie Tobyn, ORR’s director of strategy, policy and reform, said: “New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. But the west coast mainline is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers.” Private operators such as First Group, owners of Lumo, have been looking to increase open-access routes as Labour has renationalised major rail contracts in the transition to Great British Railways. London-Wrexham direct trains briefly ran from London Marylebone from 2008 to 2011 as an open-access service but stopped owing to financial losses.

events.title: Bahrain F1 race in Malaysia delivers $108.1 million windfall to local micro SMEs
events.summary: Based on the success and economic spillover effect, Malaysia could benefit from international sporting events such as the G1 as a platform for SMEs to have wider opportunities and market access. Malaysia’s Bahrain F1 Grand Prix at Sepang brought over RM345 million in spillover effects for local micro, small and medium enterprises, said Minister Steven Sim. Almost half of the 261,000 spectators were foreign tourists, who spent more on hotels, food, transport, shopping and leisure. The government says big sports events can help SMEs grow by boosting tourism, local demand and links with larger firms and event organisers. KUALA LUMPUR – Local micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSME) reaped over RM345 million (S$108.1 million) in economic spillover effects of the Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang International Circuit. Malaysia’s Entrepreneur Development and Cooperatives Minister Steven Sim added that almost half of the 261,000 spectators were foreign tourists. “The impact reflects the important role of large-scale international sporting events in stimulating economic activities, especially through the rise in tourism expenditure and demand for local goods and services. “The Bahrain F1 GP in Malaysia has had a very drastic impact on the SMEs, especially those in the hospitality, food and beverage, retail, transport, entertainment, tourism-related services and support industries,” he said in a statement on Oct 8. Those who attended the F1 race were projected to have spent 2.17 times more than ordinary events, he said, adding that foreign tourists usually spend more due to longer stays and expenditure spent for accommodation, food and beverages, transport, shopping and recreational activities. “This effort includes strengthening ties between SMEs and bigger industry players, event organisers, tourism operators and local suppliers so that the economic benefits generated by such large-scale events can be enjoyed by more small businesses,” he said. events.title: "The Axios Show": Inside Bryan Johnson's quest to make 300 the new 70
events.summary: Bryan Johnson , the face of the longevity movement, wants to make staying alive more important than making money. The famous/infamous biohacker spends over $2 million a year on his health, talks about living forever and publicly tracks everything from his erections to his sperm strength. Why it matters: As Johnson fights to "live forever," he's doing so with a wink to his 8 million social media followers, a link to his business in his bio and a knack for drawing attention to himself. What they're saying: In his interview with The Axios Show, he offered some advice for Elon Musk, said he'd love to help President Trump with his health and revealed his ultimate goal. "Will the 25th century ... be like, 'thank you' in 500 years? Will they give me a head nod? That's the goal," he said. Zoom out: His big picture focus: change the focus of society to health, not wealth. "Society says making money... is the greatest trophy one can get...we are at this inflection moment as a species where we are transitioning to 'Don't Die,'" Johnson said, referring to the title of his longevity movement. "What creates status and power and prestige is going to be different. And as crazy as it sounds, it may be your nighttime erections...It may be your ability to dunk a basketball at age 49," he said. Johnson, 49, is currently trying to dunk . Zoom out: That focus is what drives some of his more extreme experiments and interventions. In 2023, Johnson injected his teenage son's plasma , which he found to be a helpful regimen for his dad but not for himself, saying his own biomarkers are already "pretty similar to my 18-year-old." Through the help of wearables, tests and a concierge team, Johnson has gathered over 4.2 billion data points about his own body and health, and he relies on AI tools to help parse takeaways from that data. He has an in-home medical lab of sorts where he can do continuous testing, monitoring and procedures. Zoom in: Perhaps his most extreme act is his online presence , which Johnson called "performance art" in our conversation. When talking about humans dramatically increasing lifespans through scientific methods, "no one cares," he said. But "if you talk about it in performance art where it has a vibe and an energy to it, people will engage." The intrigue: Still, even Johnson recommends many of the basics for health: sleep, healthy diet and exercise. For those who want to go further, he recommends a blood draw or MRI, sitting in a sauna several times a week and testing out psychedelics. When asked which longevity treatments feel like snake oil, Johnson said "Basically everything on social media." When I pointed out that includes Bryan, he said, "you're right. I've done this for years. Most things don't work." Reality check: Johnson has multiple longevity businesses that he calls successful, though the financials of the companies are not public. Blueprint , his consumer products business, sells "the most tested healthy longevity protocols," per the company: protein powders, supplements and even extra virgin olive oil. Immortals , another one of his companies, offers concierge longevity care for a limited group of members. Prices range from $75,000 a year to $1 million per year. Johnson has "very complicated emotions about this business because I started the company to try to help other people and not to make money. ...I'd rather just be clean and be like, "I'm going to help you out." But to help people out, I have to have infrastructure to actually deliver these things." The intrigue: Johnson said he gets calls from world leaders asking for his advice, and he's in group chats with top tech leaders and influencers. When asked for his health advice for Elon Musk, Johnson said "I hope Elon would clean up his health. I mean, he's worked so hard. He has a lot of potential to enjoy what he's built." The bottom line: Johnson believes wealth is out, health and longevity are in as the new status symbols.
