events.title: 'Enough is enough': Alan Jones emails to schoolboy read in court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Complainant denies deceiving Alan Jones for financial assistance, trial hears Veteran broadcaster Alan Jones denies all allegations against him. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Complainant A is giving evidence in the Alan Jones trial in the New South Wales Local Court on Thursday. The complainant, who is now an adult, is accusing Mr Jones of kissing him and touching his buttocks when he was a 17-year-old. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. A man accusing Alan Jones of kissing him when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy has denied he and his mother tried to deceive the veteran broadcaster to obtain as much financial assistance as possible before he came forward with his allegation. The now-adult, known as Complainant A, alleges Mr Jones kissed him, put his tongue in his mouth, and touched his buttocks when he visited the radio host at his farm on the Southern Highlands as a 17-year-old. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexually touching relating to five male complainants between 2003 and 2020. Mr Jones is facing 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Complainant A said he first reached out to Mr Jones when he was 13 years old, sending the 2GB host a letter asking for help with his family's serious financial struggles. Emails read to the court showed Mr Jones had extensive correspondences with the young boy over a three-year period and used his influence to help the boy's mother re-negotiate a more favourable home loan, which included $600,000 being wiped off her initial debt. The trial heard Mr Jones also provided more than $100,000 of his own money to help with the completion of the boy's family home and to help with their legal fees. The court is hearing from Complainant A, who is the fifth and final male complainant. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Under cross-examination, defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC raised an email sent by Mr Jones to the boy, three years after they started communicating with each other, and a year before the alleged indecent assault occurred. The court heard Mr Jones informed the boy in the email about how he had provided his family more than $100,000 in support, writing "enough is enough" and "there must come a point where I have to say, no more". Complainant A said he believed Mr Jones's email expressed frustration but told Ms Bashir he did not believe the email meant the end of the broadcaster's financial support to him and his mother. "Isn't it that the case that your intention was on obtaining as much financial assistance from Mr Jones as you possibly could?" Ms Bashir suggested. "That is not true," the complainant replied. "It's the case that your mother had the intention of obtaining as much financial assistance from Mr Jones as she possibly could?" Ms Bashir asked. "That is a lie," the complainant said. The court heard the boy replied to the email, writing that his family was "happy to make arrangements to make repayments", with Mr Jones's reply asking about when a legal matter would end and that "he was not a mobile bank". Ms Bashir questioned the complainant about whether he had drafted specific emails to Mr Jones or whether his mother also had some level of involvement. Complainant A repeatedly told the court he could not remember who may have drafted specific sections of emails but said there was certain information contained in correspondence that he would have only been able to obtain from his mum. "You were you trying to deceive Mr Jones about the author of the email when you sent emails signed off just from [your name] that your mother had input into?" Ms Bashir suggested. "I suggest that you were, what do you say to that?" Ms Bashir said "[I say] that you're wrong," he answered. The trial heard Mr Jones and the boy met in person on several occasions, including at his Circular Quay apartment, at the boy's home and alone at a pub. It is alleged that after many invitations over several years, the boy agreed to spend two nights at Mr Jones's Fitzroy Fall's property when he was 17 years old. Complainant A said the alleged indecent assault occurred on the second day at the property and that it left him feeling "violated". The court heard, the boy later wrote a letter to his mother saying, "something happened at Fitzroy Falls" and took his allegation to police the next year.

events.summary: Chinese assets likely to continue attracting attention amid relatively low valuations and elevated external uncertainties, analyst says Global active long-only funds have raised their average allocation to Chinese equities to benchmark-neutral from underweight since June, according to a recent Bank of America analysis of 2,767 global funds. The change ended four years of underweight positioning, with the funds managing US$562 billion in Chinese stocks, the bank added. Meanwhile, BlackRock remained neutral on Chinese equities but saw opportunities in physical AI, according to its fourth-quarter global outlook published in September. UBS Asset Management also said in a report published on October 1 that China remained “a key opportunity”, citing attractive valuations in selected sectors including technology, AI and advanced manufacturing. “Chinese assets are likely to continue attracting greater attention from global investors,” said Kenny Ng, a strategist at Everbright Securities International. “Valuations, particularly in Hong Kong, remain relatively low, while external uncertainties remain elevated.”

events.summary: To mark their 10th partnership anniversary, DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong are supporting enhanced round-the-clock digital mental health resources for approximately 90,000 Hospital Authority healthcare workers. [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] As DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong celebrate the 10th anniversary of their bancassurance partnership, the two organizations are marking the milestone with a HK$1 million donation to Oasis – Centre for Personal Growth & Crisis Intervention, a centre under the Hospital Authority's Corporate Clinical Psychology Services. The milestone also reflects a decade of collaboration in helping customers protect their wealth and plan for their long-term financial needs. Over the past decade, the partnership has expanded substantially, with annual insurance sales, measured by annualized premium equivalent, increasing by more than 400%* since the partnership was launched. The figure is based on internal sales data from DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong, verified as of August 31, 2026. Oasis has long been providing psychological wellness and mental health support to the Hospital Authority staff. The funding from DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong will expand the resources available through myOasis, allowing staff to access additional support around the clock. Around 90,000 healthcare workers across Hong Kong's public hospitals are expected to benefit from the initiative. Beyond commemorating a decade of partnership, the initiative reflects the companies' shared commitment to creating lasting value for customers and society. Sebastian Paredes, Head of North Asia and CEO of DBS Hong Kong, said the partnership had helped customers protect their wealth and plan for their long-term financial needs over the past decade. As the two companies marked the anniversary, he said they also wanted to support the wellbeing of healthcare workers who care for the Hong Kong community. “Their dedication to caring for our community deserves our collective support, and we hope this contribution will help strengthen their resilience and wellbeing for years to come,” said Paredes. Wilton Kee, CEO of Manulife Hong Kong and Macau, said the companies had combined their strengths and shared vision throughout their decade-long partnership to deliver insurance and wealth solutions that help customers secure their financial future. The anniversary, he said, also provided an opportunity to support the wellbeing of Hong Kong's healthcare workers and contribute to a healthier community.

events.title: Asahi and Kirin among Japan beer giants raided over alleged price-fixing cartel
events.summary: Japanese officials have raided the country's biggest beer makers over allegations they worked together to raise the price of their beverages. Asahi, Sapporo, Kirin and Suntory Spirits confirmed to the BBC that their premises had been searched by the Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC), adding that they would fully cooperate with the regulator. The four firms dominate Japan's beer market, with their drinks a common sight in supermarkets and convenience stores across the country. Asahi, Kirin and Sapporo all saw their share price fall after news of the investigation broke on Wednesday. Suntory's beer business is not publicly-listed. "I do not deny that an investigation is being conducted today, but I'd like to refrain from commenting on the details as a preliminary review is underway," JFTC Secretary General Iwanari Hiroo said, according to local media. The BBC has contacted the JFTC for comment. According to the Japan Times, the investigation centres on the companies raising their prices in April last year and in October 2022. All four companies announced increases, citing the rising cost of raw materials as well as other factors such as energy and transportation. Kirin Holdings said its subsidiary, Kirin Brewery Company, was searched "on suspicion of a violation of the Antimonopoly Act". It said it takes the matter "very seriously", adding it would "fully cooperate with the Japan Fair Trade Commission's investigation and any requests for cooperation". Kirin Holdings said: "At present, the impact of this matter on the company's financial results has not been determined. The company will promptly disclose any material developments as they arise." A spokesperson for Suntory confirmed "an on-site inspection" had taken place "in connection with a potential violation of Japan's Antimonopoly Act relating to domestic alcohol trade practices". The company said: "We sincerely apologise for any concern or inconvenience this situation may cause to our customers, business partners, and other stakeholders. We will cooperate fully with the JFTC's investigation." Asahi said it was "subject to investigation by the Japan Fair Trade Commission" and that it will fully cooperate with the regulator. It follows an investigation by the regulator in June over alleged cartel activity by some of Japan's biggest ice cream makers , including Meiji and Pocky maker Ezaki Glico. events.title: Singapore’s central bank wants all FinTech AI use cases subject to independent review
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Failures of third-party services no excuse for island nation’s financial sector Singapore’s government creates a dating app 7 days ago DeepMind bigbrain calls for America to set AI standards before it's too late July 14, 2026 Singaporean sovereign wealth fund Temasek thinks AI is going to pay off July 9, 2026 OpenAI job listing suggests ChatGPT could someday replace junior analysts at Goldman Sachs July 8, 2026 UN warns of need for global governance to avoid an AI-pocalypse July 2, 2026 Singapore’s Monetary Authority, which acts as both central bank and finance industry regulator, wants all local industry players to seek independent review of AI use cases before deployment. The island nation’s combination of strict regulation and low taxes have made it one of the world’s premier finance hubs. One of the roles of Singapore’s Monetary Authority (MAS) is ensuring the nation retains that status, but in its first Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions , published on Wednesday, warns that AI increases risk. “The use of AI can improve performance across business and functional areas but its complexity and probabilistic nature can lead to greater uncertainty, as well as unexpected or more biased behaviour that is harder to identify compared to the use of simpler methods,” the guidelines state. And that’s MAS’s view of old-school AI: it rates generative AI as even riskier. “The greater complexity of Generative AI gives rise to even greater uncertainty and unexpected behaviour compared to AI,” MAS warns, citing “noise that is inherent in training data, training data that may not be representative, or when the model encounters scenarios that are not present in its training data” as sources of risk. The regulator fears agentic AI “could further amplify these risks.” MAS therefore calls for financial institutions (FIs) to expand their risk management frameworks to cover AI and expects board and senior management to make that happen. The regulator also wants all AI use cases to undergo independent review before going into production. “Prior to deployment, an FI should subject the AI use case, including its underlying systems or models, to reviews by parties not involved in its development to ensure that the relevant controls, such as evaluation and testing, have been adhered to,” the guidelines state. MAS also wants regulated entities to run technology and cybersecurity reviews “to ensure that AI can be deployed into the production environment in a controlled and secure manner.” If an AI project survives those reviews, MAS wants ongoing monitoring of both the FI’s own systems and any third-party AI powering an application. “Given the uncertainties associated with AI, their dynamic nature and the potential for model staleness and performance degradation due to data or model drifts over time, ongoing monitoring is critical to ensure that deployed AI operates as intended and remains fit for purpose over time,” the guidelines state. MAS does not see failings by third-party AI suppliers as an acceptable excuse for AI problems at entities it regulates, and it wants FIs to monitor their suppliers’ products and services to ensure they remain stable and secure. “FIs remain accountable for AI used in the services they deliver, including AI developed, operated or provided by third parties,” the regulator explained. “FIs should obtain sufficient assurance from third-party providers, assess whether third-party AI is suitable for their intended use, and apply compensating controls where practical constraints or assurance gaps arise. If the risks cannot be brought within the FI’s risk appetite, it should consider limiting, suspending or replacing the use of the third-party AI service.” The regulator also wants Singaporean FIs to maintain up-to-date inventories of all AI used in their business.

events.title: Fuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soar
events.summary: The prices will be displayed when people search for fuel, as well as listed underneath descriptions of forecourts Published 8 October 2026, 00:50 BST Google Maps will now show fuel prices to help motorists find cheaper petrol and diesel in the UK as costs continue to soar. From Thursday, a search for forecourts on the app will display their locations as well as their pricing, using data supplied via the government's Fuel Finder scheme. It is a legal requirement for UK forecourts to add their prices to Fuel Finder within 30 minutes of changing them. It comes days after the price of diesel topped £2 per litre for the first time , which RAC policy head Simon Williams described as "a price threshold no one wanted to cross". There are multiple apps dedicated to finding the cheapest fuel around, but Google Maps is used by 77% of Britain's adult population for general navigation, according to Ofcom. Fuel costs around the world have been dramatically impacted by the US war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine. Diesel price has since fallen by 2p but the AA says an average 55 litre tank of diesel still costs around £110, with the petrol equivalent coming to around £96. The feature is already part of the navigation app Waze, which is used by around 2 million people in the UK. Apple Maps does not show the price of fuel, although some third-party apps can link to its maps on iPhones. Some experts say Fuel Finder is not entirely reliable. "At the moment, we still have to supplement the Government's Fuel Finder feed with other data sources because, on its own, it does not provide the level of coverage and accuracy needed to deliver a complete and reliable service to motorists," said Clare Lafferty, director at the price comparison site PetrolPrices. "There are still sites that have not registered with the scheme at all, alongside sites that have registered but are not consistently updating their prices within the required timeframe." She said the firm identified 200 forecourts in September which it did not believe had updated its diesel prices in time. Sarah-Jayne Williams, director of product partnerships for Google Maps and Waze, said the firm would check the data independently, and would not display prices it believed were not up-to-date. "Accuracy is very important, so we will still show the petrol station and where it is, but you'll only see a price if we have high confidence that it's the right price," she said. The Petrol Retailers Association, which represents thousands of UK forecourts and petrol retailers, said its members were complying. Fuel Finder was launched in February by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who said at the time it could save households £40 per year. events.title: Fuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soar
events.summary: The prices will be displayed when people search for fuel, as well as listed underneath descriptions of forecourts Published 8 October 2026, 00:50 BST Google Maps will now show fuel prices to help motorists find cheaper petrol and diesel in the UK as costs continue to soar. From Thursday, a search for forecourts on the app will display their locations as well as their pricing, using data supplied via the government's Fuel Finder scheme. It is a legal requirement for UK forecourts to add their prices to Fuel Finder within 30 minutes of changing them. It comes days after the price of diesel topped £2 per litre for the first time , which RAC policy head Simon Williams described as "a price threshold no one wanted to cross". There are multiple apps dedicated to finding the cheapest fuel around, but Google Maps is used by 77% of Britain's adult population for general navigation, according to Ofcom. Fuel costs around the world have been dramatically impacted by the US war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine. Diesel price has since fallen by 2p but the AA says an average 55 litre tank of diesel still costs around £110, with the petrol equivalent coming to around £96. The feature is already part of the navigation app Waze, which is used by around 2 million people in the UK. Apple Maps does not show the price of fuel, although some third-party apps can link to its maps on iPhones. Some experts say Fuel Finder is not entirely reliable. "At the moment, we still have to supplement the Government's Fuel Finder feed with other data sources because, on its own, it does not provide the level of coverage and accuracy needed to deliver a complete and reliable service to motorists," said Clare Lafferty, director at the price comparison site PetrolPrices. "There are still sites that have not registered with the scheme at all, alongside sites that have registered but are not consistently updating their prices within the required timeframe." She said the firm identified 200 forecourts in September which it did not believe had updated its diesel prices in time. Sarah-Jayne Williams, director of product partnerships for Google Maps and Waze, said the firm would check the data independently, and would not display prices it believed were not up-to-date. "Accuracy is very important, so we will still show the petrol station and where it is, but you'll only see a price if we have high confidence that it's the right price," she said. The Petrol Retailers Association, which represents thousands of UK forecourts and petrol retailers, said its members were complying. Fuel Finder was launched in February by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who said at the time it could save households £40 per year. events.title: Africa launches credit rating agency
events.summary: The News Africa’s long-planned credit rating agency launches in Mauritius on Wednesday, the continent’s most concrete answer yet to years of complaints that the world’s biggest agencies overstate African risk and drive up borrowing costs. The creation of the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) comes as global agencies face growing criticism for relying on offshore models that some African leaders and policymakers say misread local realities — a debate sharpened this year by Afreximbank’s public break with Fitch . AfCRA will rate governments, cities and companies, and it is meant to complement the three US firms, which control 95% of global ratings markets. The new ratings agency “ will add another opinion in the market place of opinions ,” said Marie-Antoinette Rose-Quatre, head of the AU body that incubated it. She called it “a very tangible outcome of our aspiration to build our own financial institutions”. Only three African sovereigns hold investment grade ratings, according to a background note from the AU’s African Peer Review Mechanism (ARPM). Thirteen are rated at very high risk or in default, and 23 have no rating from the big agencies, which cuts them from international bond markets. The AU has also said the continent’s external debt service costs climbed from roughly $60 billion in 2010 to more than $160 billion in 2024. Know More The launch is part of a wider push by developing countries, at the G20 and the UN, to change how global finance prices their risk. South Africa used its 2025 G20 presidency to put borrowing costs on the agenda. In an op-ed published in Africa Renewal, the UN magazine, Rose-Quatre and Ahunna Eziakonwa, the UN secretary-general’s special adviser on Africa, said unfair ratings cost Africa $74.5 billion a year — an estimate which was first published by the UN Development Programme in 2023. Key details of the new agency remain unclear. The APRM describes it as privately owned and self-funded but has not named its shareholders, chief executive, or board. Mauritius Commercial Bank and the pan-African lender Afreximbank took part in a 2025 meeting to raise support for the project. According to the APRM note, AfCRA “will require a licence” from Mauritius’ financial regulator. People close to the project say trust will take time. “Credibility in credit rating is accumulated rather than declared,” said Daniel Cash, a UK-based law professor who has advised the APRM on credit ratings. The real test, he told Semafor, will come when AfCRA issues a rating that a member state, “particularly an influential one” strongly dislikes. “Independence is demonstrated at the point of disagreement.” The launch also comes as global agencies expand on the continent. Moody’s owns GCR, the largest issuer of ratings in Africa, and in July S&P agreed to buy a majority stake in Nigeria’s Agusto & Co. S&P Global declined to comment, while Moody’s and Fitch did not respond to requests for comment. Tiisetso’s view For half a century, the cost of African borrowing has been set largely in New York by three firms that rate the 55 countries from a distance. AfCRA is the continent finally taking a seat at the table where its risk is priced. Every 10 basis points shaved off a $1 billion Eurobond saves an issuer $1 million a year. Twenty-three states have no rating from the big agencies at all, which locks them out of mandates that require one. That’s the prize. True, AfCRA has no track record and no named shareholders, but the quickest route to credibility runs through pain: an early, well-argued downgrade of one of the governments that cheered the launch. Room for Disagreement Critics question whether investors will trust any agency created by the governments it rates. David Lubin of UK think tank Chatham House asked whether AfCRA amounts to Africa “marking its own homework,” adding that fund managers compare African borrowers with the rest of the world and an African agency “does nothing” for them. Misheck Mutize, AfCRA’s chief architect, acknowledged that the agency’s main role would be to steer Africa’s $4 trillion savings into African assets rather than changing how foreign investors see the continent. “The challenge here is that this is the bare minimum disclosure required before international investors can even begin to take AfCRA seriously,” said Bright Simons, head of research at IMANI, a think tank based in Accra, writing on public policy platform Katanomics Society. Notable Nigerian President Bola Tinubu made the case for an African rating agency , arguing that the Big Three misjudge African risk and that a homegrown agency could spot progress early, which the global firms would later confirm.

events.title: China’s succession crisis: a generation of entrepreneurs is retiring, but are their children ready to take over?
events.summary: Family run private businesses helped power China’s economic miracle, but the next generation is finding it difficult to carry on the work of their parents G rowing up, Ayu would watch his parents put together hand made leather shoes on the ground floor of their three storey home in the Chinese city of Wenzhou. Their relatives in Europe would send photographs of designer products from Italy for the workers to base their designs on, and in the decades that followed, the tiny family-run workshop transformed into a 700 person factory. “The factory and the home were the same place. I watched them make shoes by hand, piece by piece, using small machines,” Ayu recalls of watching his parents work in the 1980’s. By the mid eighties, Chinese economists had a name for this type of bottom up economic growth story: the Wenzhou model. It was a system that saw small companies secure finances through family connections and operate underground factories to produce cheap goods that would end up on the busy streets of China and beyond. But now many of the family-run manufacturing businesses that helped to fuel China’s economic success are facing a succession crisis, with the children of factory owners unable or unwilling to take them over. Ayu – who today runs an online e-commerce platform – says it’s not that his generation doesn’t want to take them over, but that the market is much more competitive than when their parents started, and the crucial institutional knowledge and commercial relationships that powered their success will be impossible to pass on. Personal relationships, experience and instincts are difficult to hand over to the next generation, says Hanqing Fang, an associate professor at Missouri University of Science and Technology. “Shares can be passed to a son or daughter overnight,” Fang says. “But the heir is being asked to take over something that looks like a company on paper but, in practice, is closer to the founder’s personal belongings.” “The network is very difficult to inherit,” Ayu says. “You have to build it yourself. In the end, some people inherit an empty shell. On paper they’re the boss, but the people underneath them have already begun to leave. “We inherited the wealth, but we couldn’t inherit the industry.” ‘I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy’ According to HSBC Life research, two-thirds of wealthy Chinese people have no legacy plan. In a study led by the University of Ningbo, just 10 out of 114 private companies surveyed said they were being managed by the families’ second generation. Many of China’s second generation business owners speak of a profound anxiety about taking over the family firm. “I really don’t want to take over because there are so many interpersonal relationships and financial connections that I’d have to handle and learn about,” says Wu, a graduate who works in marketing in Hong Kong. His family own a snack processing factory in the Chinese city of Shanwei, as well as dozens of stores in Shenzhen and Hong Kong. But he is reluctant to join the family business. “Most young people dream of getting rich overnight, but I know there’s no such thing. When inheriting a fortune, you also have to consider all the complicated paperwork and whether you really have the ability to handle those responsibilities,” Wu says. According to official estimates, China’s private sector accounts for more than half of the country’s tax revenue and 60% of its GDP . Economists say unsuccessful handovers can lead to firms losing value or even closing. Because family-run companies represent such a large percentage of China’s private sector, if they fail in their thousands it could threaten the country’s future growth. “The risk is not that these family firms simply disappear. It is that the capabilities embedded in the founder – including the knowhow, the supplier networks and the relationships – are lost in the handover,” Fang says. For Wu, the idea of one day taking control of the family business is not completely out of the question, but he concedes he still has a lot to learn. “I’d say that one day my parents’ company will be mine. But I’m not ready yet, because it’s not easy,” Wu says. “If I could just have the money without any responsibilities, I’d take it without hesitation. But the thing is, it’s not that simple.” Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

events.title: How oil-rich Alberta's economy might fare if it broke away from Canada
events.summary: Albertans will vote on 19 October whether to hold an independence referendum in the future Published 8 October 2026, 00:10 BST For Alberta independence supporter Keith Wilson, the western Canadian province is in a league of its own. With its wealth of rich oil and gas reserves, a significant agricultural sector and a young and skilled workforce, its economy is one to be reckoned with, says Wilson. The province will hold a referendum on 19 October, giving residents two options: vote to stay in Canada, or vote to move ahead with a formal binding referendum on independence at a later date. The vote, despite not being a cut and dry "stay or leave", still stands to be among the most consequential in recent Canadian history, and a significant test of national unity. One key issue has become central to the debate: Would Alberta be richer if it were to become an independent country? "Alberta's economy is unique. is fundamentally different than the rest of Canada's - we have the people, the institutions, the infrastructure to excel," he says. Alberta separatists have long argued that the province has been short-changed by being part of Canada, and that more of the oil and gas wealth would be kept within its borders instead of being shared with Ottawa, delivering it tens of billions in savings. But many disagree with their accounting. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who opposes independence, predicts a more sober outcome. She says the province could risk paying C$400bn ($283bn; £213bn) in transition costs alone, while bleeding billions more in lost investments and trade due to the political upheaval. A report commissioned , external by her government released earlier this month calculated the costs of separation as between C$50bn and C$170bn over five years - and a highly unpredictable outlook over the long term. The report cautions that the to-do list for a newly independent Alberta would be long and costly. It would have to set up agencies to manage taxes and national security, develop its own constitution, legal and court systems, and pension plans, and negotiate the division of federal assets like national parks and military bases. At Canada's biggest rodeo, the starting gun is fired in the fight over Alberta separation Published 11 July Alberta will vote on whether to remain part of Canada. What now? Published 23 May Lennie Kaplan, a former finance official in Alberta, says the province would be expected to take on a share of Canada's national debt, among many other fiscal challenges and responsibilities. A report on Alberta independence by the CanadaWest Foundation , external , a non-profit Alberta-based think tank, estimates that the province could be stuck with additional debt ranging from C$258bn to C$333bn. With a projected hit to Alberta's GDP and the additional costs, the report estimates separation could hit Albertans' bottom line and reduce their disposable income by 5.8% on average. "Why do we have to create all this uncertainty that might impact and impair the province's fiscal position going forward? Why wouldn't we just work within Canada to address these issues?" Kaplan asks. Opinion polling indicates that around 20% to 25% of Albertans plan to vote in favour of moving ahead with a binding separation referendum, with higher support among younger, rural and conservative voters. Behind the separatist push is the belief that Alberta is misunderstood and overlooked by decision-makers in Ottawa. For decades, that sentiment fuelled a sense of "western alienation" in the prairie province. Once a fringe movement, a number of factors pushed it to the forefront of Alberta politics. There was anger over environmental and political pushback that killed proposed pipelines from landlocked Alberta to coastal waters. A decade of Liberal government in Ottawa has also caused frustration in reliably conservative Alberta. And, in addition, there is also leftover distrust of the federal government over what some Albertans saw as excessive lockdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic. Over the past year, separatist organisers held townhalls across the province to gauge interest from the public. They then launched a citizen-led petition to separate earlier this year, which got more than 300,000 signatures. Smith, the premier, decided earlier this year she would authorise a vote. Alberta is home to Canada's oil and gas sector, with oil reserves estimated to be the fourth-largest in the world. Crude oil is by far Canada's most profitable commodity, accounting for C$142bn in export value in 2025 alone. Most of it is sold to refineries in the US. The province has the highest GDP per capita in the country, and it contributes billions a year to the federal tax pool because of its strong economy. It has not received any "equalisation" payments - money that so-called "have not", or less wealthy, provinces receive from the federal government - since 1965.

events.title: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
events.summary: The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran , U.S. officials said. Why it matters: The directive didn't include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump hasn't made any final decisions. But U.S. and Israeli sources say it could happen before the U.S. midterm elections and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier. The big picture: If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say. Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterm elections, in part because oil prices might rise in response. "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told Axios. A White House official said Trump has all options available at any time. "The U.S. is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." The Atlantic reported earlier Wednesday that Trump is weighing striking Iran before the midterm election. Driving the news: On Friday, Trump's national security team met at Camp David for several hours to discuss the war and other issues. An Israeli official told Axios that part of the meeting focused on a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that it focused on "long-term" foreign policy planning. Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran haven't made any progress. Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian response to a U.S. counterproposal that included demands for nuclear concessions. "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out. After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly," a second Israeli official said. Behind the scenes: President Trump spoke Wednesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was their second call in days , after barely speaking for many weeks. A U.S. official said Trump and Netanyahu spoke about "remembrance and respect for the victims of the October 7 massacre." The call took place after Netanyahu held a meeting with his national security team about Iran, the first Israeli official said. Netanyahu spoke to Rubio on Monday. If major combat operations resume, they will most likely be with the U.S. and Israel working in tandem and with the Israeli military participating. The two Israeli officials said the Iranian regime is desperate and paranoid, which might lead it to strike first. They said the Iranians have suffered two surprise attacks and don't want to experience a third. Between the lines: Resumption of the war could also affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. A renewed escalation — or even a heightened state of tension or emergency — could benefit Netanyahu politically and prevent his opponents from attacking him in the final stretch of the campaign.

events.title: The wildlife winners set to appear on your banknotes revealed
events.summary: Published 8 October 2026, 00:01 BST Banknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money. The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote. The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said. Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians. 'Four distinct and inspiring animals' "We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes," said Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier. A panel of wildlife experts drew up a shortlist of 18 mammals, birds, amphibians insects and fish which were put forward to public nominations . Respondents were invited to select up to six. More than 2.5 million votes were cast by 478,531 people, ranging from wildlife enthusiasts to primary school classes. The buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) was a clear winner, receiving 360,399 votes, nearly 90,000 more than the barn owl (Tyto alba). The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was most popular in the mammals category. The red fox, in the mammals category, and the common kingfisher, among the birds, received more nominations than the Atlantic puffin. The puffin (Fratercula arctica) was still selected because it was the most popular marine animal. The Bank said its inclusion added variety to the series, made the denominations easier to distinguish, and gave an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline. The puffin and bees also feature on coins, as part of the Royal Mint's redesigned 20p and £1 coins respectively . Mock-ups of the new Bank of England banknotes featuring all four winners Each of the quartet of creatures will feature as the central image of a £5, £10, £20 or £50 note, which will also feature other elements from nature as part of their designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The monarch will still feature on the other side of the notes. Rhys Phillips, the Bank's incoming chief cashier who will be responsible for the roll-out of the new series of notes, said the process of designing, testing and printing banknotes could take years. He said the Bank needed to make sure they were high-quality, resilient and accessible. As the designs were only in the very early stages, they would be unveiled closer to their launch. "We'll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we've announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science," he said. Wildlife already appears on banknotes in the UK, with mackerel, otters, red squirrels and osprey featuring on notes issued by the Royal Bank of Scotland , external . Churchill's granddaughter happy with his picture being replaced on the £5 note Yet it will be the first time since 1970 that the reverse side of Bank of England notes will no longer feature notable figures from history. On notes circulating currently, in ascending order of value, are former Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill, author Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and mathematician and wartime codebreaker Alan Turing. The proposed removal of wartime leader Churchill angered Reform leader Nigel Farage, and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch describing the move as "a silly thing to do". The Bank said the move was primarily to stop counterfeiting so all images needed to be replaced on banknotes over time. events.title: The wildlife winners set to appear on your banknotes revealed
events.summary: Published 8 October 2026, 00:01 BST Banknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money. The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote. The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said. Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians. 'Four distinct and inspiring animals' "We have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes," said Victoria Cleland, the Bank's chief cashier. A panel of wildlife experts drew up a shortlist of 18 mammals, birds, amphibians insects and fish which were put forward to public nominations . Respondents were invited to select up to six. More than 2.5 million votes were cast by 478,531 people, ranging from wildlife enthusiasts to primary school classes. The buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) was a clear winner, receiving 360,399 votes, nearly 90,000 more than the barn owl (Tyto alba). The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) was most popular in the mammals category. The red fox, in the mammals category, and the common kingfisher, among the birds, received more nominations than the Atlantic puffin. The puffin (Fratercula arctica) was still selected because it was the most popular marine animal. The Bank said its inclusion added variety to the series, made the denominations easier to distinguish, and gave an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline. The puffin and bees also feature on coins, as part of the Royal Mint's redesigned 20p and £1 coins respectively . Mock-ups of the new Bank of England banknotes featuring all four winners Each of the quartet of creatures will feature as the central image of a £5, £10, £20 or £50 note, which will also feature other elements from nature as part of their designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The monarch will still feature on the other side of the notes. Rhys Phillips, the Bank's incoming chief cashier who will be responsible for the roll-out of the new series of notes, said the process of designing, testing and printing banknotes could take years. He said the Bank needed to make sure they were high-quality, resilient and accessible. As the designs were only in the very early stages, they would be unveiled closer to their launch. "We'll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we've announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science," he said. Wildlife already appears on banknotes in the UK, with mackerel, otters, red squirrels and osprey featuring on notes issued by the Royal Bank of Scotland , external . Churchill's granddaughter happy with his picture being replaced on the £5 note Yet it will be the first time since 1970 that the reverse side of Bank of England notes will no longer feature notable figures from history. On notes circulating currently, in ascending order of value, are former Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill, author Jane Austen, artist JMW Turner and mathematician and wartime codebreaker Alan Turing. The proposed removal of wartime leader Churchill angered Reform leader Nigel Farage, and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch describing the move as "a silly thing to do". The Bank said the move was primarily to stop counterfeiting so all images needed to be replaced on banknotes over time. Please enter a search term. The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will represent UK wildlife and feature as the central images on our next series of banknotes. The decision comes after nearly 500,000 people responded to a public consultation asking which native wildlife they would like to see on our banknotes. They chose from a shortlist of 18 options across three categories – mammals; birds; and amphibians, insects and fish – developed in collaboration with a panel of UK wildlife experts. The Bank used the feedback from the consultation to decide on the four animals, one for each denomination of banknote. The selected animals meet the Bank’s objectives for a distinctive set of banknotes that can support counterfeit resilience and are representative of the UK. The barn owl (Tyto alba), buff-tailed bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) and European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) were the most popular animals in their respective categories. The Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica) was selected because it was the most popular marine animal. The inclusion of a marine animal will add variety to the series, making the denominations easier to distinguish and will provide an opportunity to celebrate the British coastline. The decision on which animal will feature on which denomination will be made in due course and announced closer to launch. While the selected animals will feature as the central imagery for the next series, the banknotes will also feature other elements from nature to complete the designs, potentially including other shortlisted animals. The next series will continue to include a portrait of the monarch. It takes a number of years to design, test and print banknotes, to make sure they are high-quality, resilient and accessible. The expectation is, therefore, that the first denomination from the next series will be launched over the next few years. Victoria Cleland, Bank of England Chief Cashier, said: ‘I am delighted that nearly half a million people responded to our wildlife imagery consultation, showing that cash still matters. I would like to thank everyone who engaged, including those who I met at our events. With their support, we have chosen four distinct and inspiring animals that not only showcase the great variety of wildlife we have in the UK but will also enhance the security of our banknotes.' Rhys Phillips, the Bank’s incoming Chief Cashier who will be responsible for delivering the new series of notes, said: 'It’s fantastic to see how engaged the public have been in this choice. With these animals as the focus for the design we can deliver a new series of banknotes that are secure and represent the UK at its best. We’ll now work to design, test and produce the banknotes, combining the imagery we’ve announced today with cutting-edge security features and materials science’. 1. In July 2025, the Bank announced that work would begin on designing the next series of banknotes, with the important goal to increase counterfeit resilience. As part of this, it also launched a consultation on the theme for the new images for the notes. The July 2025 theme consultation received over 44,000 responses and in March 2026, the Bank announced that nature had been chosen as the theme for the next series of banknotes. Nature received the highest proportion of nominations in the July 2025 consultation, with 60% of respondents nominating it as one of their preferred themes, as well as support in focus groups commissioned by the Bank. 2.

events.title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK
events.summary: Dame Julia Hoggett says negative sentiment about the UK market has pushed companies to leave in the past Published 8 October 2026, 00:00 BST The UK needs to do more to back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC. Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth. Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market , are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors. The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations. "If we want Britain to back Britain, which is what I hear the chancellor and the prime minister saying, then let's make sure that we're creating structural incentives to do so," Dame Julia told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast . "We need to take the handbrake off." The LSE's main market is made up of around 930 companies with a total market value of about £4.9 trillion. Almost 40% are international businesses, hailing from over 80 countries. But in the last few years, many firms have delisted or moved away from the LSE, including takeaway chain Just Eat, which joined the Amsterdam stock exchange, travel giant Tui which opted for Frankfurt, and Paddy Power-owner Flutter which now trades in New York. Meanwhile, the number of companies newly listing their shares in London has dwindled. Last year, there were 23 initial public offerings (IPOs) on the London market, with £2.1bn raised. In the US, which has much larger capital markets, there were 354 with $44bn (£33bn) raised. It has coincided in a big rise of UK investment money flowing into US stocks in search of better returns. "We talk as a nation about wanting growth in every postcode, but at the moment, a lot of us are funding growth in every zip code," Dame Julia said. There was "no shortage of great companies and no shortage of capital", she added. But negative sentiment about the UK market - which was often exaggerated - had contributed to companies leaving in the past, she said. "We need to stop throwing shade at ourselves as a nation... it's a national habit." Big Boss Interview: LSE's Dame Julia Hoggett The boss of the London Stock Exchange speaks to the BBC about the attraction of the UK as a place for companies to list. However, she said British people needed more "incentives" to invest in UK stocks. She wants the government to scrap the 0.5% tax , external Britons pay when they purchase UK shares, pointing out there is no tax when they buy foreign stocks. She also supports the idea of tax credits for Britons investing domestically. The UK had such a scheme until 2016. Business lobbying group the Confederation of British Industry has called for urgent action to halt the exodus of firms from the London Stock Exchange. It said that lighter regulation, better marketing and incentives for investors were needed to stem the outflow. The government declined to say if stock market reform would be part of its Budget this month. "As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals," a spokesman said. events.title: Hong Kong banks grow cautious on One Stanley mortgages amid investigation
events.summary: Banks are taking a cautious approach to mortgages related to the luxury Hong Kong development, which faces building defect allegations The furore over alleged construction defects at luxury development One Stanley threatens to cast a shadow over Hong Kong’s recovering super-prime property market, as banks hold off on mortgages and property agents suspend viewings at the complex while an investigation continues. “Most [banks] are adopting a wait-and-see approach,” said Eric Tso Tak-ming, chief vice-president at mReferral Mortgage Brokerage Services, adding that lenders were likely to take a more cautious approach to mortgage applications at the development while the investigation was under way. Loan approvals would be assessed on a “case by case” basis, said a banking industry source, adding that lenders would look at whether buyers had a high net worth or were otherwise considered reliable customers. A property agent handling sales at One Stanley, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said their company had suspended viewings at the development unless clients proactively requested a visit.

events.summary: French authorities suspended the use of stun grenades Wednesday after a teenager lost his hand during clashes with police, as demonstrations over school conditions spread to more than 40 cities. Protesters’ weekslong blockade of schools is the most visible aspect of a multifaceted national crisis, as public workers strike, bond yields rise to multidecade highs , and France’s traditional parties reckon with the far-right. But one proximate trigger of public discontent may have been overlooked: a ban on phones in schools enforced last month. Following the loss of this “comfort object” — which provides entertainment and connection — the “high school student has opened their eyes to a situation that has suddenly become unbearable ,” a French teacher argued in Grand Continent. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Seafood shop owners fear being forced to close due to gillnet ban
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gillnet ban will lead to seafood shop closures and fishers retiring, businesses warn Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Neil Green says the ban might see him out of the industry. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) A couple running a seafood restaurant say they may be forced to close if commercial fishers leave the industry when gillnets are banned in the Great Barrier Reef Zone. In 2023 the state and federal governments made the commitment to phase out gillnets in the zone. Temporary gillnet licences are set to expire on June 30, 2027, with the state government running trials with fishers to find alternative fishing methods. Business owners in north Queensland are concerned about the economic flow-on effect of the looming Great Barrier Reef gillnet ban. Some commercial fishers fear they will have to leave the industry and seafood shops may be left with no other option than to close. Peter and Heather Bradford are worried about the future of their business. ( ABC News: Brooke Tindall ) In Ayr, Heather and Peter Bradford serve locally caught seafood to about 150 families a week and say their business will not survive without gillnet fishers on the water. "Next year we'll have to probably close the shop," Mr Bradford said. "Cut out the netting, there's 80 per cent of our business, so we've got no other option but to close." Gillnets are used to catch certain species of fish, including barramundi, by their gills. In 2023 the Queensland and federal governments made the decision to phase out the use of gillnets in the Great Barrier Reef fishing zone by June 30 2027. The governments provided financial assistance to licensed fishers at the time of the decision and established the temporary NX licence, which allowed fishers to use gillnets under strict on-board camera monitoring. The state government has been working with fishers to find an alternative fishing method in the last three years, such as trapping and line fishing. Barramundi is largely caught using gillnets. ( ABC News: Brooke Tindall ) But as the expiry of the NX licences approach, no solutions have been rolled out to fishers. South of Townsville, Alva Beach commercial fisher Neil Green said the other options trialled had not been successful so far. "The intent was to have alternative gear running by 2027. That's been a failure," he said. Neil Green is one of 25 NX licensed fishers in Queensland. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) Mr Green said without change he would probably be forced to retire, but he was worried about more than his own future. "It's not about me — it's about the next generation of fishers that are coming on that we're talking about," he said. Mr Green is among several fishermen in the industry pushing for a three-year extension to the ban, which has the support of Shadow Minister for Northern Australia Susan McDonald. "It will allow [the fishers] to demonstrate that gillnet fishing is incredibly targeted on the species that the fishermen are taking," she said. Susan McDonald supports the seafood industry's call for a three-year extension on NX licences. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Senator McDonald said the 2027 deadline would increase reliability on imports. "If we allow more seafood to be imported from offshore, we are handing over seafood production to countries that don't have the same high standards that Australia does," she said. Back in Ayr, Ms Bradford said importing seafood had not worked for her and her husband's business in the past. "We couldn't compete with [the major supermarkets] price-wise, so it's not going to be viable for us at all," she said. Ms Bradford said other small seafood businesses were in the same boat. "Fish and chip shops will be gone, especially all up along the north coast," she said. Not everyone agrees that putting off the eventual gillnet ban is a viable option. Australian Marine Conservation Society (AMCS) Great Barrier Reef fisheries campaign manager Simon Miller said a three-year extension of the NX licences would come at a cost to wildlife. "The current gillnet fishery, the NX fishery, is still catching thousands of threatened species each year," he said. "We do urge the Queensland and Australian governments to fully deliver their commitment to phase out gillnet fishing from the reef by June 30 next year." The AMCS is against extending temporary licences but Mr Miller says there is support for finding alternative fishing gear. "We need to be looking to the future for genuinely sustainable ways to catch these fish and put them on Queenslanders' plates, but without this impact on threatened species," he said.

events.title: Microsoft is about to let Copilot loose on your file system
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters But don't worry, it's totally safe because the agents and models will (probably) be running locally. Routers never break right? AI giants promise to play nice with personal data after UK watchdog scrutiny 52 minutes ago Windows Search learns to take orders 2 hours ago Microsoft unveils 'Surace' Laptop Ultra 3 hours ago Embedding the human factor into AI agent adoption 5 hours ago Singapore’s central bank wants all FinTech AI use cases subject to independent review 12 hours ago If you thought Windows Recall was creepy, buckle up. Microsoft is about to shoehorn even more AI into its desktop operating system, giving Copilot access to every file on your PC. But don't worry, Redmond insists it's totally secure and safe since the agents powering the functionality will run entirely on your PC — some of the time. Microsoft describes the new functionality, announced alongside a new Nvidia N1X powered Surface Laptop, as "hybrid intelligence." Built atop Microsoft's HydraFusion model router, Windows apps and Copilot features will soon be able to use local models when it makes sense and cloud-based models when it doesn't. For example, Windows might use a local model for simple or privacy-sensitive tasks, or decide complex or performance-sensitive requests need OpenAI's GPT-6 or Anthropic's Claude. Local agents will run in Microsoft's Execution Containers (MXCs), agent sandboxes with fine-grained permissions applied at runtime. According to Microsoft EVP of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri, MXCs mean Windows is now "the most secure platform for agents." (That claim will surely age well because models never escape their sandboxes and routers never misbehave.) To support this hybrid intelligence functionality, Microsoft is extending support for Windows ML, its inference framework built on the ONNX runtime, to Llama.cpp – one of the highest-performing inference engines for local AI inference. By adding support for Windows ML, Llama.cpp should be able to take advantage of a broader range of accelerators. Microsoft is rolling out its hybrid intelligence functionality to GitHub Copilot — its AI code assistant — next week and its Copilot app over the next few months. The new Copilot features look and sound suspiciously like OpenClaw in a business suit. Copilot's agentic functionality will not have access to your entire file system, opening the door to advanced search functionality and productivity tasks through integrations with Microsoft Office. In a demo, Microsoft showed how Copilot could be used to find and organize a user's tax documents, then draft an email with those files attached, addressed to an accountant. Microsoft insists it'll only go snooping through your docs if you ask it to. Windows is also getting AI-enhanced search functionality enabling users to surface settings like dark mode. The OS will also get a conversational interface to perform tasks like sending a text message to a friend. Finally, for those interested in coloring outside Microsoft's agentic lines, the company is rolling out a new onboarding experience to make deploying agent harnesses like OpenClaw a bit easier and more secure. Keeping sensitive tasks on device may help to assuage anxieties over privacy, which have dogged Microsoft since the first Copilot+ PCs arrived in 2024 alongside Qualcomm's Snapdragon X Elite SoCs. It should also help to reduce the load on Microsoft's servers by keeping low-priority, low-complexity requests on devices. That said, the impact of running these models locally on battery life, fan noise, and workload quality could prove a turnoff for many users.

events.title: Brazilian students in Rio de Janeiro march against the prospect of another Bolsonaro presidency
events.summary: Thousands of Brazilian students have marched in Rio de Janeiro against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro winning the presidency RIO DE JANEIRO -- Thousands of Brazilian students marched in downtown Rio de Janeiro on Wednesday to protest against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro winning the presidency, after the far-right candidate received more votes than incumbent and left-leaning Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election . A sea of red-clad demonstrators made their way between two historical squares in Rio’s center, chanting and holding signs referencing Brazil’s sovereignty and democracy in the South American country , which they said were under threat. “We’re fighting for Brazil, not for Lula,” said Talita Amaral, a 19-year-old environmental science student at a nearby university. She was wearing Brazil’s yellow and green soccer jersey, often worn by supporters of Bolsonaro, which she said was a gesture aimed at reclaiming the national colors. “We don’t have time to be sad, we need to be doing this, occupying the streets, sending messages in WhatsApp groups, trying to convince people,” Amaral said, as the chant “Olé olé olé ola, Lula Lula” rang out across Cinelandia square. Neither Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup, nor Lula received more than the required 50% of the vote needed to become Brazil’s leader on Sunday. Therefore, they will face each other in an unpredictable runoff on Oct. 25. But Flávio Bolsonaro has at least two advantages: He received 2 million more votes than Lula on Sunday and the candidates who placed third, fourth and fifth are all on the right of the political spectrum. They gathered more than 8 million votes between them. Bolsonaro is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion because of his ties to the failed Banco Master — a case that many protesters in Rio made reference to on Wednesday. Some pointed to Jair Bolsonaro's handling of the coronavirus pandemic , during which 700,000 people were reported to have died from the disease, while others held signs emblazoned with messages such as “Brazil isn't anyone's backyard” and “I don't vote for someone who sells Brazil.” Many on the left fear a Flávio Bolsonaro presidency would fully align the Brazilian government with the United States because of the proximity in ideologies between U.S. President Donald Trump and the Bolsonaro family. Last year, Trump imposed a 50% tariff on Brazilian goods and imposed sanctions on a Brazilian Supreme Court justice, citing Jair Bolsonaro’s trial, which he called a “witch hunt.” Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Army to execute Fort Hood mass shooter by firing squad Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys “If Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become a colony of the United States,” said João Victor Vieira, 20, who studies literature. He said that Bolsonaro represented a threat to minorities such as people of color, women and the LGBTQ+ community. Bolsonaro's father was notorious for homophobic remarks. Vieira said that while he was initially dispirited following the results on Sunday, he has since regained hope. “This protest shows that social movements are still very much alive,” he said. “We will resist.” This story corrects a previous version that stated the candidates who placed third, fourth and fifth gathered 6 million votes. The correct number of votes is more than 8 million. events.title: Student protest unrest spreads across Europe
events.summary: Police and protesters clashed in Liège, Belgium, on Wednesday as student anger over education costs and school conditions grew, echoing massive protests in neighboring France. Why it matters: The protests are exposing broader anger across Europe over school funding and classroom conditions. Catch up quick: Protests that began in Paris in mid-September as a localized demonstration by high school students have escalated into a massive nationwide movement, with students, parents and teachers' unions demanding more education funding. There have been clashes between French police and protesters in recent days, culminating in a 15-year-old boy's hand being blown off by a police-fired stun grenade. More than 6,500 people — most of them minors —have been arrested since the protests began in France. In Belgium, police have made at least 139 arrests in Liège since the protests began Oct. 1. The big picture: The current wave erupted in France, but education grievances across Europe predate it, with crowded classrooms, teacher shortages, university cuts and soaring education costs fueling protests over government investment in education. In Greece, students called nationwide school actions for Thursday, according to Euronews , including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and potentially occupations. In Italy, high-school occupations began in Turin and Rome on Monday under the slogan "Let's do as in France." Italian students cited underfunding, deteriorating school buildings and rising living costs among grievances they share with French students, and a delegation traveled to Paris in solidarity, ANSA reports . In Ireland, thousands of university students demonstrated in Dublin earlier this month, demanding lower fees, more higher-education funding and affordable accommodation, per RTÉ . In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions rallied in September to demand greater education investment, more teachers and a more equitable school system, according to Tagesschau . In Austria, student groups are preparing fresh demonstrations in mid-October after the country's university association warned of possible cuts of around €1 billion from the next three-year university budget, ORF reports . Between the lines: The education unrest comes as several European governments face mounting pressure to rein in deficits while higher borrowing costs make their debts more expensive to service. France and Belgium are each running budget deficits of more than 5% of their GDP this year, while Austria's is above 4%, according to European Commission forecasts. That squeeze is forcing governments to make difficult choices over public spending. The bottom line: The protests aren't one coordinated European movement, but students across several countries are mobilizing around their shared concerns. events.title: OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Persistent agents appeal to AI companies, but demand isn't obvious AWS launches open-source AI agent sandbox to prevent YOLO mode disasters 19 hours ago Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism 1 day ago COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in 1 day ago South Korean president calls for creation of tools that stop all cyber-attacks 1 day ago Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says 1 day ago When OpenAI introduced dots last month , it pitched them as "always-on agents" running in their own cloud computer, but that may be overstating the readiness of the technology and of the people trying to use it. Presently, multiple users are reporting task failures and connection issues with their dots. Others have flagged cloud connectivity problems, dots that disappear , and dot refusals that appear to be related to abuse prevention. And the OpenAI Developer Community forum shows several similar concerns . OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment about the usage of dots. ABI Research argues that "AI claws" – always-on agents – will shape enterprise AI adoption. The biz sees "a market evolving from isolated assistants toward modular agent ecosystems built for longer-running, enterprise-grade automation." Despite the hiccups that have afflicted dots, some skepticism on social media forums, speculation that OpenAI rushed dots out in response to Meta Muse and Grok Bot , and security issues , dots have some enthusiastic users in addition to detractors who just don't see the point. They also have competition from companies and developers who believe they can deliver a similar service more affordably, with fewer restrictions. A company called Tawkit that makes an SDK called CopilotKit has released OpenDots . "OpenDots is completely open source and gives you the same thing [as OpenAI Dots] as a template you host yourself," the biz said in a post last week. "Bring any agent through AG-UI, use any OpenAI-compatible model, and make every part of it your own." The company previously released OpenMuse and OpenBot . These projects essentially separate the user interface, the AG-UI agent layer, and the backend to provide an alternative personal agent. This doesn't eliminate the token expense of whatever agent is deployed, but it does mean that OpenAI may not be doing the billing. Then there's a potentially lower cost option, called (confusingly) Open Dot , powered by AI models running on OpenRouter. And as it's open source, the code could be altered to run using a local model – a feature that we understand is planned. "Open Dot is an open source version [of OpenAI Dots] that runs on your own Mac with your own OpenAI key, or with open models like Kimi, DeepSeek and Qwen through OpenRouter," the project repo explains. It allows users to connect to various apps like Gmail, Calendar, Slack, Notion, and GitHub via Composio . Prathit Joshi, the project's creator, told The Register , "I enjoy building and shipping tools for developers, especially tools that can support use cases that closed model companies aren't necessarily incentivized to support, like allowing open source models." Joshi is based in Bangalore, India, and works as a growth engineer at Composio. He said he's been using Open Dot to handle personal tasks like setting "to do" lists for the day based on Slack messages and summarizing posts on social media. Open Dot is based on the Electron framework, Joshi said, because he wanted it to be a desktop app. Distinguishing between OpenAI dots, OpenDots, and Open Dot may be confusing, but don't expect things to get any better in the near future. Everyone is busy wrapping increasingly commoditized models in a gatekeeping layer, in the hope of developing a sustainable business. For example, Elon Musk said on Tuesday that Grok Bot would become a model router rather than a front-end for a specific model.
