events.title: IEEE Report Predicts Tech That Will Transform Lives
events.summary: By 2028, genetic engineering and gene therapy will be used frequently to treat a variety of diseases, thanks to advances in artificial intelligence, according to the recently released 2030 Technology Megatrends Report from IEEE. “We are seeing a fundamental shift in how technology evolves,” says IEEE Fellow Dejan Milojicic , chair of the IEEE Future Directions Committee ’s Industry Advisory Board, the group responsible for the report. “ Artificial intelligence is no longer operating in a vacuum; it is now deeply connected to our energy, infrastructure, and physical systems.” Milojicic, a Hewlett Packard Enterprise Fellow, is a vice president at HPE Labs in Milpitas, Calif. AI underpins many of the report’s 30 technologies and five “megatrends,” which are technology shifts with the potential to reshape industries and everyday life for decades. A megatrend isn’t a single breakthrough but a collection of related technologies. For the 2030 report, 166 experts—from 38 countries across six continents—drawn from industry, academia, and government identified 30 breakthrough technologies across the five megatrends: AI, energy, health, space, and physical AI. The experts graded the trends against five criteria: likelihood of success, impact to humanity, maturity, market adoption, and horizon to adoption. AI as a common thread Interconnected systems drive the megatrends, and the connection among them is AI. The report notes that AI technology is advancing faster than any previous revolution, including industrial, electrical, and digital. The pace has turned the technology into general-purpose infrastructure, Milojicic says. That evolution carries risks, though, the experts say. The report cites the lack of computing infrastructure and energy sources as constraints on the ability to scale up AI, and it says the technology’s growth will require reshaping the workforce. Workers have always needed to adapt to stay competitive, Milojicic says, adding that AI adoption isn’t an all-or-nothing approach. Businesses should decide when and how to apply it, he says. The experts say long-term success will require both technical capabilities and attention to the human-AI relationship. Conditions including trust, security, explainability, and policymaking will determine which AI-supported technologies are most likely to scale, they say. “This report shifts the conversation to something far more important: how these advances will intersect with one another to shape human lives,” Mary Ellen Randall , 2026 IEEE president and CEO, said in a news release about the report. “The data makes clear that trust, safety, and human connection must guide every major breakthrough in the decade ahead.” Health care is a high-impact bet The experts scored personalized medicine as the study’s highest-impact technology, at 4.93 out of 5, for its potential to improve human life. The report credits AI-driven breakthroughs in personalized diagnostics and therapeutic treatments, driven by innovative biotech startups. Within two years, the experts predict, genetic engineering and gene therapy will be used in therapeutic areas. Within five years, earlier disease diagnoses will move out of the lab and into day-to-day medical practice, the report predicts. Meanwhile, it says, researchers likely will be able to manufacture simple synthetic proteins—molecules engineered from scratch, rather than found in nature—to perform a specific job in the body, such as targeting a tumor or supplying a missing enzyme. Energy wakes up for AI Increased power demand by AI is outpacing the energy sector’s ability to keep up. Tech infrastructure—data centers, networks, and computing hardware—already uses an estimated 10 percent of electricity globally, according to the news release. The experts predict that within two to three years, energy storage will double in developed countries. The energy industry has been relatively dormant for years, Milojicic says, with little breakthrough innovation since the times of Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla. “Data centers can ramp up within milliseconds, yet it takes months for the power and energy sector to ramp up,” he says. “The governments of various countries will have to rethink their approach to power generation to stay ahead of demand.” The experts cite the Jevons paradox —the idea that efficiency gains tend to increase overall consumption. As AI chip efficiency improves, organizations will run more hardware to build ever-larger frontier models—those advanced AI systems currently in development—the experts say. Data centers will draw as much power as grids can supply, leaving no surplus, the experts predict. Physical AI moves the fastest Physical AI refers to systems embedded within machines that sense and act in the world, including robots and autonomous vehicles. In the report, the category originally was called “hyper-automation and robotics,” a broad, software-driven process automation paired with physical machines. The Industry Advisory Board later folded it into the single physical AI megatrend. The experts found that human-AI interaction has the shortest adoption horizon of any of the 30 scored technologies, at two to three years. They also say physical AI has the biggest chance of technical advancement of any megatrend during the next four years. “The data makes clear that trust, safety, and human connection must guide every major breakthrough in the decade ahead.” —Mary Ellen Randall, 2026 IEEE president and CEO Smarter, more efficient robots will substantially cut energy consumption in the next two years, the experts say. Communications between humans and AI—whether in an android or another device—will shift from text-based commands to predominantly audio and video instructions within two to three years, the experts predict. Androids used in factories will use tactile and haptic feedback within two to five years, letting them sense what they’re touching and adjust their grip or force in response, the experts say. Bio-inspired skin, tissues, and sensors will advance in the same timeframe, the experts predict, giving robots perception that better mirrors human touch. Space is just getting started Space technology , as the report defines it, covers more than exploration. It spans satellite communications, in-space manufacturing, launch technology, and other infrastructure. It is one of the lower-profile megatrends in the report, not for lack of promise but because of where the sector presently sits. “It’s not lagging,” Milojicic says. “It’s the current state of maturity. People are talking about satellite communication right now because it’s very cool and practical. events.title: Australia wants to sell Singapore solar power. But does anyone want it?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts What Singapore really thinks of Sun Cable, the Australian solar power export plan Tiny, rich Singapore has big power needs and wants to go green. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) Australia and Singapore are neighbours, but not exactly close. As the crow flies, the distance from Darwin, the capital of Australia's Northern Territory, to the South-East Asian island nation is 3,400 kilometres — by most standards, a very long way. And yet it is this distance over which an Australian energy company is vying to lay the world's longest subsea electrical cable in the hope of tapping into a green dream. That company is Sun Cable, a renewable energy developer backed by Australian tech billionaire Mike Cannon-Brookes. Sun Cable aims to generate colossal amounts of solar power in the endless, sun-drenched expanses of Australia's Top End, supplying Singapore's 6 million consumers via a 4,300km transmission cable through the Indonesian archipelago. "I'm not aware of too many other projects on this scale," James Bowen, an energy and geopolitical analyst, said. Indeed, the exact scope of Sun Cable's $35 billion ambition is hard to comprehend. It would involve building solar panels to produce up to 10 gigawatts across as much as 12,000 hectares — an area twice the size of Manhattan. Battery storage on a similarly massive scale would back up the solar farm when the sun was not shining. A computer-generated image of Sun Cable's proposed solar farm in the NT. ( Supplied: Sun Cable ) Electricity would be transported 800km from the desert to Darwin, where some of it would support the local grid. The vast majority, however, would be sent onwards to Singapore. There, Sun Cable would supply up to 1.75 gigawatts of power, or about a quarter of the country's typical demand. Amid persistent questions about the feasibility of Sun Cable's grandiose plans, the ABC travelled to Singapore to speak to potential customers. Puah Kok Keong, chief executive of the Singapore Energy Market Authority, is the regulator of the nation's power and gas industries and one of its most senior energy officials. Puah said his country's energy needs were intense. Puah Kok Keong runs Singapore's Energy Market Authority, a regulator. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) He said air-conditioning in the famously steamy climate ran around the clock while industry chewed up as much as 80 per cent of power demand. Added to the challenge of meeting that demand, he said Singapore wanted to become carbon-neutral. Plus, Singapore is tiny — at fewer than 750 square kilometres, it is 13 times smaller than greater Melbourne. "We have set for ourselves a goal of reaching net zero by the year 2050," Puah told the ABC. Singapore, Puah said, was doing what it could within its own borders. Solar panels are being installed everywhere — on roofs, on car parks and even on the city's reservoirs as floating installations. With land at a premium, Singapore has resorted to floating solar farms. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) But he acknowledged it was a strategy with severe limits. Even with the feverish activity, Puah said solar only supplies about 3 per cent of Singapore's power, a figure unlikely to increase by much more than double. To reach net zero by the middle of the century, he said Singapore had started to look further afield. "We are also looking at importing electricity from around the region," he said. "We have set for ourselves a target of importing up to around 6 gigawatts of clean energy from the region by the year 2035." It is into this equation that Sun Cable hopes to insert itself. Currently, Singapore gets about 95 per cent of its electricity from natural gas, more than half shipped into the country as liquefied natural gas (LNG). Singapore is heavily reliant on gas supplied by the likes of Shell. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) The rest is sourced via pipelines from neighbouring Malaysia and Indonesia. Christophe Inglin from the Sustainable Energy Association of Singapore said the island state would have to do with renewable electricity what it had long done with fossil fuels. "We've imported the oil and gas," Inglin said. According to Inglin, Singapore already imports some electricity from Malaysia through a high-voltage transmission line, but these imports do not amount to much. There are plans to dramatically increase the amount through a regional "super grid" that would much more closely weave together the electricity systems of South-East Asia. From the highest levels, Singapore is seeking a more integrated Asian grid.

events.title: AWS launches open-source AI agent sandbox to prevent YOLO mode disasters
events.summary: AWS has offered multiple open-source strategies for holding AI agents accountable, and now it’s adding a full-on sandbox to this stack. Dubbed Strands Box, the new solution uses OS-level isolation and some of AWS’ other recent open-source AI control tools to, ostensibly, retain greater control over autonomous AI agents’ behavior. “Agents increasingly run in ‘YOLO mode,’ approving every action without human review,” the AWS team explained in its announcement. “The usual solution to this problem is a sandbox … but access is only part of what we want to control.” The problem with containers and microVMs typically used to isolate AI agents, as AWS explains it, is that their strong isolation doesn’t come with contextual rule enforcement. In other words, when a containerized or virtualized agent gets hold of a tool, there may be no stopping it from doing whatever it wants - like deleting a production database, or gaining access to the internet and doing dog knows what. That’s where the other open-source tools inside Strands Box come in: It uses the Dogwood Local Engine to give the policy engine in Box temporal awareness, so tool calls can be checked against not only what the agent wants to do, but what it’s already done. As one example, AWS noted that an agent could be allowed to post status updates to Slack, but no more than three times every ten minutes to prevent it from spamming its human operators. An AWS spokesperson further explained that Box could be used to control when an agent can perform a Git push, or it could be used to put a cap on API calls that could end up costing a small fortune. Additionally, Strands Box includes Strands Shell and Monty for Python, which expose shell and Python operations to the same Dogwood policy engine and event history, making agentic actions clearer to developers and allowing policies to account for what an agent is trying to do. AWS VP and distinguished engineer Marc Brooker, one of the folks behind Dogwood and Strands Box, explained to The Register that the interpreters are a key part of making agentic behavior more intelligible, which allows for devs to write more precise policies to prevent agents from taking bad actions. “Box’s Shell and Python interpreters expose operations such as file deletions, while its gateways expose API requests and tool calls,” Brooker told us in an email. “Policies can then account for the action being attempted and earlier activity.” Box, Brooker added, enforces those rules without trusting or relying on agents to actually follow instructions, which should ideally prevent them from running roughshod over their operators’ wishes. As for the reason behind AWS’ push to develop open-source tools like Dogwood, the Dogwood Local Engine, and Strands Box, Brooker said that AWS wants to find the right balance between boundaries and policies that prevent agentic AI disasters of the kind we regularly report. “Box enforces the policies developers configure, deterministically, and the agent can't talk its way around these rules,” Brooker explained, though he added that, even with properly configured permissions, an agentic action can still produce an unwanted result. “Developers remain responsible for deciding what access to grant and where human review is needed,” Brooker added - in other words, don’t let your YOLO mode go too YOLO. A bit of human oversight is still necessary. “Agent safety is an area where the industry still has significant work to do, and we're committed to continuing to invest in it, both inside the AWS cloud and in open source,” Brooker said. Strands Box supports any agent or harness one wants to confine within its walls and is available on GitHub now, though only for macOS for the time being. Linux support is in development, and AWS told us a Windows client is “on our radar,” but neither has a planned release date. Deployment to platforms like AgentCore, ECS, and Kubernetes is also planned. ®

events.title: Americans don't want taxpayer dollars funding campaign ads: poll
events.summary: Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Nearly nine in 10 voters say using taxpayer money to pay for election-related ads featuring the president or Cabinet members is inappropriate, including 80% of Republicans, according to a recent Reuters-Ipsos poll . Why it matters: The administration's decision to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on Trump-fronted ads weeks before the midterms is facing an uproar and overwhelming public opposition. While the administration insisted the ads were actually PSAs, Trump later announced that a super PAC affiliated with him would foot the bill for future ads (but not reimburse the taxpayer dollars already spent). Friction point: New polling suggests the TV spots, which the White House said "are a reminder for Americans to love their country," might not get much love from voters. The poll of 4,506 adults found that just 9% of Americans find it appropriate to tap taxpayer funds for election-related television ads featuring the president or cabinet members. Zoom out: A majority of Americans also panned other actions Trump has taken: 68% say it's inappropriate to block media outlets from entering the White House, and 72% say the same about naming federal institutions and buildings after a sitting president. Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Zoom in: A White House official contended in a statement to Axios that the "PSAs are clearly not political," saying Trump "is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action." But one is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad, using the same footage and narration, with the campaign sponsorship tagline replaced with a disclaimer: "Paid for by the U.S. Government." Earlier this month, Democrats called on the Government Accountability Office and the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate the use of taxpayer money to produce and air the ads. Between the lines: Axios' Alex Isenstadt scooped late last month that the ads released so far were "just the beginning" and that Trump himself — pleased with the war-room-style social media posts his digital team regularly pumps out — was hand-picking the ads himself. And it's not just the White House that's gotten in on promotional hype that blurs the lines with campaign content: The FBI's rapid response account released a video Tuesday applauding director Kash Patel — and criticizing Democrats, including Senate candidate Abdul-El Sayed. The bottom line: As an election approaches where cost-of-living concerns are paramount, Americans have strong feelings about how their taxpayer dollars are spent. events.title: US states sue popular kitmaker TP-Link over China risks
events.summary: The attorneys general of Florida, Iowa, Montana, and Nebraska have sued ubiquitous networking and smart home tech maker TP-Link, alleging its security claims were misleading and it hadn't properly disclosed ties to China. The company has a large presence in US retail and the tech channel, especially in consumer routers, with stats from Circana asserting it had around 36.6 percent US market share by units and 31 percent by dollars in 2024. The complaint [PDF] accuses California-based TP-Link Systems, whose brand originated in Shenzhen, of deceptive and unfair marketing practices concerning its routers' security and its connections to China. It cites exploitation of TP-Link devices by Chinese and Russian state-backed hackers. The suit also claims TP-Link allegedly concealed facts about its "past and ongoing ties to the People's Republic of China," accuses it of having a supply chain that's reliant on PRC players, repeated firmware vulnerabilities, and being subject to Chinese laws that force companies to cooperate with state intelligence. According to the states' attorneys general, the hardware vendor still relies on Chinese companies for research and development and manufacturing operations, despite previously claiming to have moved into Vietnam after severing ties with China. The complaint alleges that only 0.5 percent of components used at TP-Link's Vietnamese plant, measured by value, are bought in Vietnam, with "all other inputs" imported "from or through China." The complaint also claims that a US-designated Chinese military company carried out construction work at the Vietnamese factory, challenging TP-Link's assurances about its supply chain's security. The complaint cites 2025 testimony [PDF] from former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce that TP-Link's share of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and small-office/home-office (SoHo) routers at at least 60 percent. Lawyers pointed to various snippets from TP-Link's marketing materials. These included claims that its HomeShield product "covers all security scenarios" and, on a version of its website available in November 2025, provides a "100 percent safeguard" for network security. The complaint argues that TP-Link's security assurances were misleading because its routers contained critical vulnerabilities. It further cites Joyce's that TP-Link routers were among the brands exploited in the China-linked Volt Typhoon and Flax Typhoon campaigns. The complaint also alleges that TP-Link's privacy policies permit it to collect customer data and share it with affiliates without disclosing how its Chinese connections and China's intelligence laws could expose that information to Chinese intelligence agencies. "Iowans' sensitive data and our national security is at risk because of TP-Link and their connection to the communist Chinese government," said Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird. "TP-Link tells Iowans its routers are safe, our personal data is secure, and that they have no ties to China. They are not telling the truth. It's time to hold China and China-backed companies accountable." "TP-Link's false statements and deceptive advertising are a violation of Montana law," said Attorney General Austin Knudsen. "As a result of their nefarious practices, millions of Americans have unknowingly invited a foreign adversary into their living rooms and put their personal information at risk. "I will do everything I can as Attorney General to hold TP-Link accountable and protect our privacy and security." Steve Kovsky, corporate affairs officer for TP-Link Systems Inc., said the lawsuits were based on false premises, did nothing to advance national security, and unfairly penalized a US company. Kovsky added that the company has spent months providing officials with clear documentation showing that it is not owned or controlled by any foreign government and that its devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam. "Any claims that our products present a threat to user security or grant unauthorized network access to foreign governments are baseless," he said. "TP-Link Systems is a US company that complies with US privacy and data protection laws. We perform comprehensive security testing and rely on trusted third-party security labs for additional scrutiny to ensure our products meet the highest security standards and are recognized as among the most secure on the market. "We meet or exceed all industry best practices for monitoring and preventing vulnerabilities and actively support our customers to mitigate any issues that occur as they are identified. We do not, and will not, share customer network data with foreign governments or unauthorized third parties. "We stand fully behind the security of our products, the integrity of our company and our people, and our commitment to serving the best interests of our customers in the United States and globally. We look forward to refuting these baseless allegations in court." The allegations echo those made by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose office sued TP-Link earlier this year over its Chinese connections and router security. US officials began weighing restrictions on TP-Link router sales in 2024. In March 2026, the FCC imposed broader restrictions [PDF] on new foreign-produced router models, barring new equipment authorizations unless an exemption is granted. Previously authorized models were not automatically banned. ®

events.title: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense | Heather Stewart
events.summary: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense The Tory leader’s proposal to slash the tax would shovel £6bn of taxpayer money to the already-wealthy Kemi Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit is a Conservative classic. After all, it was George Osborne’s high-profile pledge to “take the family home out of inheritance tax” in 2007 that put Gordon Brown off calling a snap general election. In practice, Osborne’s plan involved a £1m threshold for inheritance tax – and given the global financial crisis had blown a hole in the public finances by the time the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition came to power in 2010, it never came to pass. But the promise was grabby enough to change the political conversation – and contributed to Brown’s fateful decision not to go to the polls early. So politically, Badenoch’s flagship policy may have merit. IHT, as policymakers call it, is notoriously unpopular. Families never likely to be liable nevertheless fret about their kids having to paying it, while a cacophony of highly paid tax advisers offer to help them avoid it. The furious response to Rachel Reeves’s reform of the inheritance tax regime for family businesses and farms, with tractors streaming down Whitehall , underlined how unpopular it is. But whatever its political logic, the Tory plan makes little economic sense. First, it’s worth pausing to underline how very wealthy the beneficiaries of this new policy are likely to be. The latest data from HMRC shows that less than 5% of estates – the wealthiest 5%, that is – were liable for any inheritance tax at all in 2023/24. And under current rules, by combining their tax-free allowances, a married couple can already pass on a property worth up to £1m to their children or grandchildren, without them being liable to pay a penny in inheritance tax. Badenoch’s new, much more generous regime would permit a couple to pass on the entire family home, however valuable, without paying any tax on it at all; and for good measure an additional £1m in other assets. And the more valuable the property, the bigger the gain. Clearly, in a sluggish economy where resources are stretched, there’s a question about whether that is the best use of the £6bn of taxpayers’ money the policy is reckoned to cost – compared with, say, investing in infrastructure where there might be the prospect of a return. Total revenue from IHT is forecast to be about £9bn this year, rising to £15bn by 2030-31 – Badenoch’s plan would wipe out about half of that. Worse than that though, it will create perverse incentives for older homeowners to do exactly what the economy needs them not to do, and hang on in a valuable property, for fear the proceeds of downsizing would be grabbed by HMRC . Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The Tories claim they’ll also abolish stamp duty, helping to oil the wheels of the property market and encourage downsizing; but for the most valuable homes, the benefits of not paying 40% inheritance tax above the current threshold would be likely to more than overwhelm the boon of a tax-free move. And that would be likely to mean far fewer family-size homes coming on to the market in the places up-and-coming buyers most need them to be available. As Arun Advani, of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at the University of Warwick, points out, the biggest beneficiaries would be in areas where housing is expensive. He says: “‘Where housing is expensive’ mostly means ‘where lots of people want to live’, usually because there are good jobs. Reducing housing sales here will make it harder for young working families trying to upsize. By staying put, they will in turn make it harder for school leavers and university/college graduates to move to the area for work. This is bad for growth,” he said. Indeed, he points out there would even be an incentive for those who can afford it to “upsize” – moving to a larger house, which would then effectively shelter the asset from inheritance tax. If Badenoch and her party want to shovel an additional £6bn of taxpayers’ money to the already-wealthy in the hope of winning back votes in the stockbroker belt, so be it – but she should not be able to claim the policy would be anything but bad for economic growth.

events.title: AI video startup Higgsfield launches tool to build custom AI influencers
events.summary: There’s a new kind of AI influencer flooding social media feeds — and they’re not even pretending to look like real people. Higgsfield — which recently announced it hit a $1 billion run rate , and which boasts 30 million users — has updated its AI influencer tool, making it easier for users to insert a character of their own creation into existing videos. The characters are peculiar: They look realistic, but not quite of this world. Many have geometric haircuts, elongated necks, or other extreme bodily proportions that make clear they’re artificial. That’s by design. “A flawless face is the fastest way for a character to read as generic AI,” a Higgsfield spokesperson told Semafor. This odd aesthetic plays to AI’s strengths: Creating uncanny characters is a better use of the technology than trying to pass as human. It’s a more transparent way to create content that doesn’t deceive the audience the way deepfakes can. Some of these AI-generated influencers have racked up millions of views and thousands of followers across platforms (some users are already using them to promote memecoins). — Jake Angelo

events.title: Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash Owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its investors for £550m after sewage spills South West Water owner taps investors after sewage spills W ater is “a service where the shareholders never lose and the public never win,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told the Labour party conference last week , reflecting the popular feeling towards the industry in England. And, of course, his big-picture point is familiar: the £80bn, or thereabouts, that has been paid in dividends over the past 35 years represented over-the-top rewards for investors in many cases. It is easy to agree the public was taken for a ride. But the idea that shareholders never lose is not correct – and has been out of date for a while. For starters, the current owners of Thames Water have been wiped out. Their shares are worthless whatever the outcome of the interminable talks over whether to put the company into administration or opt for a recapitalisation by the creditors (who will get a sharp haircut on their debt in all circumstances). Meanwhile, the owners of Southern Water have been obliged to shove in cash on dilutive terms. Now comes something similar at Pennon Group. The owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its shareholders for £550m via a rights issue to fund, in effect, the cost of clearing up past failures. The new-ish Pennon chief executive, Keith Haslett, outlined an extra £1bn of capital investment on top of the existing £2.6bn in the current five-year period. Of the new £1bn, only £400m represents spending on new infrastructure that can be charged to bills (an extra £10 a year for South West customers if Ofwat gives a thumbs up). The other £600m hits shareholders directly and is the catch-up cost of fixing things that should not have gone wrong in the first place. Reading between the lines, Haslett seems shocked by what he found. The rights issue document talked about sustained improvement requiring “a fundamental change in how we plan, deliver and maintain our assets” and how previous efforts have been “held back by the way accountability sits within the organisation and gaps in the capability”. Mr Fixit is not saying it’s an overnight job. All the biggies of water companies’ performance – pollution, leaks and supply interruptions – got a mention as items in need of improvement. The plan is merely to reduce regulatory penalties by 50% in the current period. Haslett’s hope is that, come 2030, Pennon will be closer to earning a few rewards via Ofwat’s incentive mechanism. The point is that none of this will feel like a case of “shareholders never losing” if you’re unfortunate enough to own Pennon’s shares. Anybody who bought at virtually any point in the past five years has lost a packet. The price was £13.30 in July 2021. Now it is 361p, down 20% on Wednesday with the rights issue to a 22-year low. For good measure, the dividend is being cut by 30% on a per-share basis to reflect the new equity issuance. Reality has arrived at Pennon. Burnham might reflect that private investors can have their uses: the capital has to come from somewhere and shareholders can sometimes be forced to swallow some financial medicine. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning One could take the view that those investors deserve something even sourer, such as outright nationalisation. It’s a point of view but, since Burnham has pretty much ruled it out for water as a blanket policy (we wait to see what happens at Thames), the argument feels academic at this point. If Burnham, despite it all, is going to live with a privatised system, he could do everybody a favour at this point by hurrying up and deciding what he means by his “public control” overlay. Keir Starmer’s water bill, based on Sir Jon Cunliffe’s 2025 review of the water sector and including a stronger regulator, would have been published about now. Instead, we’ll get Burnham’s “strengthened” version some time next spring, according to the Westminster whisper. Given that it could take 12 months to become law, that will be four years for the Labour government to reform the water sector. That is shockingly slow. As Pennon’s fundraising demonstrates, even the current rickety system is moving faster.

events.title: Changing Your Career Isn’t Easy
events.summary: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum ’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written i n partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! When I changed careers at 30 to become a software engineer, I expected it to be hard. I expected to struggle to fit in, and I expected to bomb a lot of interviews (I did). What I didn’t expect was how few people would support me. As a parent, I get it now. A career change is a risk, and the people who care about you tend to project their fears onto you. They don’t want to watch you struggle or fail, so they discourage you or just don’t offer much enthusiasm. Right now is a strange time to be in engineering, or knowledge work in general. Plenty of us are excited about what AI means for our jobs. More of us are nervous, and I think that fear is justified. Employment for entry-level software developers has fallen nearly 20 percent since late 2022, according to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index , and it can feel like the knowledge we spent our careers building is being commoditized. Lately I’ve seen a flood of social media content telling software developers to go into the trades. YouTubers are telling you to become a plumber or a goat herder. But before you do that, I want to warn you, there is no EASY path. Even if you want to become a goat herder. I’ve changed careers once so far, but my business has forced me through several pivots that felt a lot like career changes—new audiences, new skills, new identity. Here’s what I’d tell anyone considering a change, whether you’re moving into engineering, leaving it, or finding a new speciality. Find someone who’s done it and ask how This is exactly what I told my oldest son, who’s getting ready to enter the job market full-time. Outside of the primary social media feeds, the internet is full of free and paid communities on Facebook, LinkedIn, and other sites. Reddit works, too, if you can stomach the trolls, because there’s valuable information buried in there. Many of these spaces are flooded with people trying to break in, so look for the ones full of people who already do the work and talk openly about what is and isn’t going well. Then find one or two people in your own circle who’ve done it and ask what the job takes. You’ll often find the degree matters less than you assumed. Indeed Hiring Lab found the share of U.S. postings requiring a bachelor’s degree fell from 20.4 percent in 2019 to 17.8 percent in early 2024, and more than half listed no education requirement at all. Build proof of work, even if it’s unpaid Yes, you’ll probably need to do some work for free, or at least far cheaper than you’re used to. I’ve had to do this in my business over and over. Nobody cares that I’ve been a software engineer for 12 years. They want to know whether I can do the thing they need. When I started pitching businesses, I offered to build something for free as a case study, then used it to land clients who paid well. You can copy this in most fields. Say you want to get into marketing: Learn how Facebook ads work, find a friend or small business that needs help, and run the campaigns at a low price. Now you’ve picked up the jargon, and you have something concrete to show a hiring manager. Stability is a myth It may be corny, but change is the only constant. If you’re a software engineer, you could argue you’re in the middle of a career change already, whether you opted in or not. Programmers in the 1990s had the same experience when the web showed up and they had to quickly learn new tools just to stay relevant. If you’re looking for stability, you’re in the wrong place, and I think it will get scarcer as AI and other forces reshape work. The best move is to build a strong foundation so you can adapt when the ground shifts. I wrote about the foundational skills to focus on if you’re interested. —Brian Barbara Mazzolai Wants to Build a New Field of Robotics Roboticist Barbara Mazzolai is a prime example of someone who advanced her career by switching fields—and now, she’s helping to create a new one. Learn how her background in biology led her to co-author a manifesto on “sustainability robotics.” Read more here . Turning Tech Talent Into Leadership Legacy The transition from a technical role to a leadership position can be challenging. To help seasoned professionals navigate the shift, IEEE is hosting its first International Leadership Conference in Budapest. Read more here . IEEE Celebrates Innovators Shaping the Future Every year, IEEE recognizes engineers whose technical achievements and leadership have made a lasting impact with its Technical Field Awards. See who’s on the 2027 list of awardees, which was announced in late September. Read more here .

events.title: The West’s open-source AI race kicks into high gear
events.summary: J.D.’s view The race in the West to become the top open-source AI model shifted into higher gear this week, as both Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French lab Mistral unveiled new models they hope will break China’s open-source monopoly. The challenge looming over Beam and Le Chonk ’s debuts (immediately my new favorite model name) is that they lag the top Chinese models and the leading closed systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on prominent benchmarks. But Reflection and Mistral boasted in their announcements that they do beat other open Western models, such as those from Thinking Machines and Nvidia, suggesting the companies care just as much about the race against each other as the one with Beijing — despite US and European companies’ shifts to using more Chinese models over the past year. Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told me his goal isn’t necessarily to dismantle the foothold Chinese models have achieved among developers and large companies. Instead, he sees a market in entities that can’t or won’t use Chinese models — think heavily regulated industries and governments — and might otherwise have no choice but to pay for closed American AI. The timing of that pitch is opportune: Many businesses are heading into year-end budget reviews with eye-popping AI spend figures to account for. Governments are also bracing for sticker shock as $1-a-year pilot deals expire. New data from Ramp suggests companies are switching which AI providers they use more than ever. The question that will determine the fate of these and other Western open-source players is whether businesses and agencies will tolerate less advanced models for some tasks in exchange for affordability and control. Notable Businesses are finding it hard to budget for AI because the number of tokens a task will consume is hard to predict, The Wall Street Journal reported.

events.title: Beware rightwing economic myths such as ‘maxing out the nation’s credit card’ | Letters
events.summary: Beware rightwing economic myths such as ‘maxing out the nation’s credit card’ Readers respond to an article in which Larry Elliott argues that Andy Burnham must challenge neoliberal nostrums Larry Elliott’s column on the rightwing economic myths constraining Andy Burnham’s government should be required reading before John Healey’s budget ( Rightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes, 1 October ). I spent 20 years trading bonds, and agree that the household budget analogy bears no relation to how the UK state finances itself. Parliament votes on the spending, the Treasury instructs the Bank of England , and the Bank credits accounts in the private sector. Taxes withdraw money afterwards. The same accounting exposes the “black hole”: every pound of government borrowing ends up as a financial asset held by households, firms and pension funds. That money hasn’t disappeared into any hole, black or otherwise. The triple lock is debated as a question of whether Britain can afford its pensions, yet a government that issues sterling cannot run out of sterling to pay them. John Maynard Keynes and Clement Attlee understood this, and so did an unlikely ally. Asked in 2005 whether US pay-as-you-go pensions were secure, Alan Greenspan, then chair of the Federal Reserve, told Congress that there was “nothing to prevent the federal government from creating as much money as it wants and paying it to somebody”. The same is true of sterling. The real question, he added, was whether the economy creates the real assets those pensions are used to buy. Deciding how to provide the care workers, homes and medicines is a political and moral question of the kind democracies exist to settle. Elliott warns that Burnham risks becoming the prime minister who asked the right questions without finding the answers. Ending Treasury-Induced Decline, a report that I co-wrote, sets out the institutional reforms he needs. He could start by dropping the wrong question: “How will we pay for it?” Vince Gomez The 99% Organisation Larry Elliott is right: Burnham’s government needs to challenge neoliberal ideas, “the nostrums of the past four decades”, like the one about the government being like a household, if it is to repair the damage done to our social services by the Tories. There are others which Elliott didn’t mention. The Laffer curve cannot be accepted by a government when chronically underfunded public services are crumbling, and the richest 1% in the UK own 36.5% of all financial assets, with a value of £1.8tn. We must reject arguments against equalising capital gains and income tax and imposing wealth taxes – and of course increasing income tax when fiscal rules allow – which use this old and long-disproved Tory economic myth. The same applies to the silly notion of trickle-down economics when tackling the excessive profits of banks and companies cashing in on the effects of war. That leads to the Bank of England’s inevitable blaming of wage increases for inflation, ignoring the relatively recent research in the US showing that that most price inflation comes from “ companies seeking to maintain profit margins ”. Bernie Evans Liverpool Grateful thanks to Larry Elliott for demolishing the conditioned belief that we must not “max out the nation’s credit card”. Producing and spending is fundamentally important to the ultimate revival of the UK economy and the restoration of industrialisation. My late husband always insisted that we could afford what we needed to and I didn’t believe him. I do now. Val Bynner London Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

events.title: ‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already left
events.summary: TaxWatch contradicts claims about David Reuben’s departure and questions stories of super-rich exodus Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground When the Sunday Times broke the news that David Reuben, one of the richest men in the UK, had apparently fled to the tax haven of Monaco, there was much pearl clutching. Reuben had moved from his Holland Park house in London to live full-time in the principality. Labour’s tax regime was blamed and there were said to be fears there would be a cascading effect across the economy, with wealth draining from the UK. It was reported that he had probably left because of potential taxes on wealth in the upcoming budget. However, research by T axWatch has found that Reuben, 88, has been a tax resident in Monaco since at least 2014. A spokesperson for the Newcastle United shareholder, who with his brother Simon, 85, shares a combined estimated wealth of almost £28bn, confirmed this was the case. Simon Reuben has lived in Monaco for 40 years since moving on health grounds while having cancer. The principality is a popular place for those who do not wish to pay UK taxes as it does not impose income tax, capital gains tax or inheritance tax. In July 2019, when David became a director of the Reuben foundation, the paperwork filed at the UK company registry stated he was “usually resident” in Monaco. In 2024 he provided a signed declaration to a Los Angeles court stating: “I reside in Monaco. I have resided there for approximately 10 years.” It was reported that the Reuben brothers were “non-doms” , which allowed them to pay UK tax only on income generated in the UK. The then chancellor Rachel Reeves axed this system in April last year, prompting a reported exodus of foreign super-rich individuals. Asked whether Reuben would have been caught by changes to these rules if he had not decided to move out of his UK residence, a spokesperson said: “That’s an entirely hypothetical question to which it would be impossible to give an answer.” Mike Lewis, the director of TaxWatch, told the Guardian: “When we started looking into this, we were surprised that publicly available documents completely contradicted a major news story. Sadly, these kinds of stories dominate the UK’s public and political conversation about our tax system. “The autumn budget may see some of the biggest changes in years to how gains from wealth are taxed. Perhaps it’s time that our politicians, and our media, debate these changes based on public facts and verifiable numbers – not anecdotes and anonymous reports from billionaires and their spokespeople.” The Labour MP Clive Lewis, who campaigns for a wealth tax, said: “If you want to live in this country, being British, having access to the culture of London, people want that, and there are lots of billionaires and millionaires who do stay because of that. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters “It’s instructive that there is a grouping of commentators who put on the scare tactics to say the wealthy are leaving this country. We can see that many of these billionaires don’t reside here anyway, many of them do stay here, and those who want to go, we can’t stop them anyway. This has always been the case.” Some of the super-rich are leaving . Analysis of Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index has found that super-rich UK residents worth a combined £121bn have either left or loosened ties with the UK since the Labour government came to power in 2024. This represents more than half of all billionaire wealth. Among those who have left are the steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, the Aston Villa co-owner Nassef Sawiris and the shipping magnate John Fredriksen. Inheritance tax changes in Reeves’s budget were also blamed for pushing the wealthy out, and it is thought capital gains tax may be increased this autumn. The Reuben brothers were born in Mumbai, moved to London in their teens, and went to a state school in Islington, leaving education aged 17 with no A-levels. They started businesses in metal trading and carpet importing. Since then, they have built a property empire. They own prestigious locations including Mayfair’s chandelier-festooned Burlington Arcade, Admiralty Arch, which is being developed into a five-star hotel, and Millbank Tower in Westminster.

events.title: UAE seeks to boost Gulf industrial integration and supply chain resilience
events.summary: The UAE is seeking to boost industrial integration with Gulf states, as the region explores ways to strengthen supply chain resilience at high-level meetings in Bahrain. A UAE delegation led by Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology, is participating at the GCC Industrial Co-operation Committee and the Ministerial Committee for Standardisation Affairs meeting being held in Bahrain. The UAE’s participation focuses on “strengthening industrial integration among GCC countries, building more resilient and competitive Gulf supply chains, accelerating the deployment of advanced technology and artificial intelligence in the industrial sector, and enhancing the role of the private sector in building partnerships and joint industrial opportunities”, the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology said in a statement on Wednesday. The meetings, which began Tuesday and will continue until Thursday, highlighted the need for co-ordination in standards. Dr Al Jaber emphasised the importance of advancing joint efforts to develop a more advanced industrial sector that supports the diversification of national economies and strengthens the GCC's position as a global hub for industry and innovation. “Industrial integration is a cornerstone of Gulf competitiveness,” he added. The meetings took place on the sidelines of the inaugural Made in GCC Forum and Exhibition 2026 being held in Manama. The event is aimed at boosting collaboration and partnerships across investment, manufacturing, supply chains and technology. Key outcomes of the meetings include the launch of the Gulf Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution and its digital platform aimed at enhancing the digital maturity of factories and supporting industrial transformation, the GCC Council said in a statement. The evaluation period for the amended rules on exempting industrial inputs from customs duties was extended until the end of 2027. UAE manufacturing push The UAE’s participation comes amid a strong push towards domestic manufacturing in the country. The industrial sector plays a key role in the national economy, with its contribution having reached Dh200 billion ($54.45 billion) – an increase of 70 per cent. Its industrial exports reached Dh260 billion last year, including Dh92 billion in medium-and high-technology industrial exports. The Emirates also launched its industrial strategy, Operation 300bn , in 2021, to position itself as a global industrial hub by 2031. The UAE’s overarching agenda is focused on priority industries including chemicals, electrical, construction, machinery and equipment, food, transport, metals, pharmaceuticals, rubber, plastic and fibreglass, and wood and paper. The Emirates has in recent years also invested heavily in advance technology and AI, with multibillion-dollar projects being built. In May, the UAE launched the Dh1 billion National Industrial Resilience Fund to support the industrial sector and announced a national strategy to secure supply chains and boost local food, medicine and industrial production. Meanwhile, the country's National In-Country Value (ICV) programme has redirected more than Dh473 billion into the national economy. The UAE is pushing for deeper industrial co-operation across the Gulf as countries seek to localise supply chains and reduce their reliance on imports following disruption exposed by the Covid-19 pandemic and other global shocks, Dr Farah Al Zarouni, assistant undersecretary for the Standardisation Affairs sector at the ministry, told The National . “We need to benefit from all the resources available across the GCC countries,” she said. The Made in GCC event is expected to involve the signing of a number of initial pacts between UAE entities and Gulf companies, the ministry said. The UAE is participating with 23 Emirati companies spanning sectors including basic industries, pharmaceuticals, defence and spare parts. “We no longer look at industry as simply traditional manufacturing. We are moving our national industry towards more advanced manufacturing,” Ms Al Zarouni said. “Technology is a very important and fundamental component of our national industrial sector.” The experience of the six years since the pandemic has highlighted the vulnerability created when countries depend heavily on overseas suppliers for relatively small components for manufacturing. “If I had been able to source that small component locally, the component that enabled me to produce the final product, I would not have been affected to the same extent,” she said. The priority now should be to identify which raw materials and components can be produced within the UAE or elsewhere in the GCC, she said. “Supply chains are long, so you need to benefit from all the resources available across the GCC countries.”

events.title: The five takes that will define this midterm campaign
events.summary: David’s view Prick up your ears, and you can hear it — the sound of many different kinds of Democrats grabbing credit for midterm victories that aren’t official yet. There’s Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, assessing that when (not if) Abdul El-Sayed wins his Senate race in Michigan, the left will “break open the entire political calculus in America” — i.e., that progressives like them can win the Midwest. There’s Pete Buttigieg, making sure we know how many states he’s campaigned in (37) and how many candidates he’d endorsed (more than 100). At this time in any campaign cycle, groups, candidates, and strategists pepper reporters with early claims that they were right. The election, they say, will be a referendum on issue, a validation of spending strategy, proof that ideas moved votes. These takes aren’t immaculate. I’ve never deleted the October 2017 email from a strategist who was ready to explain why Ralph Northam lost the election for governor of Virginia. In fact, Northam won easily, and that strategist got strategically quiet. As preposterous as it is, though, the pre-spin cycle matters, because anyone not ready to contextualize what happened to their benefit will lose face. It mattered in 2020, when centrist Democrats burst out to blame “defund the police” activists for their party underperforming the final polls. It mattered after President Donald Trump’s win in 2024, when Sen. Bernie Sanders instantly blamed defeat on the party having “abandoned the working class.” That quick analysis shaped the conversation. Populism won. This is the Sanders project — progressives’ entire project, really. The goal of recruiting swing-seat populists and getting them through primaries was to prove, as Ocasio-Cortez said, that their kind can win anywhere, which should matter for 2028. This theory may be tough to sell. One of its proof points was supposed to be Maine, where Graham Platner humiliated the party establishment, then himself. Progressives won the insta-caucus that replaced him, nominating Troy Jackson to face GOP Sen. Susan Collins, and Sanders will campaign for Jackson this weekend after some internal grumbling about whether consultants not approved by the left were ruining his campaign. Michigan’s the ballgame now. An El-Sayed win would, for progressives, be the story of the midterms. Most of the movement’s primary victories came in safe seats, but to take control of the 2028 story, they want to be talking about El-Sayed winning, Will Lawrence flipping back a mid-Michigan district, and Randy Villegas unseating Rep. David Valadao in California. They want to say that hand-wringing moderates were wrong, and pure populism can flip or hold swing seats. But if El-Sayed becomes the first Democrat to lose a Michigan Senate seat this century, progressives will enter 2028 with empty hands. Gerrymandering didn’t matter . This will be the biggest conclusion if Republicans don’t hold the House. And they’re already conceding partial defeat. “We’re not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., told Axios this week. Indeed, Democrats are competing for most of the seats that Republicans tried to lift beyond their reach z– three in Texas, three in Florida, one in North Carolina, one in Ohio, one in Alabama, and as of this week, one in Tennessee. When Trump first urged Texas to eliminate five Democratic districts, the most ambitious response was that Democrats could moderate and compete for them anyway. That did happen. Four of the Democrats whose seats turned redder voted with Republicans on a recent transgender health proposal; a fifth, Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, is running the most critical ads about “transgender ideology” of any Democratic incumbent. While it might not decide who controls the House, gerrymandering did matter. It won’t have mattered enough if most of the remapped districts don’t flip. Anti-trans politics stopped working. This is a complicated topic to spin; both LGBTQ rights groups and more cautious Democratic strategists are trying to set themselves up for it. “I hope that the headline coming out of November 4 is that equality voters won and anti-trans ads lost,” Kelly Robinson, the president of the Human Rights Campaign, told reporters on Monday. Robinson wants that to be proven by victories for candidates who followed her group’s playbook, of responding to GOP attacks on a candidate’s gender voting record by answering them and pivoting. A small group of Democrats, like Kaptur, have used the language that activists find offensive; the HRC is ready to point to those defeats as evidence that using a conservative frame won’t win votes. [Insert 2028 Candidate] was the strongest surrogate. There’ll be fast post-midterm calculations of which Democrats and Republicans endorsed, and campaigned for, the most winners in congressional races. The model for taking a scorecard into a presidential primary comes from Richard Nixon, who refurbished his reputation by campaigning across the country for Republicans in 1966 and got some credit for a good GOP year. But every would-be president has approached this differently. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., has endorsed scores of candidates, some of them extreme longshots. He’s not going for a batting average; he’s trying to show people that his politics, and the attention he got by releasing the Epstein files, give him broad appeal. Buttigieg has gotten the word out that he can draw crowds in Republican districts, and that the candidates are happy to have him. So has Sen. Mark Kelly; he doesn’t have Buttigieg’s reach but he’s made it known that Democrats in the toughest seats are happy to campaign with the astronaut from a swing state. And isn’t it convenient that Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who leads the Democratic Governors Association, has to keep going back to Nevada? Every 2028 Democrat will get a scorecard, and there’s already some chatter about how few Democrats want to appear with Kamala Harris — the only potential candidate who several have said they won’t appear with. The Latino vibe shift is over. This argument is already being written: Texas Republicans, and maybe even Florida Republicans, misinterpreted the 2024 Latino vote as a permanent shift away from Democrats. Public and private polling has found the Latino vote slipping back to Democrats, who are recovering to where they were in 2018 and 2020, wrecking the GOP’s congressional map. The clear reason for this is Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy, which swept in people with no criminal records, but some Democrats are already warning the party not to celebrate too hard. “The vote is probably moving somewhere in the neighborhood of 15 to 20 points or more back to Democrats,” said Chuck Rocha, a strategist working for Latino Democrats in Texas. “[It’s] not because they’re in love with Democrats, but more they’re just so angry about the economic downturn with the overarching fear of ICE in their neighborhood.” There will be

events.title: IEA members support faster release of reserve oil stocks
events.summary: Members of the International Energy Agency (IEA) expressed support on Wednesday for accelerating the release of roughly 100 million barrels of reserve oil stocks previously agreed to in March. About 325 million barrels of oil have been released under the March agreement to ease oil markets after the onset of the Iran war led to a surge in energy prices. The IEA also said members had agreed to prioritise the release of diesel stocks. Member countries still hold roughly 1.1 billion barrels of emergency oil stocks, including more than 200 million barrels of diesel. “The IEA stands ready to release more of these stocks to the market if and when required,” executive director Fatih Birol said in a statement. “Participants in the meeting expressed strong appreciation for the IEA’s response to the energy impacts of the Strait of Hormuz crisis." Mr Birol said members also welcomed last week's statement by G7 leaders on global energy and security, and agreed to assess and review the situation at the IEA governing board meeting next week. G7 member countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves through the IEA, following pressure from US President Donald Trump's administration. Conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have triggered a global surge in fuel prices, adding to pressure on Mr Trump ahead of November's midterm elections. On Monday, he signed an executive order waiving restrictions on cheaper red-dyed diesel, which could ease price pressures for lorry drivers, who are facing higher costs at the pump that could be passed down to consumers. Diesel prices have risen to more than $6 per gallon in recent weeks, compared to the average price of $3.60 per gallon this time last year. The White House said the federal diesel tax is 24.4 cents per gallon, or about $60 on a 250-gallon fuel. Europe is also facing higher diesel prices, which hit a record of €2.24 per litre, compared to €1.59 before the Iran war began on February 28. The US is currently in the process of a 172-million-barrel drawdown from its strategic petroleum reserve. Once completed, the SPR is projected to fall to its lowest levels since 1982.

events.title: Starlink's plan to avoid orbital near-misses: Ephemeris sharing
events.summary: SpaceX has acknowledged the need for satellite operators to collaborate to avoid collisions and has taken the unusual step of sharing imagery showing how close spacecraft are coming to each other. The company has called on other operators to share their satellites' ephemeris (a set of parameters describing the position and velocity of a spacecraft over time) to facilitate timely avoidance maneuvers. "In 2026," the company wrote, "Starlink encountered conjunctions with about 650 unique maneuvering third-party satellites, with only about half of them actually sharing ephemeris. "Some operators don't share ephemeris out of a concern that sharing upcoming maneuvers gives away proprietary information. In other circumstances, operators are willing to share data, but are unable to receive permission from the government to do so. "Such policies are counterproductive, and largely only serve to create preventable collision risk between satellites." "Over six months," the company went on, "Starlink observed ~164,000 conjunctions where time of closest approach (TCA) was within four hours after an unannounced manoeuvre. "While not all of these conjunctions were high-risk, they represent cases where Starlink would not have sufficient information to reliably avoid the other vehicle if the other operator’s action created a high-risk conjunction. "In many cases, the lack of high-accuracy post-manoeuvre trajectory information can cause such conjunctions to go unnoticed, giving operators a false sense of confidence and not realising how much risk their actions are creating." How many sats is that again? It's all worthy stuff, until you consider that SpaceX has applied for permission to operate 100,000 Starlink satellites and up to 1 million Starmind AI satellites. Arguably that is a substantial contribution to orbital overcrowding. Not to worry though – space isn't really getting crowded, according to SpaceX. "A good analogy is air travel," the company wrote. "Airspace around the world has grown more congested since aviation began. Yet air travel is the safest form of transport on Earth in part because every aircraft publishes a flight plan and then continuously broadcasts its position during flight." Er, kind of. Although if aircraft collide, the debris falls rapidly to Earth, rather than lingering in the sky and potentially striking more aircraft weeks or months later. Plus, SpaceX is helpfully not counting other debris, from spent rocket casings to flakes of paint, that also pose a hazard in orbit. The company noted its successes, where Starlink satellites successfully dodged other vehicles. One in October 2025 occurred when the other satellite made an unexpected maneuver, reducing the predicted miss distance from 9 km to a bottom-clenching 57 meters. Another example happened in August 2026, when the risk was identified too late for the Starlink satellite to move out of the way, and the satellite had to "duck" instead, slewing to present a narrower profile. "The vehicles ultimately passed within 134 metres of each other," the company said. "This approach could have been prevented if the other object shared its manoeuvre ahead of time." SpaceX was keen for operators to connect to sites such as space-safety.com and talked up its Stargaze service, which uses star trackers on the Starlink fleet to observe nearby objects in orbit. A far cry from 2019, when a Starlink satellite failed to move out of the way of the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Aeolus Earth-observation satellite due to a bug in SpaceX's on-call paging system. There is no shortage of companies with capabilities to monitor and advise on traffic in orbit. Neuraspace, for example, springs to mind. As the company's CEO Chiara Manfletti observed, humanity has not done a particularly good job of looking after the space above the planet. While the technology used to prevent satellite collisions is impressive, and data sharing should be encouraged, we can't help but wonder whether another solution might be to not launch tens of thousands more satellites into orbit in the first place. Manfletti told The Register that the problem was very real. She said, "As the number of satellites increases, knowing where an object is today is no longer sufficient. Manoeuvrability is becoming essential, and operators increasingly need timely, accurate information about where other spacecraft intend to be, including planned manoeuvres." "Initiatives such as SpaceX's space-safety platform are certainly welcome. But the long-term solution cannot depend on every operator joining a single company's system. What we ultimately need is a federated and interoperable space-traffic ecosystem in which operators can securely exchange trusted trajectory and intent information across different platforms, organisations and national systems. "Neuraspace has reached out to SpaceX to enable such coordination on behalf of our customers. We have extended an open hand, and it would be a strong sign of leadership for SpaceX to take it — demonstrating that improving safety in orbit ultimately requires cooperation not only within individual platforms, but across them." ®

events.title: Is ‘abundance’ really dead?
events.summary: The News Whatever happened to “ abundance ,” the pro-growth movement that many Democrats were going to hitch a ride on this election cycle? They did embrace its ideas. They just don’t use the “a-word” that much. In ads and across swing districts, Democrats are running on having “built more affordable housing,” supported “all-of-the-above energy,” and sliced through “bureaucracy and red tape” without mentioning “abundance” at all. Back home, some are talking about the permitting reform bill they’re trying to push through Congress, and the housing bill they already did. “Resource development is about our survival,” former Rep. Mary Peltola says in one of her ads, highlighting how she defied climate activists to support Alaska’s Willow oil-drilling project.This year, after progressive activists accused the loose “abundance” movement, which favors targeted deregulation to spur growth, of trying to steer Democrats away from populism, groups working with local electeds forged ahead armed with polling showing how their ideas fit into the “affordability” framework that most candidate were running on. “That early criticism of ‘abundance’ being a flash in the pan was a bad faith argument from people worried about what a powerful argument it was,” said Derek Kaufman, the founder and CEO of Inclusive Abundance. “I look at New York, where I live, where you have Gov. [Kathy] Hochul Mayor [Zohran] Mamdani changing environmental reviews for urban infill; you have Mamdani doing his version of DOGE, which he called COGE.” In the Los Angeles mayoral race, Kaufman continued, “the more progressive-coded candidate is all about building housing to bring down costs.” Know More The criticism of the “abundance” concept got a wide airing in 2025. Last spring, after Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s “Abundance” hit the New York Times bestseller list, progressives attacked it as a dangerous off-ramp from populism — which could actually win elections.Skeptics commissioned their own polls to argue that “abundance” was a dead end. Last spring, Demand Progress tested a version of an anti-bureaucracy “abundance” message against a “populist” message that saw the latter winning out. Four months later, Groundwork Action released data that found “excessive bureaucracy,” while a concern for some voters, “ranks far behind other concerns and tackling it does not strike voters as a direct response to the problem of affordability.” To critics, the absence of the word “abundance” on the campaign trail is a sign of victory. Those sympathetic to the movement argue that’s not the case — and that there was never a binary choice at hand between progressive ideology and the ideas abundance advocates stand for. “I don’t use the word ‘abundance’ when I’m campaigning,” said Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., “but I say all the time that when people think that the system is rigged against them, they’re right. It is. And a lot of the reason is what we’ve layered into government, where really well-intended ideas have the opposite effect.” David’s view Democrats are feeling very good about next month’s elections, and the jockeying is already underway about which faction made it happen. Progressives hope to power a Democratic victory in the House that sees them pick up more seats — and influence — in the next Congress. When “abundance” critics went after the movement, they were trying to win the argument then as well as the argument of the future. They saw a coalition of techies and liberals who were trying to prevent what they wanted: A move to the left and away from deep-pocketed donors. They view “abundists” taking credit for Mamdani’s victory as opportunists trying to deny democratic socialists a major governing success. But the non-socialists have made a modicum of impact, even if “abundance” has faded from Democrats’ lexicon. Thompson got Mamdani to agree with some of the “abundance” principles, and both agreed that the left can’t credibly compete with the new right if people believe progressive governments are tied down by interest groups and can’t build. The argument continues. Room for Disagreement David Segal, whose group Demand Progress commissioned the first abundance-skeptical poll, argued that the abundance movement is all but dead. “Having a primary message that is populist and then having a couple of lines about zoning or permitting reform is ‘offering a sop to abundists,’” he said. “It’s not ‘running on abundance.’ And it’s totally fine to do that, but it’s just not what Abundance (™) was arguing for when they rolled out their project.” Notable In Politico, Riley Rogerson broke news of another “abundance”-pilled caucus in the House looking for a way to fund more big projects.

( Reuters. ) Asahi, Kirin, Sapporo and Suntory breweries have been raided in Japan. The four beer giants make up around 90 per cent of Japan's beer market share — and are popular brands in Australia too. Japan's Fair Trade Commission is investigating whether the beer brewers colluded to raise their prices over several years. Japanese authorities have raided four global beer manufacturers over suspicions they colluded to raise their prices. Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Sapporo Breweries and Suntory have confirmed the raids on Wednesday. Sales of Asahi's Super Dry variety in Australia have increased 40 per cent in Australia since 2020, according to the company. A spokesperson for Asahi in Australia said: "The investigation cited in media reports concerns Asahi Breweries in Japan and is entirely unrelated to Australian operations." The ABC has also contacted Kirin and Sapporo for a response about whether Australian production of the beer has been impacted. Japanese beer is suddenly everywhere Due to a combination of business and travel Japanese brewers have come to dominate our domestic beer market. Japan's public broadcaster NHK said the Fair Trade Commission was investigating whether the companies had formed a cartel and colluded to raise their prices at the same time over several years, together citing factors including rising raw material costs. The anti-trust watchdog is expected to continue its investigation and could file a criminal complaint if they were found to have breached the country's anti-monopoly laws. In statements, the four beer makers separately said they intended to cooperate with ⁠the investigation. Suntory said in a statement that it was "undergoing an on-site inspection by the Fair Trade Commission on suspicion of breaching the anti-monopoly act in relation to its alcohol trading activities". Asahi beer in Australia is manufactured locally. ( Reuters: Tim Wimborne, file ) Asahi beer in Australia is manufactured locally with the beer brewer telling the ABC earlier this year it employed almost 4,000 Australians across 17 manufacturing sites. Kirin Ichiban and Sapporo are also manufactured in Australia, with Japanese beer only representing about 4 per cent of beer imports into Australia. Japanese beverage manufacturer Kirin owns Lion, which produces many of Australia's most popular beers. ( Reuters: Issei Kato/File ) Ice cream giants alleged of cartel price fixing in Japan Six of Japan's biggest ice cream companies are under suspicion of forming a cartel to hike up prices. Earlier this year, in the midst of a heatwave, six major Japanese ice cream companies were similarly raided over suspicion of colluding to hike their prices. If the companies are found to have have violated anti-monopoly laws, the country's anti-trust watchdog will issue a fine and order the companies improve their business practices.
